The money can be used to hire sworn and non-sworn law enforcement personnel and other public safety workers, purchase technology and equipment, expand forensic capabilities and fund programs addressing mental health, substance abuse and recidivism.

Jacksonville's selection comes after a sharp drop in killings. The city recorded 59 murders in 2024, its lowest total since at least 1995 and less than half the number recorded a year earlier, according to the Jacksonville Sheriff's Office. DOJ said murders fell 38% between 2023 and 2025, while robberies declined 25% and aggravated assaults fell 21%.

DOJ pointed to Jacksonville's use of advanced training and technology and efforts to strengthen investigative capabilities in selecting the city. The Jacksonville Sheriff's Office, which has more than 3,600 police, corrections and civilian employees, has an annual budget of roughly $674 million.

FIRST ON FOX: DHS POINTS TO ‘COMMON SENSE’ REASON FOR COLLAPSING CRIME: ‘NO SURPRISE’

St. Louis' selection is particularly notable given the city's long struggle with violent crime. The city recorded 263 homicides in 2020, but that figure fell to 150 in 2024, its lowest total since 2013, as overall crime declined 15% year over year.

The decline continued into 2025, when homicides during the first three months of the year fell another 45% compared with the same period a year earlier.

Chicago police officers patrol downtown on Aug. 26, 2025, in Chicago. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

DOJ said St. Louis' proposal calls for expanding law enforcement personnel by more than 300, modernizing policing technology and strengthening public safety operations.

Baton Rouge is confronting a different challenge: manpower. The Baton Rouge Police Department was roughly 150 officers short earlier this year, prompting officials to approve what they described as the largest police pay raise in department history. Starting salaries increased from $40,000 to $58,000 as part of an effort to recruit and retain officers.

The department also operates a Real Time Crime Center that uses data analytics and other technology to support officers and investigators.

DOJ said East Baton Rouge Parish stood out for its partnerships among law enforcement, local government and community organizations and its broader approach to combating violent crime.

Jackson, Mississippi, meanwhile, was selected for what DOJ described as an ambitious, technology-driven strategy to address persistent violent crime.

The Jackson Police Department already operates a Real Time Command Center and specialized units focused on gun crime, vice and narcotics and other investigations, while assigning officers to outside task forces. Its proposal calls for greater coordination among law enforcement agencies, expanded investigative capabilities and targeted enforcement, according to DOJ.

"President Trump and this Department of Justice have demonstrated that Americans need not accept unsafe streets as a fact of life," Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. said. "We have made tremendous strides in restoring public safety, and the Model Cities Initiative offers an opportunity to build on that progress. These cities have the potential to set a new standard for safer communities across America."

A Florida man was arrested and picked up several charges when he ditched a "Wizzinator" device in the back of a patrol car. (Antonio Diaz)

The four winning jurisdictions will now work with DOJ to finalize and implement their public safety plans.

Blanche and other Justice Department officials will travel to all four jurisdictions over the next 10 days to present the awards in person and reveal how the nearly $300 million will be divided among them.

title: Police in Scotland launch Andrew and Epstein royal castle investigation
excerpt: Police in Scotland have opened an investigation into the time the former Prince Andrew spent with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, at the king’s Balmoral est...
body_text:
Police in Scotland have opened an investigation into the time the former Prince Andrew spent with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, at the king’s Balmoral estate.

Police Scotland, which provides law enforcement throughout the country, said on Friday that the inquiries began after it received “information” and that the investigation was at a “very early stage″.

The force provided no further detail about what the information was or what offences officers were investigating.

The investigation was first reported by The Daily Express, which said the inquiries were related to claims that women were trafficked to the king’s private estate in the Scottish Highlands.

“All inquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries,″ Police Scotland said in a statement. “We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further.”

Images released by the United States Department of Justice appeared to show Epstein and Maxwell on a shooting trip at Balmoral in 1999. The photos were among millions of pages of documents the department published earlier this year as Congress probed Epstein’s links to politicians, business leaders and other influential people in the US and around the world.

The presence of anyone’s name or image in the files is not proof of wrongdoing.

Several other UK police forces, including London’s Metropolitan Police Service, Thames Valley Police and Surrey Police, are also investigating information released in the Epstein Files.

In February, Thames Valley officers arrested the former prince, now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, on suspicion of misconduct in public office, based on information uncovered in the trove of documents released by US authorities.

The 66-year-old younger brother of King Charles III was held for several hours before being released on police bail pending further investigation.

It was the first time in nearly four centuries that a senior British royal had been arrested.

The former prince has repeatedly denied committing any crimes.

Mountbatten-Windsor’s links to Epstein have caused headaches for Britain’s royal family for almost two decades.

With US authorities preparing to release documents related to their long-running investigation into Epstein, the king late last year moved to shield the monarchy from the scandal by stripping his brother of his princely title.

Mountbatten-Windsor was also ordered to move out of the Royal Lodge, his longtime home in parkland near Windsor Castle. He now lives in a house at Sandringham, the king’s privately owned estate in eastern England.

The former prince’s reputation has been tarnished by his relationship with Epstein ever since 2008, when the wealthy American financier pleaded guilty to soliciting a minor for prostitution. In 2011, the late Virginia Giuffre alleged that she had been trafficked by Epstein and forced to have sex with Mountbatten-Windsor when she was 17.

Mountbatten-Windsor tried to silence the scandal by giving a lengthy interview to the BBC in 2019, but the strategy backfired when he was criticised for offering unbelievable explanations of his behaviour and failing to show empathy for Epstein’s victims.

title: Ceasefire allows evacuation from devastated Russian-occupied Oleshky
excerpt:
Watch: How will the evacuation of Oleshky unfold?

Hundreds of residents of the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have been evacuated, Russian and Ukrainian authorities have said, following ...
body_text:
Watch: How will the evacuation of Oleshky unfold?

Hundreds of residents of the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have been evacuated, Russian and Ukrainian authorities have said, following a humanitarian ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.

"Everything unfolded without any incidents, and both sides noted the high level of organisation," Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova said.

Ukrainian authorities confirmed the evacuees were on their way to southern Russia, from where they will travel on to Ukraine through Belarus.

Melania Trump said that "all elements of the convoy, including the safe passageway in and out of Oleshky, was established through mutual agreement between Russian and Ukrainian leaders".

A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.

Residents who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so on Friday. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.

Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.

"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning.

"At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."

Ukrainian territory lies 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa.

They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.

Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.

Oleshky residents had a four-hour window to board buses to be evacuated to either Russia or Ukraine

Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.

Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine. He will also become the first to visit Russia when he escorts the evacuees back into Ukraine on Saturday.

The Oleshky ceasefire has required close cooperation with Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.

But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.

Residents travelled from Oleshky in convoy to Armyansk in Russian-occupied Crimea

Both Lubinets and Lantratova posted videos from Oleshky on their social media channels, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine.

In one video, Lubinets can be seen meeting tearful locals. "The problem is that a lot of people are staying," he can be heard saying. "I was told that it was their own choice, we will do everything possible for the humanitarian aid to arrive."

Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.

An Oleshky resident told the BBC she had decided against leaving because "they wouldn't take my animals, so that's it."

Olena, who now lives in Kyiv, said her grandmother and wider family in Oleshky were also staying behind.

"The older generation does not want to leave," she told the BBC. "I've barely managed to persuade my father - and only because I've just had a baby, who he would never see otherwise."

Olena's grandmother's sister died in Oleshky last winter.

"She lost her legs after stepping on a landmine, covered in snow... People took her to the hospital in a garden wheelbarrow," Olena said.

"That's how locals transport all wounded and dead people in Oleshky to the hospital and the hospital's morgue: in garden wheelbarrows."

Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova spoke to journalists before arriving in Oleshky

The ceasefire is due to be in force until the end of Sunday 1 November. It has provided the first few days of peace in the Kherson region since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Residents of Kherson told the BBC they were "overjoyed" by the ceasefire. However, they are concerned the truce has given Russia time to build up its military presence on the banks of the Dnipro river, which could result in a renewed assault once the ceasefire expires.

On Friday, the Kremlin made it clear that the success of the Oleshky ceasefire should not be interpreted as willingness to extend the truce to the rest of Ukraine.

A handful of foreign journalists have been invited to witness the evacuation of the town, which Moscow is expected to present as a humanitarian mission conducted with mercy to protect the people of Oleshky.

Many Ukrainians suspect Russia's real intention is to earn credit with the White House, and to provide US President Donald Trump with a boost ahead of next week's midterm elections.

'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next

Truce begins in Ukraine city where residents ate weeds to survive

title: Arsenal boss Arteta fires ‘Disneyland’ warning at Dowman after red card
excerpt:
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta warned Max Dowman he was “not in Disneyland” after the teenage rising star was sent off in the Gunners’ shock League Cup defeat by lowly Fleetwood.

The Premier League cha...
body_text:
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta warned Max Dowman he was “not in Disneyland” after the teenage rising star was sent off in the Gunners’ shock League Cup defeat by lowly Fleetwood.

The Premier League champions suffered one of the most embarrassing losses in their history when, after the fourth-round tie ended 1-1 in normal time, they lost 5-3 on penalties away to fourth-tier Fleetwood on Tuesday.

To make matters worse for the Gunners, Dowman saw red five minutes before the end of normal time.

Although it looked a harsh decision to send off Dowman for aiming a kick towards Harrison Neal, Arteta was unimpressed with the 16-year-old, giving him a stern word as the midfielder trudged off.

Arteta’s reaction on the touchline was criticised by some pundits, who felt he should have been more sympathetic towards Dowman, who is now starting an immediate three-game ban for violent conduct after Arsenal lost an appeal against his red card and punishment.

But an unrepentant Arteta defended his response to Dowman’s red card in a pre-match press conference on Friday ahead of Arsenal’s trip to Liverpool.

“I understand. But you need to understand the context, the relationship that I have with him and what we discussed just before we went out (for the match).

“You want to see the reaction of his team-mates? When they have to play with 10, you want to see that? What do you expect? I don’t know… This is the environment and this is the reality.

“Otherwise, we are in Disneyland. We are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League.”

Dowman has been carefully nurtured by Arsenal since making his debut when he was just 15.

“We look after him so much but at the same time we’re going to be demanding because he needs to earn the right to play, just like everybody else,” said Arteta, whose side are level on points with Premier League leaders Manchester City

“It is not the first time. It happened another time this month with England (Under-19s). And it will continue to happen because of the way he plays and the way he attracts opponents and that’s it.

“We have to be able to tell each other what we think because he is 16 and we have to be very protective of him, but at the same time very straight with him about what we expect of him towards the team, individuals and the club.”

Arteta, himself a former Arsenal midfielder, insisted he had “no issues” with Dowman as the Spanish boss lamented the failure of the Gunners’ appeal.

“I’m very disappointed to be fair, especially with the reckless tackles that he received, and then his reaction is minimal in relation to the action,” he said.

title: Business secretary says UK needs to understand direction of EU before signing up to closer relationship – as it happened
excerpt:
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has suggested the UK needs to know more about where the EU is heading before it signs up to a much closer relationship.

He made the comment in an interview ...
body_text:
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has suggested the UK needs to know more about where the EU is heading before it signs up to a much closer relationship.

He made the comment in an interview with the Sun, a day after John Healey, the chancellor, also hinted that he might have reservations about Andy Burnham’s ambitions for a new relationship with the EU undoing the damage done by Brexit.

Burnham is attending a summit with the EU next month where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus. There is strong support for all these initiatives in cabinet.

But Burnham also wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election, when – if it wants – Labour will be able to dump the 2024 manifesto pledges ruling out joining the single market or the customs union.

Burnham has not said what he wants to propose in Labour’s next manifesto, and he insists ultimately the public will decide, but he has said that he would like the UK to rejoin the EU in his lifetime and he seems open to trying to rejoin the single market in the next parliament.

Asked by the Sun if he shared Burnham’s dream of rejoining the EU, Reynolds replied:

double quotation markI genuinely can’t answer that, because I don’t know what the future of the EU is – because [of] some of the very strong political currents in member states.

For me, it’s an approach to issues. What is their approach to how they regulate technology, AI? How dynamic will the economy be?

Sophia Sleigh, who wrote up the comments, said Reynolds was referring to the rise of far-right populist parties in Europe, which could fundamentally change and weaken the EU.

Although Reynolds’ comments were prompted by a question about rejoining the EU, his concerns would also apply to a proposal to join the single market.

Healey is also distinctly less pro-European than Burnham. In interviews yesterday, he did not accept that joining the single market would automatically be good for growth, he stressed the importance of accepting the referendum decision and making the best of the current relationship, and said he did not expect the UK to rejoin the EU in his lifetime.

In a bid to stop ministers disagreeing in public about the EU, Burnham sent them a letter earlier this week telling them to stay “disciplined” and not to “advocate for specific options” as the debate on the future UK-EU relationship gets under way.

Andy Burnham has admitted his first budget as prime minister was not as radical as he would have liked because of the economic uncertainty facing the country.

The Unison leader Andrea Egan has called for the same political focus to be given to NHS, education and care sector workers as there has been on those employed in North Sea oil and gas.

Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, has claimed that Andy Burnham has now accepted in principle the case for the Welsh government to get greater borrowing powers. (See 3.59pm.) He was speaking after they met at the national economic council meeting in Glasgow.

Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has suggested the UK needs to know more about where the EU is heading before it signs up to a much closer relationship. (See 1.28pm.)

For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.

Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, has released his readout from his meeting with Andy Burnham. Breaking with convention (these readouts are normally rather bland), he has included some news in his.

Ap Iorwerth claims Burnham has now accepted that Wales should greater borrowing powers. Under the current rules, the Welsh government’s borrowing powers are extremely limited. “This has led to the bizarre situation where it has been forced to rely on local authorities to do its borrowing for it (such as a school-building programme),” Will Hayward said in a recent Guardian column. Ap Iorwerth said:

double quotation markThere was an encouraging consensus that the fiscal and borrowing powers which have for so long put Wales at a disadvantage compared with other UK nations must be revised as a matter of urgency. I welcome the prime minister’s comments that this is now a matter of how and when.

He said he told Burnham that “further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd” – which sounded like a rather blunt ‘stay in your lane” response to Burnham’s “regional empowerment” proposals.

Ap Iorwerth said he was pleased Burnham had agreed to look at what has happened to the proposed £14bn transport boost for Wales. This was a promise made by Keir Starmer ahead of the May elections, but the Welsh government says the proposal has in effect been shelved.

Ap Iorwerth said he asked Burnham to lean on the Treasury “to enable the Welsh government to press ahead with our Cynnal weekly child payment pilot to support the poorest families”.

Ap Iorwerth urged him to back rejoining the EU single market and customs union “as a priority”.

The Downing Street readout did not mention any of these issues. It just repeated some of what was in the Swinney one about the NEC meeting (see 3.28pm), and said Cardiff would host the next NEC meeting in spring 2027.

John Swinney, Scotland’s first minister, has now issued a statement about today’s national economic council [NEC] in Glasgow, and Downing Street has issued a readout about Andy Burnham’s bilateral meeting with Swinney. Reading them together, three points emerge.

Swinney and Burnham were both positive about the meeting, and sounded keen to be constructive not confrontational. No 10 said both leaders agreed the NEC meeting had been “extremely positive”, and Swinney said it was “a welcome start of work to develop the UK government’s new principle of ‘devolving by default’”.

But there is still a problem because, although they both want devolution, it’s not the same devolution. Swinney’s statement is all about the devolution of power from Westminster to Scotland. No 10’s is mostly about “regional empowerment” (devolution within Scotland), although it does say the PM agreed to “review and respond to a range of issues raised by the first minister”.

They agreed to differ on independence. The No 10 statement restates Burnham’s position that a second independence referendum is off the table. Swinney could have chosen to have a row about this, but he didn’t. While not at all resiling from his pro-independence position, he politely said: “While the prime minister and I disagree on independence, we do agree that Westminster does not work for people in Scotland.”

For the record, here is the full readout from the No 10 spokesperson.

double quotation markThe prime minister met with the first minister of Scotland in Glasgow following a meeting of the National Economic Council today.

The prime minister and first minister agreed the meeting at the NEC had been extremely positive. They said it had been a valuable exercise in starting the process of exploring how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode.

They agreed that now there would be a policy sprint led by No 10 North, involving officials from both governments, to take this agenda forward.

Outside that process, the prime minister said the UK government would review and respond to a range of issues raised by the first minister.

This would not include a second independence referendum in Scotland, which the prime minister has repeatedly made clear is off the table.

double quotation markWhile the prime minister and I disagree on independence, we do agree that Westminster does not work for people in Scotland. And when the people of Scotland take issues into their own hands, the best outcomes will come about.

To that end, I will work constructively and collaboratively with him to devolve more powers from Westminster to Scotland – as long as those proposals drive economic growth that is felt in higher wages, better jobs, more opportunities for business to start and expand, and support with the cost of living.

Today’s meeting of the national economic council was a welcome start of work to develop the UK Government’s new principle of ‘devolving by default’ and the prime minister has been clear that he will not bypass the Scottish parliament in this endeavour.

I welcome that commitment, and look forward to our governments jointly developing a plan to consider further devolution to Scotland that will boost economic growth.

A rise in rough sleeping in London is a “stark reminder of the huge challenge” Andy Burnham faces in his pledge to get people off the streets, campaigners have said. As the Press Association reports, data shows there were 4,678 people recorded as sleeping rough in the capital in July to September this year. PA says:

double quotation markWhile this is a slight drop of 1% on the same three-month period in 2025, the figure has risen by almost a fifth (18%) on the previous quarter this year.

The Combined Homelessness and Information Network (Chain) figures, published today, showed that there were 819 people classed as living on the streets (a separate category) – a rise of 8% on the same time last year and up by a fifth (20%) on the previous quarter.

Rick Henderson, chief executive of Homeless Link, the national membership body for frontline homelessness services, said: “The increase in rough sleeping across London, and particularly of those spending longer on our streets, is a stark reminder of the huge challenge London and the wider country face in turning the prime minister’s ambition to end rough sleeping into action.”

Speaking to reporters after the national economic council meeting, Andy Burnham said he did not want Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to lose out on the changes that will give more financial powers to mayors in England.

Referring to the plans in the fiscal devolution roadmap, he said:

double quotation markThe agenda is moving quickly in England. There were further measures in the budget around regional devolution across all of England, and I don’t want to see Scotland left behind. I don’t want to see Wales left behind, but also crucially, I don’t want to see Northern Ireland left behind.

So it’s really important that we all move at the same pace together. And I won’t allow anything to delay that. Growth can’t wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK.

Referring to the absence of Northern Ireland’s first minister and deputy first minister, he said:

double quotation markIt’s disappointing that the first minister and deputy first minister of Northern Ireland weren’t here. There was some representation, but we will continue the discussions too with Stormont about how do we take forward the same ideas.

Andy Burnham has said the UK government will consider further devolution of employment support to Scotland and Wales.

Speaking after chairing a meeting of the national economic council, Burnham said:

double quotation markWe had a good discussion today on two fronts.

One around reindustrialisation, and the offer of more devolution of innovation funding to the regional level. It’s about creating those structures at a regional level, and that’s a matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries.

It’s not for me to impose or try to interfere there. But once there is a vehicle, that can be backed by the Scottish government, it can be backed by the UK government …

Secondly, we had a conversation about employment support, and particularly young people. There are too many young people out of work here in Scotland, in Wales, and in England too.

It’s a very big agenda that’s coming towards us. We need to localise as much as we can support for young people, employment support to help them back to work.

Now, as part of those discussions that will follow this meeting of the national economic council, we need to look at what are [the] arrangements for further devolution of employment support, particularly for young people in both Scotland and Wales.

Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has suggested the UK needs to know more about where the EU is heading before it signs up to a much closer relationship.

He made the comment in an interview with the Sun, a day after John Healey, the chancellor, also hinted that he might have reservations about Andy Burnham’s ambitions for a new relationship with the EU undoing the damage done by Brexit.

Burnham is attending a summit with the EU next month where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus. There is strong support for all these initiatives in cabinet.

But Burnham also wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election, when – if it wants – Labour will be able to dump the 2024 manifesto pledges ruling out joining the single market or the customs union.

Burnham has not said what he wants to propose in Labour’s next manifesto, and he insists ultimately the public will decide, but he has said that he would like the UK to rejoin the EU in his lifetime and he seems open to trying to rejoin the single market in the next parliament.

Asked by the Sun if he shared Burnham’s dream of rejoining the EU, Reynolds replied:

double quotation markI genuinely can’t answer that, because I don’t know what the future of the EU is – because [of] some of the very strong political currents in member states.

For me, it’s an approach to issues. What is their approach to how they regulate technology, AI? How dynamic will the economy be?

Sophia Sleigh, who wrote up the comments, said Reynolds was referring to the rise of far-right populist parties in Europe, which could fundamentally change and weaken the EU.

Although Reynolds’ comments were prompted by a question about rejoining the EU, his concerns would also apply to a proposal to join the single market.

Healey is also distinctly less pro-European than Burnham. In interviews yesterday, he did not accept that joining the single market would automatically be good for growth, he stressed the importance of accepting the referendum decision and making the best of the current relationship, and said he did not expect the UK to rejoin the EU in his lifetime.

In a bid to stop ministers disagreeing in public about the EU, Burnham sent them a letter earlier this week telling them to stay “disciplined” and not to “advocate for specific options” as the debate on the future UK-EU relationship gets under way.

At the Downing Street lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson was asked to give more details of the sort of “regional empowerment” that could be offered to Scotland and Wales on the basis of today’s summit. The spokesperson did not give any detail beyond what No 10 has said already (see 9.11am) and, like the PM (see 12.05pm), he said it was ultimately up to Scotland and Wales to say what they wanted. It sounds like we won’t be getting specific proposals today.

Downing Street has paid tribute to Patrick Stewart following the actor’s death. At the daily lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson gave a comment that was a bit more extensive than the usual No 10 contribution when a great British celebrity dies. The spokesperson said that was because Andy Burnham feels strongly about the importance of actors.

double quotation markThe prime minister was very sad to hear of the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart.

As a former culture secretary he knows how much Britain’s greatest actors mean to the country, and Sir Patrick was one of the very best.

He never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots. He brought joy to millions, and he always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.

Our thoughts are with his family and friends.

Here is our story, by Adrian Horton and Benjamin Lee, about the death of the Star Trek star.

Lee Waters, a former Labour minister in the Welsh government and a member of the Senedd until May this year, thinks it is a mistake for Andy Burnham to think Manchester-style devolution (greater powers for mayors) will help in Wales. Referring to posts earlier summarising Burnham’s thinking (see 9.11am, 9.33am and 12.05pm), Waters sent me this note.

double quotation markJust a reminder that when it comes to Wales, we are not comparing like with like. The term ‘region’ in an English context typically refers to an area covering between 1.5 and 3 million people. In Wales, regions cover much less dense areas. The Swansea Bay city region captures some 700,000 people, and similarly North Wales around 690,000 people. In Mid-Wales sheep outnumber people by 7:1. Only the Cardiff city region is comparable to English tiers, and even then at the lower end: around 1.5 million people.

Transposing an English mayoral worldview onto a very different political geography just doesn’t work. Wales may be a similar population size to the PM’s old manor but that’s where the parallel ends.
  
  
  Andy Burnham talks about the regions of England and Wales interchangeably but the role the new prime minister champions for metro mayors is, in many respects, already performed by the Welsh government. Powers over skills, employment support, economic development, housing investment and major spending programmes sit at an all-Wales strategic level (covering a similar population size to Greater Manchester.)
  
  
  His argument for England is that powers should flow from Westminster to city regions because they operate at an economically meaningful scale. Yet when the PM turns to Wales, he seems to suggest that powers already devolved to Cardiff Bay should be dispersed further down the system.
  
  
  But notably he is not calling on his successor as the mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, to fragment the powers of the Greater Manchester combined authority and redistribute them amongst its ten constituent councils. On the contrary, the whole logic of the Greater Manchester model rests on concentrating strategic authority at a regional level.
  
  
  Yet the implication of his comments is that Wales should move in the opposite direction.

Andy Burnham delivered his opening remarks at the national economic council meeting in Glasgow on camera. Here are the key points.

Burnham stressed that he wanted to be cooperative. He said:

double quotation markWhat I want to do is set the tone which is one of positive offer to work with both the Scottish and Welsh governments, in terms of looking at a model of deeper devolution in Scotland and Wales.

Referring to John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth using their first names, not their titles, Burnham also said that he hoped they had seen enough of him as PM to know that he was serious about wanting “problem solving rather than point scoring”. He also said he wanted to “draw a line”, implying previous relations with the devolved governments weren’t ideal.

He said that, while he wanted “deeper devolution” (see 9.11am), “obviously, it’s for the devolved governments to determine the shape and the structure of that”.

He suggested his experience as mayor of Greater Manchester had made him more inclined to see Westminster the way Scotland and Wales did. He said:

double quotation markObviously, speaking as a former mayor, I saw how Greater Manchester was able to go on a very different track to the one that we’d been on pre the arrival of devolved powers in Greater Manchester.

I’ll be honest, I looked at the world differently, and perhaps more from Scotland and Wales’ point of view, when we were making that case for a greater level of power.

He said, using devolved powers, as mayor he was able to set “high ambitions” for Manchester – “and a decade on the results are there to see.”

He said he wanted Westminster to work “in a more collaborative way” with the devolved governments.

He said that Britain in the past had not been particularly good at handling “industrial transition” and that he wanted to change this. He recalled visiting the site of the Ravenscraig steelworks near Motherwell recently, saying:

double quotation markI was on the site of Ravenscraig and … I used to hear that word in the news when I was growing up. I only then, when I was there, understood the scale of what that industry once was, and how the country didn’t help those communities through industrial transition.

You could say the same of Port Talbot in south Wales, he said. He said what was happening in Port Talbot was a model of industrial transition.

He expressed regret that Northern Ireland’s first minister and deputy first minister weren’t at the meeting.

John Swinney, the Scottish first minister, and Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, arrived together for the national economic council meeting in Glasgow. The SNP and Plaid Cymru are sister parties, and recently Swinney, ap Iorwerth and the Sinn Féin leaders Mary Lou McDonald and Michelle O’Neill held a meeting in Cardiff that was characterised by opponents as a summit to dismantle the UK.

This is from Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, summarising what he will be putting to Andy Burnham at their meeting in Glasgow today.

double quotation markToday, I represent Wales at the National Economic Council in Glasgow.

This is an opportunity for the UK Prime Minister to prove his commitment to a respect agenda that works both ways.

That means committing to not undermining the Senedd and to stop treating Wales as a region of England.

I will urge the Prime Minister to commit to a range of measures to improve the lives of people in Wales.

📈 A new Growth Partnership between the Welsh Government and the UK Government to boost prosperity in every part of our country.

🏴󠁧󠁢󠁷󠁬󠁳󠁿 Devolving the same powers as Scotland through a new Wales Bill.

🚂 And honouring, without delay, his commitment of £14bn for Welsh railways.

And that’s to name just a few of our demands.

Under the Plaid Cymru Welsh Government, Wales will never stay silent on issues that affect our communities.

Yesterday the Institute for Fiscal Studies (see here) and the Resolution Foundation (see here) delivered fairly negative assessments of the budget. But mostly the gloom was triggered by the thinktanks said about the overall state of the economy and the public finances; they were critical of John Healey for deferring difficult choices, but less hostile about the decisions he did actually announce.

However, according to YouGov, voters are quite positive. They regard it as one of the fairest budgets for years.

This is how Dylan Difford explains the figures in his YouGov write-up.

double quotation markThe public’s initial reaction to John Healey’s first budget is in some key respects broadly positive, with nearly half of Britons (45%) regarding the budget as being fair, relative to just 20% seeing the measures announced as not fair.

This is a notable improvement on last year, when Rachel Reeves’ second budget was declared ‘not fair’ by a near-inverse margin of 48% to 21%. In fact, on this measure, this is one of the most positively received budgets in recent times. In data going back to 2010, only George Osborne’s first budget in 2010 and Rishi Sunak’s Covid budgets of 2020 and March 2021 have been judged ‘fair’ by a greater proportion of Britons (50-55%).

The Covid budgets were both giveaway, rescue budgets, and so it is not surprising they polled well. Osborne’s first budget was an austerity budget, and it is not a model popular with Labour MPs, but it probably polled well on fairness because the pain was spread across all groups in society.

The YouGov figures also show that only 15% of people think their family finances will improve as a result of the budget. That may not sound much but, as Difford says, “this is a sharp and favourable contrast with last November’s budget, which 50% of Britons believed would leave them and their family worse off, compared to a mere 3% feeling they’d be better off.”

In fact, Healey and his first budget outperform Rachel Reeves and her budget last year on every measure assessed in the polling.

Yesterday one of the criticisms of the budget from the Resolution Foundation was that the energy cost of living support package helped the rich almost as much as the poor. That meant it was “poorly targeted”, said the RF, applying a progressive, social justice definition of fairness. What the YouGov poll suggests is that voters as a whole judge fairness differently; it is probably precisely because most households get the £100 energy payment that people regard it as fair.

In their London Playbook briefing for Politico yesterday, Sam Blewett and Megan McElroy said Healey used focus groups extensively before finalising his measures.

double quotation markGovernment officials say they focus-grouped all this relentlessly. Playbook was told these sessions helped convince ministers to go for wider support payments for council tax bands A-D rather than the initial plans to go with something more targeted. It was the supposedly better-off voters who were complaining about the pinch as well.

Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, was on the interview round this morning, announcing a new aspect of defence procurement policy. The Ministry of Defence is now saying that, if overseas suppliers win UK defence contracts, they will be required to spend the equivalent amount in the UK.

double quotation markBritish workers, businesses and apprentices will benefit from major changes which will see more defence work carried out in the UK thanks to the launch of a world-leading Offsets policy.

Under the new rules, overseas companies that win significant UK defence contracts will be required to invest back into Britain, through new British jobs and apprenticeships, opening UK factories, investing in domestic suppliers, transferring technology and innovation know-how.

This means contracts worth over £50m will be considered for offsets. The contractors will be required to deliver such benefits to the UK that could reach the same value as the contract, for example a £100m contract could see new jobs, facilities, or skills training up to the same £100m value in the UK.

The government is prioritising buying British defence contracts wherever possible. Where it must buy defence equipment from overseas, this new approach will ensure British workers and businesses still benefit.

John Healey, the chancellor, and Streeting are formally announcing this on a visit to BAE Systems Scotstoun in Glasgow today.

The MoD says countries like Poland, Norway and the Netherlands use similar offset policies. Further details of how this will work are set out in an offset policy paper published today.

double quotation markEvery pound we invest in defence should be judged by what it does for Britain. That’s why we are backing British by buying British wherever we can.

Even when that is not possible, we are acting to ensure that any investment brings jobs, skills and investment back home, strengthening our national security by boosting our domestic industry.

In the past, the conventional globalist, free market approach to defence procurement operated on the basis that cost and quality were all that mattered and that, if a foreign firm could supply kit better and more cheaply than anyone else, that was enough. But the US is not the only country that has become protectionist in recent years, and this is a good example of Europe prioritising local employment in government procurement.

In his statement ahead of the devolution summit in Glasgow today, Andy Burnham made it clear that he is interested in transferring more power from Edinburgh to Glasgow. (See 9.11am.) But John Swinney, the Scottish first minister, would rather talk about devolving further powers from London to Edinburgh. He issued this statement ahead of the meeting.

double quotation markThe prime minister has made devolution a central focus for his government. However the UK government must ensure that any devolution proposals respect devolution in Scotland. That means working with the Scottish government.

The Scottish government has put forward substantive proposals to the UK government on areas where further devolution would help grow Scotland’s economy and I will press the prime minister, and his government, to work with us to deliver those proposals.

The SNP wants Scotland to be fully independent (the ultimate version of devolution). But, pending that, it is also calling for the Scottish parliament to have power over policy areas currently reserved to London. Greater control over taxation, immigration, employment law and energy policy are particular priorities.

Andy Burnham has admitted his first budget as prime minister was not as radical as he would have liked because of the economic uncertainty facing the country, Kiran Stacey reports.

Good morning. Andy Burnham is in Glasgow today for a meeting with the leaders from Scotland and Wales and he says he wants to use it to talk about “the next stage of devolution”. According to the overnight briefing from No 10, he is less interested in giving more powers to the devolved parliaments and more interested in promoting “regional empowerment” in their countries.

In his pre-summit statement, Burnham says:

double quotation markThrough No 10 North, we are rewiring the state. I want to make sure every city and region in the United Kingdom is part of that.

Today I’ll be making an offer to the governments of each nation. Put politics aside and work in partnership with the UK government to develop models of regional empowerment that ensure communities can use their own strengths to unlock their potential.

This is the next stage of devolution. Together, there is no limit to what we can achieve.

Burnham is speaking at a time when Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have since the May elections (when Plaid Cymru won in Wales) for the first time had first ministers from nationalist parties that want to break away from the UK. John Swinney, the Scottish first minister, and Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, will be at the meeting today. But Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin first minister from Northern Ireland won’t be there. She holds power jointly with a DUP deputy, and both of them have to stay away because the DUP has vetoed their attendance due to an ongoing row about Drumcree. Some officials will attend instead.

Downing Street says at today’s meeting Burnham “will say that devolution by default shouldn’t be about the transfer of powers from one parliament to another but should go deeper within nations to empower all places and communities who know best what they need to grow and access opportunities.”

Morning: Andy Burnham chairs a meeting of the national economic council in Glasgow.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

Afternoon (UK time): Ed Miliband is attending a meeting of G20 foreign ministers in Atlanta in the US.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

title: How do we make new economic ideas a reality? – Aditya Chakrabortty answered your questions
excerpt: Guardian columnist, senior economics commentator and host of the new Radical Thinking podcast Aditya Chakrabortty answered your questions on the big ideas around economics, society and democracy, and ...
body_text:
Guardian columnist, senior economics commentator and host of the new Radical Thinking podcast Aditya Chakrabortty answered your questions on the big ideas around economics, society and democracy, and his new podcast

Thanks so much everyone for your emails and questions and for being good company to hang out with on a Friday afternoon. I hope some of what I said, at the end of an exhausting Budget week, was useful.

If you want more from me, and it’s not mandatory, there’s a Radical Thinking podcast out tomorrow morning and I’m back to writing my weekly column.
 
 
 Catch you soon, and I hope you have good weekends.
 
 
 Aditya

Alan Martin: Would you agree that we need a radical re-think on refugees and asylum seekers, to counter how they are being demonised and to reclaim our humanity?

double quotation markAditya: I agree. The ugly and inhumane treatment of refugees and those seeking safety in the UK and across the West reflects an ugliness and inhumanity in ourselves. It’s not new: whatever the mythology around the Kindertransport, the UK left European Jews stranded in the 1930s. But nearly a century later we should be doing better. It is the refugee who is attacked today, but tomorrow it will be the migrant and the day after the poor white Briton. We need to stand together.

Compassionate says: The World Bank could bundle all debt into one bond then sell it to the moon bank. And we all start over.

double quotation markAditya: But, Compassionate, the world is built on debt! And it’s not fair to dump on the moon. We’re already giving them our datacentres.

Anne Robin: I just can’t understand why economic growth seems to be the ultimate measure of a successful economy when we live on a planet with limited resources? Shouldn’t we be seeking to achieve robustness and homeostasis instead?

double quotation markAditya: Here’s another way to think about it. In the UK, every government in my lifetime and yours has promised growth. In reality, growth per person after inflation has gone down with every government since the 1970s. Thatcher oversaw less growth than Wilson and Callaghan, Blair saw less than Thatcher, and so on.

This isn’t de-growth, as greens talk about it, but the reality. What growth there has been has been captured by top earners. So yes, we should be thinking about doing something different. Will we?

Paul Hancock asks: I think all the talks have been stimulating and insightful, partly because of the guests but also because you’re a very good interviewer. What Yaroufakis said made me understand the extent to which we don’t live in a democracy. We can vote for change but will only be allowed as much as the great financial institutions allow. Given that reality, isn’t it a delusion to think we can change the course of events?

double quotation markAditya: Thanks a lot, Paul. I really appreciate it. You’ve summed up very well the key lesson from Varoufakis’s interview. To stave off any incipient gloom, I would also point out that there are times when ‘the crowd’ (to use a notoriously imprecise concept) can compel their leaders into following. Brexit is an example, whatever I think of it and how we got there. The legacy of 2015-2019, of millions of people wanting more from politics than supine centrism, clearly lives on. Without the Green surge, you wouldn’t have got Andy Burnham.

Ariadne’s thread is long and it never runs out.

Fulya Ilbey asks: Why are all the guests sort of ‘famous’ ones? Wouldn’t it be eye opening to have the man on the street on the microphone?

double quotation markAditya says: In my writing, ‘ordinary’ people often take centre stage. Take my recent column on the redundant workers of Vauxhall in Luton. The Guardian does a lot of ‘on the ground’ video reporting – such as my colleagues John Harris and John Domokos in their Anywhere But Westminster series.

George Fidler asks: A second and related question. Would you consider interviewing Andreas Malm?

double quotation markAditya: George, I forgot to answer your second question. I was just discussing with colleagues an interview with Malm. I would, not least because his book on blowing up pipelines raises very profound questions.
  
  
  The continued crackdown on free speech by supposedly left wing governments is a danger not just to academics and pensioners but to all of us.
  
  
  Let Malm come!

Cathy247 asks: There is no shortage of truly inspirational new ideas about how to change economics for the better – some have been covered by you, other current ‘radical’ thinking is being championed by others such as Amol Rajan. These include the huge benefits of rewilding, new approaches such as doughnut economics. My question is, how do we get those currently in power in politics to take these ideas on board and actually start to roll them out?

double quotation markAditya: In 2018, I wrote about an initiative of a citizens’ economics class. It was in a church in Levenshulme, where two women were running weekly classes and discussion groups on economics. It was a really good way for lay people who felt unconfident in economics and politics to feel some agency over their lives, at a time when the country was being hit by austerity and they themselves were suffering with chronic illnesses and debt.
  
  
  This isn’t systemic change and it doesn’t involve Westminster. But community organising often gets overlooked and is so valuable.

Helen Griffiths asks: What do you think that the ordinary man or woman (‘the man on the Clapham omnibus’) can do that would help positive change, or contribute to change, in this country. We are not all politicians or leaders.

double quotation markAditya says: A great question, Helen, thank you. I am neither politician nor leader, and for me the answers are the same as they ever were: you try and keep informed, to work in your communities, and to be a good neighbour.

During Covid, I went to report on a food bank in the area in which I grew up. Standing there with a notepad made me feel like a lemon, so I began mucking in. I met more people and had a better time. For years, I’ve also been a trustee for my local CAB, which stands in one of the most deprived stretches of Britain. It’s not as good as being a volunteer or a staffer but it does give me some meaning.
  
  
  Lastly, the man on the Clapham Omnibus should not insist on me listening to his phone as he scrolls through TikToks.

thegreatfatsby asks: Do you think the fact that Gabriel Zucman, who is a recognised authority on wealth tax is given more respect, time and attention by the mainstream media than Gary Stevenson, who has worked eloquently and tirelessly to spread the debate about the terrible consequences of inequality and whose ideas and analysis are almost identical is because of our cultural fixation on class prejudice?

double quotation markAditya says: I’ve followed Gabriel Zucman (and Emmanuel Saez and Thomas Piketty) for a long time, and find his work rigorous and thought provoking. I don’t always agree, but I appreciate their acceptance that taxes on wealth are part of the fight against ever-increasing inequality.
  
  
  I think Gary Stevenson is eloquent and compelling and is fighting a good fight. His book tells a story very well. But I don’t accept the insistence on a ‘wealth tax’ (as opposed to taxes on wealth) as being the only way we fight everything from inequality to the far right. We have to look at workers’ rights, housing, public ownership, greater democracy in economics and politics as well.

In the age of algorithm, simple, strong messages cut through. But the truth is often more complex.

Marija asks: How do you maintain peace of mind in your daily life during the unsettling times we live in?

double quotation markAditya says: What a nice question, Marija. I try to read a lot and write a diary. Unfortunately, I have the handwriting of a GP so I can’t read old entries. The other thing is I try to shirk my mobile phone.

Perspectiverox asks: The government has an enormous amount riding on AI to deliver future economic growth. Do you think this strategy will work? And is the government’s heavy investment in this vision, and its apparent determination to pursue it, contributing to a failure to properly acknowledge or address serious public concerns about the environment and jobs? More fundamentally, what happens if the anticipated AI-driven growth doesn’t materialise? Is there a Plan B?

double quotation markAditya says: In their book When Nothing Works, the Foundational Economy collective of economists and analysts point out that after decades of successive governments in the UK talking up the ‘knowledge economy’, technology accounted for less than 5% of GDP. That wasn’t just a British failure – the story is same across much of Europe. This is before we get intot who benefits from AI.

I find the slavering of the UK’s politicians and press before America’s AI oligarchy vulgar and idiotic, especially when all the indications are that these trade deals work against the interest of Britons.

The other clear thing is that AI hyperscalers and Trump are forcing Americans through a bubble. When it pops it will be a political failure, a market failure, an economic failure.
  
  
  Your question about Plan B is interesting. What does the Left do when the AI Bubbles pops? I think my first ever column for the Guardian was in August 2008, before the collapse of Lehman Brothers, where I said the Left should get ready for a looming crisis (Call me Mystic Meg, why not).
  
  
  The former editor of the Economist, Bill Emmott, told me I was a silly boy and this would all blow over.

Odourcolon asks: Do you think it’s possible to get rid of the neoliberalist thought process that seems to have dominated, and ruined (?), the UK over the past few decades?

Doodah70 asks: Aditya, what does getting rid of neo liberalism actually mean? It seems to be a narrative of taking us back to the economic policies of the 1970s and has a rose tinted view of that period ignoring inflation, IMF bailouts and mass industrial unrest and strike action. Is there an example of a country that doesn’t follow neoliberal ideas, that is successful, that we can emulate?

double quotation markAditya says: Hello both, these are very good questions. I rarely use the term neoliberal in my own writing. Partly because I am not sure enough readers will have a clear sense of what it means, as Doodah says, and partly because when I am talking about neoliberalism I might be referring to:
  
  
  1) handing public assets to private actors

2) reducing the active role of the state in providing essentials

4) the bulldozing of institutions such as trade unions and the BBC

Some of these processes are well described by the political economist Will Davies when he describes the ideology of neoliberalism as “the disenchantment of politics by economics”.
  
  
  The reality is that few countries have gone as far down the same path as the UK: the first country to industrialise and the first rich country really to de-industrialise. The first social democratic polity to privatise at this scale. Filleting the BBC, an institution which so many other countries envy
  
  
  Not all of this can be reversed, at least by much. I can’t see a quick path back to major manufacturing status – not now we’ve destroyed our supply chains. After starting on his March of the Makers, George Osborne did not make it far. (For a different view of this problem, look at Reindustrialise Britain, by Costas Lapavitsas, my dear former colleague Larry Elliott and Doug Nicholls).
  
  
  But other avenues look more promising. Look at what Angela Rayner has begun with employment rights and renters rights – many in politics know some of the problems, it’s just that their solutions are too bitty.

John Buckler asks: Please, can you justify for me private education in our society when it sucks up our scant resources to over-educate the mediocre, elevating them to positions of power eg Mogg, Gove, Johnson, Farage ?

double quotation markAditiya says: Thank you for your kind invitation, John, but I must decline.

George Fidler asks: On your podcast Radical Thinking why did you interview Michael Gove – someone whose politics are as orthodox as they can be in Britain? A similar thing happened with Rayner’s Beyond the Bubble. You would be hard pressed to find someone more central to the bubble than Gove. Genuinely, I don’t think there’s anything “radical” that can be learned from him. A second and related question. Would you consider interviewing Andreas Malm?

double quotation markAditya says: Thanks for listening, George. Your question is the one with which I start that interview: why is something called Radical Thinking spending time with Michael Gove? The answer comes in two parts:
  
  
  One, across the West (and elsewhere) the radical politics that is taking the lead is not from the Left, but the Right. Think of Nigel Farage in the UK, Alice Weidel of the AfD, Giorgia Maloni running Italy, her past in neo-fascist politics.
  
  
  And two: Gove is a thinker, an intelligent man who has both led the Right (one of the fathers of Brexit, don’t forget) and followed it (think of what he publishes as the editor today of the Spectator).
  
  
  FWIW, I found that interview fascinating. Here was a man accepting that the Conservatism that he’d previously championed was dead, and that its successor was a new, nastier, nativist right that derived much of its legitimacy from the failures of him and his colleagues. Think about living with that knowledge.

redstar1000 asks: Britain has some of the highest levels of deprivation in Europe. Millions of people in one of the richest countries in the world cannot eat well, keep their homes warm and take part in social life. Why is this seen as acceptable? Where is the moral outrage?

double quotation markAditya says: This is a great question that chimes with the one above. I share your outrage and so do others. Confronted with the situation you describe - around 300,000 households in England homeless, many of them with children - in one of the richest societies in human history, they would agree this is unacceptable, outrageous. But in a highly-unequal country, not everyone sees or feels or even brushes against this deprivation.

Flaxborough asks: Hi Aditya, can you answer truthfully, do you think we are heading for total economic and social collapse? How soon? Will we rise from it afterwards?

double quotation markAditya says: In truth, I think the UK is in economic and social collapse – it’s just that some people can’t see it, and others are too polite or arrogant to point it out. But what else should we call the most miserable period for wages and growth since Napoleon Bonaparte was on his horse charging around Europe? The worst decade for living standards since the end of rationing? Shit in our rivers? Joke prime ministers who blunder about, get booted offstage, then earn £££s? And no, not just Liz Truss, but Cameron and Johnson too.

The reason this isn’t recognised is because Britain is a highly unequal country where pain is heaped on those most hurt. Even in a collapsing country, some people always do well. Look at Argentina in the 1990s/2000s for an example.

Flaxborough, my friend, don’t ask when collapse will arrive: recognise it’s here already. And push for something better.

Michael Holmes asks: I have enjoyed all the talks. I am just a bit confused that the title of the talk varies between ‘Radical thinking’ and ‘Politics’, are they different categories? They seem to have the same production team. Also, the earlier programming had suggestions by you for further reading. This now doesn’t seem to happen? I thought that was valuable. I really enjoy the thoughtful interaction between you and your guests, with the time allowed for thoughtful and creative content. Great stuff! Thanks

double quotation markAditya says: Thanks so much for this, Michael. It’s great to get your feedback on the Radical Thinking podcast – and I’d love to hear more from viewers and listeners about what they are enjoying from the series so far.
  
  
  Just to explain: Radical Thinking began as a one-off series of conversations. The idea was to capture some of the energy and ideas of this particular moment – a change of prime minister in the UK, Trump and the midterms, the rise of the far right. We publish every weekend here as well as YouTube, Spotify, Apple. This Saturday’s episode is with two of the best dissenting economists around on some of the central issues in this week’s Budget – it’s a corker.
  
  
  You’re right – part of our (tiny) team is from Politics Weekly and because it’s a one-off we don’t have a separate channel. HOWEVER! The reaction so far has been astonishing, so strong that we’re thinking about more. So: watch this space
  
  
  Glad you like the further reading. Again, I started it as an experiment – and I know it hasn’t appeared everywhere – but if it’s useful i’ll keep it up.

Aditya Chakrabortty is the Guardian’s award-winning senior economics commentator. Through his regular opinion column, he shares his thoughts on the economy and its impact on society and earlier this year he was awarded an MBE for services to public understanding of the economy and wider social issues.

This month he launched a new Saturday podcast Radical Thinking, where he interviews major thinkers about the ideas that have shaped our times. He has conducted conversations with Yanis Varoufakis on democracy and the Eurozone crisis and Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor on Gaza, fascism and climate chaos.

In his latest episode he discusses doomscrolling and democracy with playwright James Graham who suggests that our algorithms have led us into ‘a massive crisis of the new’ and are preventing us from imagining a different future.

Aditya will be online at 2pm GMT (9am EDT) today to answer your questions on economics, democracy, the future of British and global politics.

Email your questions to conversations@theguardian.com or Sign up or sign in to post one in the discussion below

title: FDA again bypasses advisers to remove black-box warnings from menopause treatments
excerpt:
Some experts express concern about ‘lack of transparency’ as agency removes warnings on three estrogen patches

Three more patches for treating menopause will no longer carry black-box warnings about ...
body_text:
Some experts express concern about ‘lack of transparency’ as agency removes warnings on three estrogen patches

Three more patches for treating menopause will no longer carry black-box warnings about cardiovascular disease, breast cancer and dementia, officials at the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said on Friday.

The FDA did not convene an advisory committee and offered few details on the scientific basis for the decision in the press briefing. The news follows the removal of black-box warnings from six menopause treatments in February, as patients across the US struggle with shortages of the patches.

When journalists asked for the evidence behind this decision, officials said it could be provided later.

“I have been concerned by the lack of transparency behind these decisions,” said Reshma Ramachandran, an assistant professor and health services researcher at Yale School of Medicine. “The blanket removal of black-box warnings regarding risks of breast cancer and cardiovascular disease without clear justification can be misleading for patients and underplays real potential harms.”

There are particular risks for certain groups of patients, such as those with histories of hormone-sensitive cancers, she said. Instead, officials highlighted the shortages patients are facing for menopause hormone treatments (MHT).

“We are working with manufacturers to strengthen supply and improve access,” said Dorothy Fink, deputy director of the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development. Manufacturing of estrogen patches has doubled over the past year, she said.

Even so, patients report stock-outs of the patches.

“We know that for some patients, these past months have been frustrating,” said Sarah Ibrahim, deputy center director for regulatory programs of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. After the change to labels in February, demand for estradiol patches “increased significantly, and patients in many areas found it difficult to get their usual patches at their usual pharmacy”, she said. “And I want you to know that we hear you.”

The FDA is working with manufacturers to ramp up production, and the agency is also working to change the labels of the remaining MHT products, Ibrahim said.

The black-box warnings “painted a broad and, in some cases, overstated pictures of risk”, she said. “Updated evidence shows that for many healthy women under 60 and within 10 years of menopause onset, the risk-benefit profile looks meaningfully different than older warnings conveyed.”

Estradiol patches are usually considered lower risk than synthetic oral medications, because they pass into the bloodstream without first going to the liver. The risks of the patches are higher with high doses, research shows.

Officials in the Trump administration have made sweeping and “data-free” claims about the benefits of MHT, including improvements in longevity, which are not supported by research, menopause experts have said. While there are benefits to the treatments for some women, the decision not to convene advisers or include research sets a troubling precedent, they said.

The FDA bypassed its advisory committees last November in announcing it would remove the warnings; at the time, a spokesperson said that the reason is because committees are “bureaucratic, long, often conflicted, and very expensive”.

Instead, the FDA convened a panel in July 2025 featuring doctors and influencers, all of whom were vocal proponents of MHT and several of whom had conflicts of interest with practices that market and sell hormone therapy, Ramachandran said.

“At the expert meeting, they also did not allow for public testimony,” Ramachandran said – including from the lead investigator of the Women’s Health Initiative, research from which formed the recommendations for MHT, who was in the audience. After audience members voiced concern, the FDA opened a docket for public comment.

The FDA is also exploring the possibility of offering vaginal estrogen products over the counter, according to an agency press release on Friday.

title: Kim Kardashian undergoes surgery after health scare echoes dad’s fatal cancer battle
excerpt:
The SKIMS founder set to confront Paris robbery gunmen in court. (Video credit: AP)

Kim Kardashian has undergone surgery to have irregularities removed from her esophagus, she revealed on her family'...
body_text:
The SKIMS founder set to confront Paris robbery gunmen in court. (Video credit: AP)

Kim Kardashian has undergone surgery to have irregularities removed from her esophagus, she revealed on her family's show, "The Kardashians."

In Thursday’s episode, the 46-year-old reality star said she had been feeling a bit sluggish, but first assumed it was just because she'd been busy.

"I’ve been feeling a little off lately. My throat is like killing me today," she said in a confessional.

KIM KARDASHIAN REVEALS NEW HEALTH SCARE WITH HAUNTING CONNECTION TO FATHER’S CANCER DEATH

Kim Kardashian said she was stressed about her esophagitis diagnosis because her father, Robert Kardashian, died of esophageal cancer in 2003. (Getty Images; Kim Kardashian/Instagram)

Early in the episode, a doctor told her that she appeared to have inflammation of the esophagus, and noted that she could have esophagitis.

She admitted in a confessional, "So, I’ve seen a couple of doctors, and it’s been heavy on my mind lately."

The doctor suggested taking a round of medicine, then coming in for a procedure so he could get a better look at what was wrong and then determine if they needed to take further action.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I haven’t really told too many people about this just because I think it’s, you know, something that really hits home for me, and I just don’t really want to go there with my dad having passed away from esophagus cancer," she admitted to the camera. "Hopefully I can just take medication, and this will go away, but I just don’t know what’s going to happen."

Kim Kardashian is seen in New York City last year. (GC Images)

Robert Kardashian died of esophageal cancer in 2003.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"The doctor says my esophagus has these irregularities and I have to have them cut out," Kardashian said in the preview for next week’s show. "That’s the same thing my dad had."

Robert Kardashian was best known for representing O.J. Simpson in his murder trial. (AFP via Getty Images)
