body_text:
Resolution Foundation says 2020s set to be the worst decade, by far, for more than half a century for rising living standards

The Resolution Foundation has now published its full 48-page report on the budget. Some of its main arguments were covered earlier. (See 8.36am.)

Here are five charts from the report illustrating five of its main arguments.

1) The amount the government is spending paying interest on its debt is “high and rising”, the report says. It says:

double quotation markDebt interest spending is now forecast to reach £147bn in 2029-30, £13bn more than in March. This leaves debt interest spending at 4.1 per cent of GDP in 2029-30 (and peaking marginally higher at 4.14 per cent in 2031-32, the highest on record since 1956-57) and above the total expected spend on universal credit, Housing Benefit and Child Benefit combined in that year.

2) The 2020s are set to be the worst decade, by far, for more than half a century for rising living standards, the report says.

double quotation markThe 2020s are on course to have the lowest growth in incomes of any decade on record when measured using Real Household Disposable Income (RHDI). RHDI is projected to rise by just 1.4 per cent in total over the decade (equivalent to £400 in 2026-27 prices), one-tenth of the growth rate achieved in the 2010s (which itself was the second-worst decade on record). Income growth this decade is set to be much weaker than GDP growth because of rising taxes and import prices.

3) Labour’s cost of living support package benefits the rich almost as much as the poor, the report says.

double quotation markTaken altogether, the Government’s £4.4bn cost of living package for 2025-26 and 2026-27 is poorly targeted. As Figure 8 makes clear, support is very widely spread. The Household Energy Payment goes to up to 20 million households in England, which are dispersed across the income distribution (87 per cent of the bottom half of the income distribution and 73 per cent of the top live in Council Tax bands A-D). The VAT cut and the Fuel Duty delay are not targeted at all. Taken together, we estimate that 52 per cent of the whole cost of living package will benefit the poorest half of the income distribution this year and next, with the other 48 per cent going to the top half (equivalent to an average £158 for poorer households, compared to £144 for richer households).

4) But, overall, the tax and benefit changes since the government took power have been progressive, the report says.

double quotation markWe estimate that annual incomes will, on average, be £320 higher for households in the bottom quintile in 2029- 30, compared to £2,000 lower for those in the top quintile as a result of the Starmer and Burnham governments’ measures. This is largely the result of policies announced before this budget: the repeal of the two-child limit and the commitment to uprate the universal credit standard allowance at a higher rate than inflation for four years, both introduced from April 2026.

5) All government spending departments apart from defence, health and education are likely to face cuts in spending per head from the end of this decade under current plans, the report says.

Andy Burnham has claimed that the British economy is going “from strength to strength”.

Economists have argued that the documents published alongside the budget suggest this parliament will be dire for living standards. (See 10.21am.) But, asked about the country’s economic prospects when speaking to reporters on a visit in Derby, Burnham said:

double quotation markThe British economy is defying the expectations of forecasters, so this year we will grow more strongly. The growth forecast has been upgraded.

The IMF [International Monetary Fund] said last week we’re the standout nation for deficit reduction, so it remains difficult because the world is difficult and the situation in the Middle East has an impact.

But I think people should look at what the chancellor said yesterday, see a country that has got a platform of stability in the economy. We’re beginning to defy those expectations, and I’m confident that we will go from strength to strength from here.

Andy Burnham has said the government is working ‘‘flat out” to cut welfare spending.

Speaking to reporters at a Rolls-Royce factory in Derby, when asked if he could confirm what John Healey was reported to have said about planning to cut welfare spending by the next election, Burnham replied:

double quotation markWe want to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible, and we’re working flat out to that end. Now that we are through the budget, the big next priority in front of us is the publication of the [Alan Milburn report on youth unemployment], long awaited, but it’s coming soon.

We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There’s no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible.

Burnham also argued that “crude cuts” on their own would just leave people “in crisis”, requiring more public spending down the line.

At the Downing Street lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson was also asked if John Healey’s comments about the EU in a GB interview this morning (see 12.14pm) were out of line with Andy Burnham’s. No, was the answer. The spokesperson said:

double quotation markThe position of the government, and the prime minister and the chancellor, is that a stronger relationship with our closest neighbours is in our national interest.

Healey did not say anything that contradicted Burnham’s views on Brexit. But if Burnham had been asked the GB News questions, he would have stressed the problems with the current EU relationship. Healey, instead, said “we’ve got a Brexit decision” and stressed the importance of making the best of the current arrangements.

Downing Street has said John Healey was not committing to cutting welfare spending before the general election in his Today programme interview this morning. (See 9.23am.)

Although one answer he gave to a question could be interpreted as saying that, the PM’s spokesperson said that was not Healey’s message. The spokesperson said:

double quotation markWe’ve never set an arbitrary target or timetable [for when the welfare bill starts to fall]. But both the prime minister and the chancellor have been crystal clear that the welfare bill needs to come down, and that we need to do that in a progressive and sustainable way and not through crude cuts which push people into hardship and puts pressure on the system elsewhere.

Asked if Healey mis-spoke in his interview, the spokesperson said:

double quotation markThe chancellor is completely in line with what the PM has said over the last few months that the welfare bill needs to come down and, as I say, we are not setting an arbitrary target or timetable on that.

The spokesperson said the government would be publishing Alan Milburn’s report on youth unemployment and Stephen Timms’ report on the personal independence payment (Pip), and that these would be followed by a white paper on welfare reform published next year. That will be followed by legislation.

Kemi Badenoch has described the Treasury clarification that John Healey is not promising to cut the welfare bill before the general election (see 9.23am) as “astounding”. In a response on social media, she said:

double quotation markThis is astounding. The government’s own figures show working-age welfare will go up by £60 BILLION by 2030, yet the Treasury has to rush out and correct the Chancellor to say there is no timetable for cutting the benefits bill. Looks like foot in mouth syndrome is spreading.

John Healey couldn’t even find £10 billion to get defence spending to 3% of GDP - the thing he quit over.

Don’t let anyone tell you this was a ‘do no harm budget’. In doing so little, Labour have harmed our economic security and they’ve harmed our national security.

Selling nicotine-free vapes to children under the age of 18 has become illegal from today, the government has said.

Children were already banned from buying vapes containing nicotine. But, under the Tobacco and Vapes Act, shops across the UK will now be banned from selling nicotine-free vapes, and nicotine pouches, to children.

In an article for the Daily Mirror welcoming the new law, Prof Sir Chris Whitty, the chief medical officer for England, said:

double quotation markVaping can be a way to help established adult smokers who are already addicted to nicotine from tobacco to swap to a less dangerous product. Vaping is considered safer than smoking, but that is a low bar. Vapes should therefore never be used by children or non-smokers.

Some children have already come to harm from bad reactions to vapes. The long-term health harms of vaping in today’s children will only become clear over time. They are however unlikely to be good; inhaling multiple, often heated, chemicals into the lungs may well do irreversible harm.

According to the Department of Health and Social Care, which has put out a new release about how the ban will operate in England, “more than a million children are estimated to have tried vaping, with more than 370,000 vaping regularly, putting them at a higher risk of developing respiratory illnesses.” Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are also implementing bans.

As Peter Walker reports, Andy Burnham has written to cabinet ministers telling them that, as he opens a national debate on improving the UK’s relationship with the EU, he does not want them to “advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process”.

John Healey stuck to this in his interviews this morning. But, speaking to GB News, he did hint that he might not be 100% enthusiastic about taking the UK back into the EU single market after the next election.

When Christopher Hope, GB News’ political editor, put it to him that more than two thirds of voters in Rawmarsh and Conisbrough, Healey’s south Yorkshire constituency, voted for Brexit and would not be happy with rejoining the single market, Healey replied:

double quotation markNo, freedom of movement is not on the agenda, and certainly for this parliament it’s ruled out.

Healey said the government would be having “a bigger discussion about how we get a better Brexit deal”. Asked if he would favour joining the EU, with freedom of movement, if that helped the economy, he replied:

double quotation markNo, I’m in favour of accepting that we’ve got a Brexit decision. And I’m in favour of the job we need to do now, which is to make the best of the terms we’ve got.

In his interviews this morning John Healey pushed back a bit against the claims that his plans are based on unrealistic assumptions about spending cuts. (See 11.29am.) Speaking to Bloomberg, he said “hard decisions” would be needed. He said:

double quotation markMy cabinet colleagues are demonstrating that they can also exert fiscal discipline and spending control, and we will take that into the spending review.

But the spending review will be framed by the priorities that we set in the 10-year plan for Britain, that’s as it should be.

Hard decisions about the top priorities for Britain in the years to come, judgments that then follow about how we fund them.

Here are some more lines from Helen Miller’s presentation about the Institute for Fiscal Studies’ assessment of the budget. (See 10.45am.)

Miller said higher inflation means John Healey would need at least £17bn to avoid real-terms cuts in some government departments under the long-term spending plans. Echoing a point made by the Resolution Foundation (see 8.36am and 10.21am), she said:

double quotation markThe chancellor left plans for overall departmental spending across the rest of the parliament broadly unchanged in cash terms. In the face of higher inflation, this means that the real-terms value of budgets has been cut. Taken at face value, and alongside the inherited plans to slow down spending growth sharply in coming years, that is a big choice. It effectively implies that some public services will see real-terms cuts in next year’s spending review. Avoiding the cuts implied by both higher inflation and tight envelopes could plausibly require a top-up of £17bn in 2030-31. That’s true even before thinking about the £11bn needed to fund defence plans.

She said she did not believe Healey would implement the future spending cuts implied by his departmental spending plans. She said:

double quotation markI want to be clear that my concern is not that it would be impossible to deliver the implied cuts to other services – that could be done. But I’m sceptical that this government would be willing to do it. I’m also sceptical because I didn’t hear John Healey starting the kind of pitch-rolling that you would expect if he intended to deliver these spending plans. And I’m sceptical because history advises scepticism. When chancellors pencil in tight spending plans in the future, they tend not to deliver.

She criticised Healey for raiding the reserves to fund the defence investment plan. She explained:

double quotation markI’m grumpy about how the chancellor decided to fund the relatively small hole in the defence investment plan – that’s the plan that gets defence spending to 2.7% of GDP next year and keeps it there until 2029–30. Much of it came from further cuts to the capital budgets of other government departments. Fine. Priorities change. But the rest came from raiding reserves in future years. This is worth drawing out: John Healey has now spent 25% of the capital reserve set aside for the next three years. He’s also spent 40% of the day-to-day reserve. This is categorically not what the reserves are for. Drawing down reserves is another way that the government has reduced its buffer against future shocks.

She said it was “sad” that the government was having to decide who should get energy support based on council tax bands that are based on property values 35 years ago. She said:

double quotation markIt is also sad that, in the time since the last energy price surge, the government hasn’t bothered to invest in the data that would have allowed a package more targeted at those most badly hit by rising energy prices. But here we are.

She said Healey was at risk of needing to put up taxes next year. She said:

double quotation markI am left with the impression that the chancellor is hoping the economic forecasts improve enough that he can make good on his plan to cut borrowing without having to also make large cuts to public spending or raise taxes. I hope that happens. And it might – a re-opening of the strait of Hormuz or AI-driven productivity growth really could create sunnier skies. But, equally, things could get worse. If they do, the chancellor now has less insurance.

A clear short-term risk with the chancellor’s choices is that next year – with low headroom and a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments – we see another season of damaging speculation about tax rises.

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies thinktank, is giving a presentation summing up the IFS’s view of the budget. Arguing that it contained plenty of “bad things” as well as welcome measures, she singled out founders’ relief for particular criticism.

double quotation markAfter years of arguing that business asset disposal relief was a bad idea – and just when I thought the relief was on its last legs – a new, similar relief has popped up. The new founders’ relief looks bonkers. It gives a lower rate of capital gains tax to a small subset of people with large gains. That will include some entrepreneurs that make investments with broader societal benefits – although most of that activity would have happened without the relief. But it will also include people that just got lucky. There are very complex rules around who gets it – rules that will incentivise people to change their behaviour in weird ways simply to be able to get the relief. I could go on. But the punchline is that this looks to me like yet another tax break for a chosen group with little economic reasoning behind it.

Since the start of 2025 Reform UK has been ahead of the Conservative party in the Politico poll of polls, a tracker which averages how the political parties are in surveys carried out by all the main polling organisations. Different polling companies use different methods, and so the poll of polls provides a reliable overview. Other poll of poll trackers are available, but Politico’s may be the most widely read in Westminster.

And today it has good news for the Conservatives. For the first time since early 2025, they have regained their lead over Reform UK.

The Resolution Foundation has now published its full 48-page report on the budget. Some of its main arguments were covered earlier. (See 8.36am.)

Here are five charts from the report illustrating five of its main arguments.

1) The amount the government is spending paying interest on its debt is “high and rising”, the report says. It says:

double quotation markDebt interest spending is now forecast to reach £147bn in 2029-30, £13bn more than in March. This leaves debt interest spending at 4.1 per cent of GDP in 2029-30 (and peaking marginally higher at 4.14 per cent in 2031-32, the highest on record since 1956-57) and above the total expected spend on universal credit, Housing Benefit and Child Benefit combined in that year.

2) The 2020s are set to be the worst decade, by far, for more than half a century for rising living standards, the report says.

double quotation markThe 2020s are on course to have the lowest growth in incomes of any decade on record when measured using Real Household Disposable Income (RHDI). RHDI is projected to rise by just 1.4 per cent in total over the decade (equivalent to £400 in 2026-27 prices), one-tenth of the growth rate achieved in the 2010s (which itself was the second-worst decade on record). Income growth this decade is set to be much weaker than GDP growth because of rising taxes and import prices.

3) Labour’s cost of living support package benefits the rich almost as much as the poor, the report says.

double quotation markTaken altogether, the Government’s £4.4bn cost of living package for 2025-26 and 2026-27 is poorly targeted. As Figure 8 makes clear, support is very widely spread. The Household Energy Payment goes to up to 20 million households in England, which are dispersed across the income distribution (87 per cent of the bottom half of the income distribution and 73 per cent of the top live in Council Tax bands A-D). The VAT cut and the Fuel Duty delay are not targeted at all. Taken together, we estimate that 52 per cent of the whole cost of living package will benefit the poorest half of the income distribution this year and next, with the other 48 per cent going to the top half (equivalent to an average £158 for poorer households, compared to £144 for richer households).

4) But, overall, the tax and benefit changes since the government took power have been progressive, the report says.

double quotation markWe estimate that annual incomes will, on average, be £320 higher for households in the bottom quintile in 2029- 30, compared to £2,000 lower for those in the top quintile as a result of the Starmer and Burnham governments’ measures. This is largely the result of policies announced before this budget: the repeal of the two-child limit and the commitment to uprate the universal credit standard allowance at a higher rate than inflation for four years, both introduced from April 2026.

5) All government spending departments apart from defence, health and education are likely to face cuts in spending per head from the end of this decade under current plans, the report says.

John Healey has denied postponing difficult decisions on the welfare system, insisting the government is making changes “now”.

Thinktanks and opposition parties have made this claim. But, when this was put to Healey in an interview on GB News, he replied:

double quotation markThis was a broken system. And two years ago we started putting back in place face-to-face assessments. We’ve changed terms of universal credit, so people don’t have to brand themselves as too sick to work.

So, those are changes we’re making now. But in the long run, as I’ve argued, and the prime minister has said, too, we have to bring the cost of benefits down.

John Healey is rowing back from his answer in an interview in the Today programme implying he wanted welfare spending to go down before the next general election. According to Chris Mason, the BBC’s political editor, Treasury sources are saying his words have been over-interpreted.

This relates to what Healey said in an interview with Nick Robinson for the Today programme. It was broadcast this morning, but recorded yesterday, and the BBC has written it up in a story on its website headlined: “Healey promises reduction in welfare bill before next election”.

For the record, here is the key exchange.

double quotation markRobinson: Let’s take welfare if we could. £19bn up in the year ahead. That’s the entire police budget for England and Wales. That’s the entire annual defence equipment budget. And yet in your speech you said, well, we’ve got a couple of reports coming next month, then we’ll have a white paper, which in non-Westminster jargon means a consultation, then you’ll have some legislation, then you’ll have a row in the Labour party. You’re not going to make any of these cuts before the next election, are you?

Healey: Well first, I’ve said clearly, the prime minister said as well, we have to bring the benefits bill down. You don’t do that by crude cuts, especially when people are feeling the cost of living pressures. We do have a big report, two big reports being produced next month, that will help us map out the way that we need to change the system for the long run. We are in fact reducing and have been over the last two years the rate of increase in the welfare bill compared to the previous period – I’m afraid to say – of a broken system the Conservatives put in place. We’re bringing back and have brought back face to face assessments which they axed for instance. We’ve been changing universal credits so people aren’t branding themselves as too sick to work in order to make that system work better.

Robinson: But you’re reducing the rate of increase in welfare spending chancellor aren’t you? But the OBR’s forecast is that £1 in every £8 will be spent on welfare by 2030 or thereabouts. You’ve got to make cuts, haven’t you?

Healey: This system is unsustainable. I’ve been clear about that. The prime minister’s been clear about it ….

Robinson: Briefly, because I want to give you the chance to talk about other things – there will be cuts in welfare before the election?

Healey: There will be there will be a reduction in the benefits bill. We’ll do that in a Labour way and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progressive to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill and I feel a moral duty to deal with these youngsters who at the moment have been written off by previous governments.

The answer highlighted in bold is what gave the BBC its story. Healey paused slightly between the first “there will be” and the second “there will be” and it would be perfectly reasonable to interpret it as:

double quotation markThere will be. [Direct answer to Robinson’s question.] There will be a reduction in the benefits bill [etc etc – Healey expanding on the answer.]

But the Treasury is implying what he meant was:

double quotation markThere will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill [Healey simply repeating three words as he launches into more general answer, not answering Robinson directly, but just explaining the government’s approach.]

Reasonable people could interpret is either way. But Mason said the Treasury had told him the first interpretation was not accurate, and that if Healey really wanted to commit to getting cutting the benefits bill before the general election, he would have announced that in the budget.

Given that Alan Milburn himself has said that his plans to tackle youth unemployment may require more spending upfront in return for savings later, and given that welfare reforms often take most of a decade to roll out, it does seem unlikely that Healey intended to say the benefits bill would be cut before the election.

But, as Mason pointed out on the Today programme, “correcting” this story means the Treasury is implicitly saying benefit spending won’t go down before the election – which is very helpful to the Tories and Reform UK.

Good morning. The day after the budget is often the moment when big initiatives announced by the chancellor the day before with a flourish start to unravel as experts pore over the small print. There is not much of that happening this morning – mainly because John Healey did not have any really big initiatives up his sleeve. Compared with a normal budget, his tax and spending initiatives were mostly relatively minor. That means that the opposition parties have been struggling to find things to attack, and so instead they have resorted to criticising Healey for what he did not do: slash welfare (the Tory/Reform UK solution), or join the EU’s single market (the Lib Dems’).

Healey has given interviews to all the main broadcasters, which are playing out this morning, but they were recorded last night and they don’t have any sensational new revelations. As Rowena Mason reports, one of the top lines was Healey saying he would cut welfare spending before the election.

But there were other lines in the interviews too. I will be posting all the highlights this morning.

The two main public spending thinktanks, the Institute for Fiscal Studies and the Resolution Foundation, are both publishing reports assessing the budget this morning. The RF has issued a news release with its main findings and its assessment of the overall economic impact of the budget measures highlights three problems.

It accuses Healey of a “complete failure” to target help with energy bills at those most in need. It says:

double quotation markThe poorest half of households will gain £158 on average from cost of living support this year and next, just £14 more than the £144 received by the richest half – highlighting a complete failure to target help at those who need it most.

It says long-term public spending plans imply a return to austerity. It says:

double quotation markTight spending plans beyond 2028-29 imply departmental budgets will take more of the strain in the future. But if the 3% defence target is met and real health spending continues to grow at 2.6%, pencilled-in spending totals imply that funding for 13 ‘unprotected’ departments will fall to just 4.7% of GDP by 2031-32, close to the post-austerity historic low.

It says people will get poorer between now and the end of the parliament. It says:

double quotation markMedian real annual disposable incomes for working age households are set to grow by a paltry £600 over the course of the parliament. Worse still, those gains are already behind us. Between now (2026-27) and the end of the parliament (2028-29), typical incomes are forecast to fall in total by £1,050 (3 per cent).

This is one reason why so many people continue to think Andy Burnham will call an election next spring (before the electorate feels the full misery of getting poorer) – despite Burnham yesterday saying he would not hold one within the next 12 months.

9am: Jonathan Haskel, chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, and Ruth Curtice, head of the Resolution Foundation, speak at an event where the RF is presenting its budget analysis.

9.30am: Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

10.30am: Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, presents the IFS’s budget analysis.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

After 11.30am: MPs resume the budget debate in the Commons.

Lunchtime: Andy Burnham is on a visit to a Rolls-Royce factory in the Midlands where he is speaking to the media.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

title: Netanyahu falls short of majority as Israel faces three possible paths to a new government
excerpt:
As coalition negotiations loom and allegations of foreign election interference emerge, Fox News Digital reporter Efrat Lachter reports from Tel Aviv, Israel.

TEL AVIV, Israel - Israeli Prime Ministe...
body_text:
As coalition negotiations loom and allegations of foreign election interference emerge, Fox News Digital reporter Efrat Lachter reports from Tel Aviv, Israel.

TEL AVIV, Israel - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition remained well short of a parliamentary majority Thursday as newly counted ballots showed a dramatic surge in support for Arab parties, potentially giving the opposition enough votes to challenge his control of parliament.

With 93.8% of ballots counted as of 4 a.m. ET Thursday (10 a.m. local time in Israel), including votes from the double-envelope count, Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc was projected to win 53 seats in Israel's 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. The two predominantly Arab parties were projected to secure a combined 19 seats, bringing the potential anti-Netanyahu parliamentary majority to 67.

The updated figures showed Netanyahu's Likud remaining the largest individual party with 26 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar party with 21 and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's Beyachad party with 12. The figures remain preliminary.

NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE

A road sign stands in front of a large billboard featuring Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on Oct. 20, 2026. (Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images)

The results leave neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with the 61 seats required to form a government independently, raising the prospect of difficult coalition negotiations or another election.

The biggest shift came from Israel's Arab voters, whose turnout surged compared with previous elections, potentially reshaping the country's political balance.

Arab voter participation reached approximately 80%, compared with 53.2% in the 2022 election, according to the Israel Democracy Institute. The 2026 figure remains preliminary.

The Joint List was projected to win 11 seats, while Ra'am was projected to secure eight. Together, their 19 seats would nearly double the Arab parties' representation from the 10 seats they won in 2022.

Overall voter turnout reached 77.7% by the official 10 p.m. closing time on election night, the highest level at that hour since 1999, according to Israel's Central Elections Committee.

The increased Arab participation could prove decisive in determining the next government's composition. Although Eisenkot and several other opposition leaders ruled out including Arab parties in their governing coalition during the campaign, their parliamentary support could allow the opposition to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, and gain greater control over the legislative agenda even before a new government is formed.

IRAN IS TRYING TO ‘CREATE A ROT FROM WITHIN’ THROUGH ‘INFORMATION WARFARE,’ ANALYST WARNS

Posters of Gadi Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu are displayed on billboards ahead of the Knesset elections, in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Oct. 25, 2026. (Nir Keidar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The political stakes intensified Thursday following a Channel 12 report alleging that substantial sums originating in Qatar may have been transferred to influence voter participation in Arab communities.

According to N12, some of the funds allegedly traveled through financial channels previously used to transfer money to terrorist organizations, including currency exchanges.

The allegations have not been independently substantiated, and investigators have yet to establish whether foreign financing occurred or whether election-related crimes were committed.

Channel 12 reported that Shin Bet Director David Zini presented intelligence concerning suspected foreign interference to Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg, prompting the judge to order an investigation.

In a letter published by N12, Sohlberg instructed the domestic security agency to investigate the allegations and identify evidence that could either substantiate or disprove them. He requested findings within one week, citing the limited time available during the election count.

The judge's letter did not publicly identify Qatar as the suspected foreign actor. That identification came from N12's reporting.

Qatar strongly denied the allegations Thursday, accusing Israeli politicians of attempting to drag the Gulf nation into Israel's domestic political disputes following the election.

"We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr. Majed Al-Ansari wrote on X.

Al-Ansari accused Israeli politicians and their allies in the media of launching a "disinformation campaign," saying Qatar had been accused of financing Netanyahu, the Israeli left and now Arab voters.

"If these claims were to be believed, Qatar would apparently own all of Israel," he wrote. "Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians," Al-Ansari added, insisting that Qatar had no involvement in Israel's electoral process and would continue its diplomatic and humanitarian efforts in the region.

Acting Central Elections Committee director general Dean Livne also rejected the allegations in a letter to Yesh Atid MK Vladimir Beliak, who sits on the committee. "The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded, and to the best of our knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."

But the allegations quickly became part of the political confrontation over whether opposition parties should cooperate with Arab lawmakers.

ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW

An Arab-Israeli woman casts her ballot during Israel's general elections on Oct. 27, 2026, in Umm El Fahem, Israel. (Amir Levy/Getty Images)

Netanyahu and Likud had already challenged the legitimacy of the Arab parties' electoral gains. On Wednesday, before the latest Qatari allegations emerged, Likud accused Arab parties of stealing the election through alleged voter fraud, accusations that had not been substantiated.

In a statement Thursday, Likud argued that the suspected foreign interference made cooperation with the Arab parties unacceptable.

"After it became clear that foreign actors attempted to take control of the Knesset, it is obvious that no Zionist party must cooperate with Ra'am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker using votes bought with cash, or establish a government dangerous to Israel," the party said.

The assertion that parliamentary seats were obtained through purchased votes has not been established by the investigation.

Hauser Tov, a political reporter for Israel's Haaretz newspaper, argued on X that the statement revealed Likud's immediate political objective: preventing the opposition from using its potential parliamentary majority to replace the Knesset speaker.

Israeli journalist Amir Tibon wrote on X, "The main reason they want to prevent this is so that the Knesset won't vote to establish a state commission of inquiry into October 7." He argued that such an investigation could examine Qatari involvement in Gaza and Israel.

Eisenkot responded to the allegations Thursday, after meeting with Israel Security Agency (Shin Bet) Director David Zini. "Foreign involvement in Israel is unacceptable and profoundly serious, particularly when it involves a country that funds and supports Hamas," Eisenkot said. "It is serious when it occurs in the Prime Minister’s Office, and it is serious if it occurs in the electoral process."

He called on the Shin Bet to investigate the allegations thoroughly and take the strongest possible action against anyone found to have attempted to compromise the election's integrity.

Eisenkot also accused Netanyahu and his allies of conducting "an illegitimate influence operation targeting the Israeli public," claiming its purpose was to delay the publication of the results and undermine the legitimacy of the newly elected Knesset.

Israeli political commentator Amit Segal also cautioned against assuming the allegations would lead to the cancellation of election results.

"The likelihood of the entire election being invalidated is extremely slim, given the time constraints," Segal wrote on X. He suggested the developments could instead intensify discussions about a unity government or another election.

Meanwhile, Democrats party leader Yair Golan urged opposition leaders to move quickly toward forming a new government.

"The people have spoken. Sixty-seven seats demanded change," Golan wrote Thursday on X, adding that he intended to spend the day meeting with political partners and coalition negotiators. "I intend to leave no stone unturned, act in every possible way and do everything necessary to fulfill the voters' will," he added.

The comments underscored the central question emerging from the election: whether parties united in their opposition to Netanyahu can overcome their differences, particularly over cooperation with Arab lawmakers.

Another possibility is a national unity coalition involving Netanyahu's Likud and Eisenkot's Yashar party, potentially excluding the Arab parties and Netanyahu's far-right allies.

Such an arrangement could also align with the preferences of figures close to President Donald Trump, who publicly endorsed Netanyahu ahead of the election.

According to Ynet diplomatic correspondent Itamar Eichner, sources close to Trump said the president wants to ensure that far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir is excluded from the next Israeli government, with Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich potentially excluded as well.

A separate Ynet report said Trump associates had contacted Israeli political figures to assess the prospects for a unity government and expressed a preference for a stable coalition without Ben-Gvir.

Trump himself has not publicly endorsed a specific unity arrangement.

Asked Wednesday by Axios whether he would become involved in efforts to establish a Netanyahu-led unity government, Trump said, "I will take a look."

A unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot would face substantial obstacles. Eisenkot repeatedly pledged during the campaign not to join a Netanyahu-led government, while Netanyahu's far-right partners have warned against efforts to exclude them.

The ultra-Orthodox parties present another potential route to a parliamentary majority. Netanyahu's projected 53 seats include 14 held by Shas and United Torah Judaism, which have traditionally aligned with him.

Those 14 seats, combined with Eisenkot's projected 48-seat opposition bloc, would mathematically produce a 62-seat majority. But such an arrangement would face major disagreements over military conscription, as Eisenkot has pledged to expand mandatory service to ultra-Orthodox men, while the religious parties have sought to preserve exemptions for yeshiva students.

Political divisions within Eisenkot's own bloc would present additional obstacles to such a coalition.

For now, the foreign interference allegations remain under investigation, while the election results continue to show Netanyahu's existing coalition without the parliamentary majority required to govern on its own.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addresses the Knesset as President Donald Trump and Amir Ohana, speaker of the Knesset, listen, Oct. 13, 2025, in Jerusalem. (Chip Somodevilla/Pool via AP)

Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed, a process that could take weeks or longer.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Healey’s budget paves way for ‘brutal’ spending review next year, warns IFS
excerpt:
Thinktank says chancellor has given himself a mountain to climb after ducking big decisions in low-key speech

John Healey has paved the way for a “brutal” spending review next year after his budget f...
body_text:
Thinktank says chancellor has given himself a mountain to climb after ducking big decisions in low-key speech

John Healey has paved the way for a “brutal” spending review next year after his budget failed to cover a £28bn shortfall in the public finances needed to avoid a return to austerity, according to Britain’s leading tax and spending experts.

A day after his address to the Commons, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the chancellor had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking several big decisions in his debut tax and spending statement.

After his low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, the thinktank said Healey had left plans for overall departmental spending across the rest of the parliament broadly unchanged in cash terms.

But as the war in the Middle East fuels a surge in inflation – raising the cost of delivering public services – the chancellor has in effect pencilled in large cuts in the run-up to the next general election.

Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP.

“It effectively implies that some public services will see real-terms cuts in next year’s spending review,” she said.

With Labour having promised there would be no return to austerity, and as Andy Burnham’s government prepares for the next election, she said it appeared extremely unlikely that Healey would follow through with such cuts.

“A clear short-term risk with the chancellor’s choices is that next year – with low headroom and a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments – we see another season of damaging speculation about tax rises,” she said.

In his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, Healey raised taxes on banks and landlords to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock emanating from the Middle East war.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – allowing a hit to the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drives up the UK government’s borrowing costs.

Faced with grim forecasts for household living standards and growth in the British economy, the IFS said it was a “reasonable choice” for the chancellor to allow for a modest reduction in headroom.

However, his deferral of some important decisions to next year’s spending review prompted the thinktank to criticise his plans for meeting the fiscal rules, because they in effect relied on him cutting public spending or announcing tax increases that he had yet to prepare the public for.

“My concern is not that it would be impossible to deliver the implied cuts to other services – that could be done. But I’m sceptical that this government would be willing to do it,” Miller said.

title: UK social media ban may lock out more than 100,000 teenagers without ID
excerpt:
Watchdog says under-16 ban may affect older teenagers without passport or licence, and that ‘motivated children’ will skirt restrictions

More than 100,000 British teenagers risk being locked out of s...
body_text:
Watchdog says under-16 ban may affect older teenagers without passport or licence, and that ‘motivated children’ will skirt restrictions

More than 100,000 British teenagers risk being locked out of social media if they do not have a passport or driving licence when an under-16 ban is introduced next year.

Ofcom, the UK’s online watchdog, said about 150,000 16- to 17-year-olds do not own a passport or driving licence, which are likely to be needed to access age-restricted platforms.

The Australia-style ban on under-16s accessing social media services, including Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, is due to come into force next spring.

The head of Ofcom, Melanie Dawes, said “motivated children” would seek to bypass the restrictions, as has happened in Australia.

On Thursday, Ofcom published an assessment of age verification measures that could underpin the ban, outlining four “highly effective” methods: checking a person’s official ID against a live selfie, a bank verifying an account holder’s age, an official digital ID service like the Young Scot card, or estimating someone’s age via a selfie.

However, the watchdog said a form of official ID would probably be needed as a “backstop” for other methods, such as facial age estimation, which could be inaccurate by several years. Ofcom said a cohort of 16- to 17-year-olds could miss out as a result.

“This means that people without a form of photo ID will likely need to take steps to obtain one to access age-restricted services,” the regulator said.

More than nine out of 10 Britons over 16 have passports or driving licences.

Facial age estimation has been a popular measure for enforcing over-18 access to pornographic websites in the UK, which have been subject to stringent age checks since last year, indicating that this method will be used by social media plaforms as well.

The UK government has not confirmed which platforms will be affected by the ban but it is expected to cover the same sites as in Australia. Those are: Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Reddit, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube.

In March, Australia’s eSafety commissioner said a “substantial proportion” of under-16s had flouted the ban since it was imposed in December last year. A survey of 900 Australian parents found 31% said their children still had one or more social media accounts after the ban, compared with 49% before the laws.

Ofcom’s chief executive acknowledged the risk of evasion and said the ban would be a “huge cultural shift for the UK”.

“We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions – just like alcohol laws can’t completely eradicate underage drinking – but there’ll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk,” said Dawes. “This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it’ll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play.”

The government is expected to introduce regulations confirming the ban by the end of the year, with Ofcom also opening a consultation on the best age verification methods before issuing official guidance on which measures to adopt.

title: Damascus, Amman contradict each other on attack that killed civilians
excerpt:
Public anger in Syria has threatened to boil over following disagreements between Amman and Damascus over Jordanian attacks on the southern Syrian regions of Deraa and Suwayda on Monday evening.

Jord...
body_text:
Public anger in Syria has threatened to boil over following disagreements between Amman and Damascus over Jordanian attacks on the southern Syrian regions of Deraa and Suwayda on Monday evening.

Jordan said its air force had killed more than 20 ISIL (ISIS) fighters in retaliatory strikes on what it called “dens of terrorist organisations in southern Syria”, linked to suspects accused of being behind last week’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the kingdom, which was claimed by the group.

But the next day, anger mounted in Syria as images spread of a slain grandmother and her three grandchildren.

While Jordan has launched attacks on Syria in the past, including assaults that led to civilian casualties, this latest episode seems to have captured public anger.

“The anger also reflects an expectation that the authorities in Damascus should now be able to protect Syrians and demand answers when they are killed or harmed,” Navvar Saban, a researcher in security and military affairs at the Arab Center for Contemporary Syrian Studies, told Al Jazeera.

“If people feel Damascus is more concerned with protecting the relationship with the Jordanians than accountability, some of the anger could turn inward.”

Monday’s attack reportedly came in response to the assault on a Greek Orthodox church that killed nine people and wounded at least 34 others in the village of Hamoud in the Karak governorate, about 120km (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.

Jordanian authorities said the attack was carried out by “extremist terrorists”.

Jordan’s King Abdullah II promised to respond with an “iron fist”.

“Jordan has absorbed many terrorist attacks before, but this one was especially brazen given the Christian church and the nature of the event being targeted,” Sean Yom, an expert on Jordan at Temple University in the United States, told Al Jazeera.

“Because of its unprecedented nature, explicitly targeting a protected Christian minority in the tribal heartland of Karak, the government instantly felt popular demands to show results from the investigation and arrest of the perpetrators. This pressure to be responsive is especially acute right now, because security and policing remain core strengths of the Jordanian state.”

Jordanian authorities arrested three men connected to the attack on the church on Monday. That evening, Jordan also launched the attack on southern Syria, which it said was carried out in coordination with authorities in Damascus.

But Damascus has contradicted that account.

The Syrian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement that it had informed Jordan of its “complete reservation” over the attacks, and said they took place “without prior coordination or notification with the Syrian side”. An official described the strikes as “treacherous”.

“Both governments have something to defend politically,” Saban said. “Amman wants to show that it acted against a serious threat through legitimate security channels. On the other hand, Damascus cannot afford to appear to have approved an operation that killed Syrian families. The investigation needs to establish who communicated with whom, when, and about which target. Until then, I would avoid either assuming Syria secretly approved everything or treating the coordination as a simple misunderstanding.”

The family’s bodies were recovered after they were killed by the Jordanian strike on a tent in the village of al-Taff, in the Lajat area of northeastern Deraa province. Syria’s civil defence said three other family members were wounded in the attack.

Meanwhile, in the al-Shayah farms near Nassib, in the Deraa countryside, an 80-year-old man named Riyad Karrad was also killed by a strike. Another man named Mutlaq Abu al-Khalil, 60, was killed in Shuhayb, in Suwayda’s northern countryside.

Syrian customs authorities closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Tuesday, before reopening it to passenger and commercial traffic on Wednesday.

Jordan has launched several air strikes on Syria since 2023. It says those strikes generally target arms or drug smugglers.

Under the regime of former President Bashar al-Assad, southern Syria became the site of cross-border drug smuggling, including the stimulant captagon. Some of those operations are believed to have continued after the fall of the Assad regime. At times, the Jordanian strikes have killed civilians, such as a January 2024 attack that Human Rights Watch said killed women and children.

Since the fall of the regime in December 2024, relations between Amman and Damascus have been lukewarm, though slowly improving. Analysts say this is down to shared interests.

“Syria needs healthy trading and commercial partners like Jordan, and Jordan wants Syria to become more secure and coherent for three reasons,” Yom said.

“A strong and friendly Syria can accept more repatriated refugees from Jordan, where there are still hundreds of thousands. It can also help seal the porous border and prevent arms and drug smuggling activities along their shared frontier. And lastly, a stronger allied Syria helps Jordan resist Israel’s creeping annexation, including the West Bank as well as more parts of Syria and Lebanon. So both have mutual interests tied to their sovereignty in maintaining good relations.”

Amman was also the site of a July 2025 trilateral agreement signing between Syria, the US and Jordan aimed at resolving internal disputes over violence in Suwayda.

“Only days before the strike, the two foreign ministers were discussing a strategic partnership and preparing another meeting of their High Coordination Council that is a significant investment in the relationship,” Saban said. “My expectation is that this is a serious strain rather than a rupture. Both governments have strong reasons to keep cooperation over the border, armed groups smuggling, etc. But this incident raises an uncomfortable question for Damascus.”

For its part, Syria’s Foreign Ministry condemned the strikes as a violation of the country’s sovereignty but seemed to indicate relations with Amman would continue to be strengthened. It said Damascus is coordinating with ⁠Amman to establish a joint security committee to strengthen border security and prevent similar incidents.

In the meantime, Saban said that regardless of coordination with Damascus, accountability is needed to subside public anger.

“Even if an investigation established that Damascus approved some part of the operation, that would not explain why those people were killed or remove the need for accountability,” he said. “Ultimately, the families deserve a specific answer about the strike that killed their relatives, their friends, their family. Syrians need to understand why their families got killed.”

Cappadocia is a popular tourist destination known for its distinctive rock formations, known as fairy chimneys (file image)

At least two people have been killed after a rock formation collapsed at a tourist site in Turkey's historical region of Cappadocia, local media is reporting.

One of the formations, known as "fairy chimneys", reportedly collapsed at the popular Göreme Open Air Museum.

Ambulances and rescue teams have been deployed to the area, and a search and rescue operation is now under way.

The cause of Thursday's incident was not immediately known, however local media reports there had been heavy rain in the region.

This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17bn in major grocery delivery consolidation
excerpt:
Acquisition will supercharge DoorDash’s grocery delivery, ‘one of the hardest things to get right online’, CEO says

DoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17bn acquisition that will supercharge its ...
body_text:
Acquisition will supercharge DoorDash’s grocery delivery, ‘one of the hardest things to get right online’, CEO says

DoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17bn acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business.

DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said.

Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the US and Canada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” – who are independent contractors – completed 338m orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14bn.

DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3bn orders last year using a network of 9m independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73bn.

DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.

The partnership with one of the nation’s largest grocery chains expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 US Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco .

Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said the acquisition will combine Instacart’s expertise in grocery with DoorDash’s expertise in logistics and delivery.

“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” Xu said in a statement. “Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”

DoorDash’s aggressive market-share gains have hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on US delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash’s share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats’ share held steady at just under 20%.

It’s not yet clear what the deal will mean for some partnerships. Instacart offers delivery from Walmart, for example, but DoorDash stopped providing Walmart delivery in 2022.

title: Israel election results live: count of absentee ballots under way as coalition talks set to begin
excerpt:
With the final count unlikely to shift results significantly, experts say Gadi Eisenkot’s hopes of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu rest on his willingness to work with Palestinian parties

Full report: C...
body_text:
With the final count unlikely to shift results significantly, experts say Gadi Eisenkot’s hopes of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu rest on his willingness to work with Palestinian parties

Full report: Coalition talks loom in Israel

Analysis: Israel’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalition

Hello and welcome to our continuing coverage of the Israeli election.

With 91% of votes now counted, the current results show prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc projected to receive 53 seats, with the grouping of his opponent Gadi Eisenkot on 48 and the Palestinian parties on track to receive a record 19 seats.

The final tally of absentee ballots is not expected to significantly shift the results, and with no grouping managing to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, Israel could be in for weeks of uncertainty, as both sides try to gather enough support to form a government.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s bloc, has told Israeli media that he will meet leaders on Thursday for coalition talks. According to the Times of Israel, he will hold talks with Eisenkot, the leading opposition candidate and chair of the Yashar party, and Yair Lapid, the number-two in the opposition B’Yachad party.

This would mark the official start of coalition talks, and Golan has been the only opposition leader so far backing working with the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, voiced hope that the country could avoid a second election. “We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” said Herzog, who is tasked with determining which candidate to tap to form a government, urging parties to keep “an open mind”.

Israel’s future hangs in the balance after it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s historic elections. Indeed, Gadi Eisenkot and his allies face a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.

Yousef Jabareen, head of the Arab-majority Joint List, said the Israeli public had voted for new leadership and “anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu’s blood-soaked government will have to talk to us”. He told AFP that while he was willing to cooperate with an opposition-led government to unseat Netanyahu, he was not open to joining such a coalition outright. The ad hoc support of Palestinian lawmakers could enable Eisenkot to maintain a minority government, although few observers believe such an arrangement would survive for long.

Israel’s Central Elections Committee said it had received a Likud party complaint alleging that Arab parties had compromised election integrity and would examine the claims as part of its routine post-election review. Netanyahu’s party responded to partial election results showing Arab-led parties could play a king-making role in forming a new government by accusing them – without evidence – of “stealing” the election and demanding that the police and Shin Bet security service investigate the allegations.

UN rights chief Volker Turk has said that he hopes the next Israeli government will “change course massively” and respect international law. “The message is: don’t continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that’s what we have frankly seen in the current environment,” Turk told reporters in New York. He added: “Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them, and I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively.”

Israeli news website Ynet is reporting that just over 29,000 of the absentee ballots have been counted so far, out of an estimated 500,000.

According to Ynet, Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is leading among these ballots, with 18.5% of the votes of far. The Together alliance of Naftali Bennet and Yair Lapid comes in second with 15.6%, while Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar is third, with 14.8%.

The absentee ballots are afforded to people unable to return to their registered polling stations on election day. They include many in the IDF, as well as diplomats, prisoners and people in hospital.

Experts say that the final tally of the absentee ballots is unlikely to significantly shift the current seat projection.

Yousef Jabareen, the leader of the Joint List – which represents a number of Israeli Arab parties – has told the ⁠Reuters news agency his party will seek to use its projected 11 seats “to facilitate getting rid of Netanyahu’s government and hopefully help to change the political situation in Israel.”

Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc is currently projected to receive 48 seats, well short of the 61 needed to form a majority government, but many in his bloc have ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties which are projected to win 19 seats in total.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, and a junior partner in Eisenkot’s bloc, has backed the idea of working with the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel. But he is so far the only opposition leader making that call.

Jabareen said the Joint ​List could not join an Eisenkot-led government because of its support for Israel’s ‌military campaign in Gaza and occupation of southern Lebanon. But ‌he has left open the possibility of bolstering Eisenkot’s bloc from the outside, propping up a minority government through confidence votes.

double quotation markWe have our demands to protect our community, to ‌advance the rights of our community and to promote equality for our community.”

The other main Palestinian party, Ra’am, is led by Mansour Abbas, who joined Naftali Bennett’s government in 2021, the first time an independent Arab party had entered an Israeli coalition. That government collapsed after 18 months, partly because of disagreements over the occupied West Bank.

Abbas has said he would ‌join an Eisenkot-led government. Speaking to Israeli media after voting wrapped on Tuesday night, Abbas said

double quotation markI believe we can overcome the difficulties … and I think that most voters for the [Eisenkot] bloc do want to see a government with the Ra’am party.”

Throughout the elections campaign, Israel’s far-right demonized Palestinian citizens of Israel and branded Palestinian political participation as a threat to ​the state.

Eisenkot himself ruled out forming a government with Palestinian parties during the campaign, citing what he called a lack of shared values, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state. However Abbas has claimed that senior members of Eisenkot’s bloc discussed ​a possible deal with him even before the election.

Ameer Fakhoury, a political sociologist at Jerusalem’s Van Leer Institute, said that Palestinian votes may block Netanyahu and make an alternative government possible.

double quotation markThe Jewish opposition may need Palestinian ⁠votes while refusing Palestinian partners. That is the central paradox.”

Israel’s ⁠currency, stocks and bonds came under ⁠pressure on Wednesday after initial election ​results showed prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc performing better-than-expected but falling short of a parliamentary majority.

With 91% of votes tallied, Israeli media project Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc could win 53 seats, ahead ⁠of the 48 forecast for rival Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc but short of the 61 needed for a majority.

On Wednesday the shekel weakened more ⁠than 2%, on course for its worst day since the aftermath of the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks and erasing Tuesday’s ​gains, when high voter turnout had raised expectations of a change in government.

Tel ‌Aviv’s key benchmark stock index was ‌down 2.5%, its worst performance in more than four months.

Opinion polls ahead of the election showing Eisenkot in ‌the lead had helped gains, with some investors expecting a change in government to improve relations with western allies.

“Israel’s financial markets have reacted negatively to the result,” said William Jackson, chief emerging ‌markets economist at Capital Economics. He said the initial results offered Netanyahu more paths to remain in power, though any government that emerged was unlikely to be robust.

double quotation markThe next government will probably be fragile.”

If neither Netanyahu nor ​Eisenkot can form a government, Israel could be facing another election, with Netanyahu remaining at the helm of a caretaker government in the meantime.

Israel’s left-leaning newspaper Haaretz has published an editorial calling on the country’s opposition bloc to form a government with the Palestinian parties.

With the combined number of Knesset seats for Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc and the grouping of Palestinian parties projected to be 67, the paper writes that Netanyahu’s government has “lost substantial support since the last round of elections.”

double quotation markThe figures clearly point to an unprecedented achievement by the Arab community, which voted en masse for political partnership with Jews. Despite the challenges and reservations about voting, and amidst a particularly racist incitement campaign, a record 19 Knesset seats loudly and clearly declare: We are an inseparable part of this country.”

The editorial goes on to say that there is reason to believe that the leaders of Eisenkot’s change bloc will discard these “19 Knesset seats simply because they belong to Arab voters.”

double quotation markThis would be a slap in the face to the citizens who went to the polls in droves to vote for integration.”

Hours before the final results from Israel’s elections were in, several things were clear. Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition had lost its mandate, and the opposition had a firm majority.

But most of Israel’s Jewish opposition ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties, in the course of a racist election campaign in which Netanyahu painted Palestinian citizens as an enemy inside the state.

The self-imposed ban on a broader opposition alliance, if it holds, offers Netanyahu the prospect of turning his defeat into another term in office – or at least a prolonged mandate as caretaker prime minister and perhaps another round of elections.

This confected barrier to unseating Netanyahu became the focus of Israeli media and analysts. “No Clear Government” announced the newspaper Israel Hayom. “Road to Unity Government Has Been Paved”, read an article on Channel 12.

Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, attacked that framing. “Netanyahu lost. I know how to count,” he said in a statement calling for a government with Palestinians, who make up about 20% of Israel’s population.

“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said. “We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Arab citizens of Israel.”

While Palestinian-led parties do not describe themselves as Zionist, neither do some of the ultra-Orthodox groups who are a key part of Netanyahu’s current coalition.

A survey taken as polls closed on election day showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with the Palestinian-led Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu, political psychology researcher Eran Halperin said.

But opposition leaders were silent on Wednesday, as they apparently tried to balance their desire to unseat Netanyahu with promises against working with Palestinians.

Former general Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the biggest opposition party, has not directly ruled out governing with Palestinians but laid out conditions that made it politically impossible for them to join a coalition.

Palestinians have been clearer about their priorities. “We are ready and prepared to pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government,” Yousef Jabareen, leader of the larger Joint List, said on Wednesday. “The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership.”

Israel’s elections committee has said it began counting absentee ballots at 1am local time. That count is expected to last until Thursday evening, with an estimated 500,000 ballots from military personnel and diplomats to be tallied up.

They are not expected to significantly change the results.

Under Israeli electoral law, each voter is assigned a specific polling station and can only vote at that station. However in exceptional circumstances, some voters are allowed to cast their ballot at special polling stations they are not registered at. Among those afforded this exception are soldiers stationed at IDF bases, diplomats working abroad, prisoners and prison guards and people in hospital.

These absentee ballots are transported directly to the Knesset where they undergo a series of checks before they are counted, which is why they arrive in the final count much later.

Hello and welcome to our continuing coverage of the Israeli election.

With 91% of votes now counted, the current results show prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc projected to receive 53 seats, with the grouping of his opponent Gadi Eisenkot on 48 and the Palestinian parties on track to receive a record 19 seats.

The final tally of absentee ballots is not expected to significantly shift the results, and with no grouping managing to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, Israel could be in for weeks of uncertainty, as both sides try to gather enough support to form a government.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s bloc, has told Israeli media that he will meet leaders on Thursday for coalition talks. According to the Times of Israel, he will hold talks with Eisenkot, the leading opposition candidate and chair of the Yashar party, and Yair Lapid, the number-two in the opposition B’Yachad party.

This would mark the official start of coalition talks, and Golan has been the only opposition leader so far backing working with the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, voiced hope that the country could avoid a second election. “We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” said Herzog, who is tasked with determining which candidate to tap to form a government, urging parties to keep “an open mind”.

Israel’s future hangs in the balance after it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s historic elections. Indeed, Gadi Eisenkot and his allies face a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.

Yousef Jabareen, head of the Arab-majority Joint List, said the Israeli public had voted for new leadership and “anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu’s blood-soaked government will have to talk to us”. He told AFP that while he was willing to cooperate with an opposition-led government to unseat Netanyahu, he was not open to joining such a coalition outright. The ad hoc support of Palestinian lawmakers could enable Eisenkot to maintain a minority government, although few observers believe such an arrangement would survive for long.

Israel’s Central Elections Committee said it had received a Likud party complaint alleging that Arab parties had compromised election integrity and would examine the claims as part of its routine post-election review. Netanyahu’s party responded to partial election results showing Arab-led parties could play a king-making role in forming a new government by accusing them – without evidence – of “stealing” the election and demanding that the police and Shin Bet security service investigate the allegations.

UN rights chief Volker Turk has said that he hopes the next Israeli government will “change course massively” and respect international law. “The message is: don’t continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that’s what we have frankly seen in the current environment,” Turk told reporters in New York. He added: “Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them, and I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively.”

title: Europe’s wealth gap: Older households eight times richer than young ones
excerpt:
Student protests that began in September in France have spread to more than 11 European countries as anger rises over high rents and fuel prices and cuts to public services.

Many young protesters sai...
body_text:
Student protests that began in September in France have spread to more than 11 European countries as anger rises over high rents and fuel prices and cuts to public services.

Many young protesters said they no longer expect to be better off than their parents, and household wealth data show a wide gap between generations.

Across the eurozone and two other European countries, households headed by someone under 35 have a median net wealth of about 25,000 euros ($27,870) while those headed by 55- to 64-year-olds are worth about 208,000 euros ($231,882), more than eight times as much, according to the European Central Bank’s (ECB’s) 2023 Household Finance and Consumption Survey.

In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera compares wealth by age groups across 22 European countries and looks at how much more expensive life has become since 2000.

The Household Finance and Consumption Survey, run by the ECB and national central banks since 2010, tracks household wealth and debt in the eurozone, the Czech Republic and Hungary.

It measures net wealth, which includes property, cars, valuables and savings, minus debts. Under-35s hold just 2.8 percent of all household wealth in the 22 countries while 55- to 64-year-olds hold the largest share at 24 percent.

In Finland, under-35s hold 0.8 percent of household wealth, the lowest share of any country surveyed, while over-55s hold more than 71 percent. Young people’s shares are also small in Ireland (1.4 percent), Austria (1.6 percent), Greece (1.8 percent) and Germany (2 percent).

Rising housing costs mean many young people cannot afford what their parents or grandparents could.

Wealth is more evenly spread in Central and Eastern Europe. In Lithuania, under-35s hold 13.2 percent, against 15.9 percent for 55- to 64-year-olds. Their share is 12.3 percent in Croatia, 10.1 percent in Slovakia and 9.8 percent in Estonia. Malta, at 11.1 percent, is the exception outside the two regions.

The graphic below shows how household wealth is split between age groups in each country surveyed.

“What we’ve seen is actually a very strong increase in housing prices both in terms of the rental market as well as the ownership market,” Evelyn Astor of the European Social Observatory told Al Jazeera’s Counting the Cost programme.

“All of this is also reinforcing a sense of inequality because ultimately ordinary families are struggling to pay their rents or be able to purchase their homes whereas wealthy people with capital are able to make rather significant investments in the European housing market,” she said.

Prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, energy, transport and household bills, have risen by 67.2 percent in the eurozone, Hungary and the Czech Republic since 2000.

Of the countries in our chart, Hungary has seen the steepest rise with prices more than tripling, according to Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics agency. Its harmonised index of consumer prices is the EU’s official measure of how much everyday goods and services cost.
