The chart below shows how consumer prices have changed in each country since 2000 with prices in 2000 set at 100 on the index.

Eastern European countries have seen the sharpest increases – particularly since 2022 when Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began – because many relied heavily on Russian energy supplies.

Prices rose by about 2 percent a year on average until 2022 when annual inflation in the EU hit 9.2 percent.

The surge was driven mainly by energy costs. Inflation has since eased, but the price rises of the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine have not reversed.

title: Chelsea beat Liverpool 6-5 on penalties to reach League Cup quarterfinals
excerpt:
Liverpool beat Chelsea 6-5 in a dramatic penalty shootout to reach the English League Cup quarterfinals.

In a clash between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso, it was the Liverpool manag...
body_text:
Liverpool beat Chelsea 6-5 in a dramatic penalty shootout to reach the English League Cup quarterfinals.

In a clash between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso, it was the Liverpool manager who took the bragging rights in the last-16 tie at Anfield on Wednesday.

A 1-1 draw in normal time set the stage for the shootout as Chelsea’s Morgan Rogers netted from the spot, only for Cody Gakpo to equalise with a penalty of his own just before half-time.

Chelsea’s Valentin Barco hit the post in the shootout before Liverpool’s Kostas Tsimikas wasted a chance to win it when he blazed over.

Ryan Gravenberch was denied by Chelsea keeper Mike Penders, but Giorgi Mamardashvili saved Emmanuel Emegha’s kick to keep Liverpool alive.

After Joe Gomez scored for Liverpool, Blues defender Wesley Fofana miscued into the Kop as the hosts advanced.

It was former Liverpool midfielder Alonso’s third defeat in his three visits to Anfield as a manager, following losses with Bayer Leverkusen in 2024 and Real Madrid in 2025.

In their debut campaigns at Liverpool, Jurgen Klopp and Arne Slot both reached the League Cup final, and Iraola is on course to follow in their footsteps with the 10-time winners of the competition.

“We are really happy. Three wins at home in a row is very important. We were struggling at home in the league but now we go against Arsenal on Sunday,” said Iraola, who will face his former club Bournemouth in the last eight.

Alonso added: “Every time you reach the penalties, someone will feel it is harsh to go out of the competition.

“We were showing a good level and this is what it takes to come to these stadiums. The Premier League is the main focus.”

Alonso made just four changes to the Chelsea side that lost 2-0 at home to Tottenham on Saturday, while Iraola made seven changes from Liverpool’s 2-0 win against Brighton on Sunday.

Rogers put Chelsea in front with a 40th-minute penalty after Gravenberch clattered into Moises Caicedo.

But Liverpool were level three minutes later with a penalty of their own as Gakpo converted from the spot following Fofana’s handball.

title: Russia’s alleged sabotage campaign in Europe raises fears of escalation
excerpt:
Russia appears to have escalated its shadow war in Europe this year.

European officials have alleged that Russian fighter planes have veered inside Polish, Lithuanian and Estonian airspace, testing r...
body_text:
Russia appears to have escalated its shadow war in Europe this year.

European officials have alleged that Russian fighter planes have veered inside Polish, Lithuanian and Estonian airspace, testing reaction times. Suspected Russian drones have been downed over Poland, Finland and the Baltic states.

And Moscow has been accused of bringing trouble to the Black Sea.

In two separate operations in October, Ukraine accused Russia of using aerial and surface drones to sink four cargo ships just outside the territorial waters of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member, in an apparent warning that Ukraine’s grain exports through NATO territorial waters may not be safe for long.

Russia and Belarus have also been accused of trying to destabilise the Baltic states by making their borders appear fluid.

“Masked and most likely armed individuals on the Belarus side of the border escorted and attempted to push groups of illegal migrants into Latvia,” Ieva Cesniece, Latvia’s ambassador to Greece, told Al Jazeera. “Those individuals expressed threats to Latvian soldiers and border guards. On the same day in a separate incident, masked individuals crossed into Latvian territory and carried out deliberate sabotage. Bborder infrastructure was damaged, and surveillance equipment was removed.”

Latvian media have reported that asylum seekers and undocumented migrants who tried to run back from the Latvian border were rounded up by Belarusian authorities and pushed towards Latvia again.

Cesniece drew a direct link between the Russian war in Ukraine and its shadow war in Europe.

“The weaker Russia appears in Ukraine, the more it tests our resilience, trying to weaken NATO and EU resolve and support for Ukraine,” she said.

As European governments warned of an imminent escalation of a Russian shadow war on the continent, experts said the bloc needs to do more to deter Russia as well as defend itself.

“Protecting critical infrastructure, strengthening intelligence services and preventing attacks are essential, but deterrence is about more than preventing the next incident,” said Olena Tregub, cofounder and head of Ukraine’s Independent Anti-Corruption Commission. “It is about convincing your adversary that continuing these operations will become too costly. And I’m not sure Russia currently sees those costs as sufficiently high.”

As an expert on following money trails, she believes European governments have not done enough to identify the networks behind operations, expose the command structures, disrupt their financing and logistics, and impose consequences.

Meanwhile, Russia’s war is going badly on the ground.

Two Ukrainian counteroffensives have blunted Moscow’s main thrust to capture the eastern region of Donetsk and in effect have deprived it of any territorial gains this year.

Since a failed August operation to blow up cargo planes at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport, which was later verified by the European Commission as a Russian operation, warnings of further escalation have multiplied.

Czech spy chief Michal Koudelka warned in September that Russia might attempt a military attack on a NATO member in “months, not years”.

Days later, Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova openly declared that European defence industries supplying Ukraine were legitimate targets for Moscow.

“Russia does not necessarily distinguish between the military capabilities Ukraine uses on the battlefield and the European infrastructure that makes those capabilities possible,” Tregub told Al Jazeera.

“From Moscow’s perspective, a factory producing military equipment for Ukraine, a logistics hub transporting that equipment or a company providing critical technology can all become potential targets of disruption.”

This month, representatives of five EU intelligence agencies told the Financial Times that Russia was seeking to “kill” European defence bosses and target their supply chains.

That followed a report from a German newspaper, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, that Russia had planted incendiary devices in the offices of defence companies Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing in Munich. It also followed a report on the Politico news site in which EU security officials said Russia was planning to move beyond messaging and claim lives on European soil.

European officials have spoken of strengthening the resilience of their data centres, telecommunications, and other vulnerable networks and industries, but they have not spoken of retaliation.

From the Ukrainian point of view, though, Europe has been slow to see sabotage, manned and unmanned military operations, cyberattacks and information warfare as the early stages of a multidimensional war with Russia, and that failure of perception is itself a weakness.

“Where will he stop if he is currently testing all these drones against European countries, even NATO countries?” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked journalists on October 16, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin. “They are not talking about it very loudly yet. They don’t want escalation, … but you will talk very loudly when there are ballistic and cruise missiles and also thousands of drones.”

“Ukrainians don’t know about any war in Ukraine. They know about war in Europe,” said Oleksandr Danylyuk, a long-serving adviser to the Ukrainian Ministries of Defence and Foreign Affairs and now a Russian warfare expert with the Royal United Services Institute.

Like Zelenskyy and Tregub, he believes the lack of retaliation to its apparent hybrid war encourages Russia.

“Russians are limited right now only by their capabilities because they do whatever they want. There is no reaction,” he said.

He said he believes NATO needs to place more forward troops in the Baltic states to create “deterrence by denial” and to strengthen Ukraine.

Minna Alander, a leading European researcher in security and defence with the Center for European Policy Analysis, said denying Russians travel visas, carrying out retaliatory cyberattacks, further interdicting the Russian oil fleet and sanctioning Chinese suppliers of defence goods to Russia were all realistic retaliations Europe could impose immediately.

Danylyuk said money remains the most potent tool of deterrence.

“The most direct way to punish Russia is to actually increase support to Ukraine,” he told Al Jazeera. “Each time we detect Russian intelligence operations in Europe, we will increase combined support of Ukraine [maybe] 10 percent, 20 percent.”

Yet Ukraine’s allies are signalling the opposite, he observed.

The United States withdrew its military and financial support in January 2025 and recently placed the dependability of its satellite services in doubt. In France and Germany, the governments trail opposition leaders who want to stop aid to Ukraine.

Ukraine has performed better than many expected.

Since 2023, it has designed and built its own weapons and developed its own strategy to halt the Russian advance. It has punished Russia by striking oil installations and weapons factories deep inside its territory.

To reverse the tide of the war and reclaim its occupied territories, it is asking for more money, and it is asking it from the people providing the vast majority of it – Europe.

“Next year, the war will cost 155 billion euros [$170bn]), and we need at least 70 billion euros [$80bn] more from you,” Zelenskyy told the European Council on October 16.

“We could double or even triple the production of drones,” he said. “Just imagine how much more pressure we could put on Russia if we could do two or three times more.”

title: Cambodian police and soldiers helped guard abusive scam compounds, Amnesty alleges
excerpt:
Survivors tell rights group that serving officers who worked as guards administered electric shocks and beatings

Cambodian police and military officers worked as private security guards in scam compo...
body_text:
Survivors tell rights group that serving officers who worked as guards administered electric shocks and beatings

Cambodian police and military officers worked as private security guards in scam compounds where thousands were forced to work in the online fraud industry, according to a report by Amnesty International.

The global rights group alleged they worked for security companies as part of a system that enabled slavery and rape in the compounds, with some guards using electric batons to keep people trapped.

“For years, survivors of these nightmarish compounds described encountering members of the Cambodian military or police inside. These accounts could not be independently verified – until now,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general.

Based on 151 survivor interviews, visits to 82 scam compounds and social media videos from dozens of guard accounts showing them in company uniform, the investigation said it could link illicit operations with five well-connected private security companies.

“Our findings begin to expose the long-suspected links between Cambodia’s billion-dollar criminal scamming networks and politically connected figures who have remained largely beyond scrutiny,” Callamard said.

“At the heart of these connections are security companies whose guards controlled compound exits, hunted down people who escaped and enforced compliance through fear and violence. Without them, this system of mass exploitation could not have functioned.”

Hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked into south-east Asia from across the world, according to the UN. In many cases, they have been lured by the promise of an office job and then forced to carry out online scams, targeting victims globally.

Among these is so-called pig butchering, a type of romance fraud where criminals build a fake relationship with a victim, slowly “fattening them up” before stealing their money.

The Amnesty report, titled Official Business: Security companies and authorities at scamming compounds in Cambodia, alleges that a company called Leap Somnang had the largest footprint and was linked to at least 15 compounds across eight provinces. Twelve survivors identified the company’s guards, uniforms or logo, the report says.

Amnesty alleges that Leap Somnang is believed to be controlled by Ban Sophat, who publicly served as its chair while also being a colonel in the armed forces. It provided photos it claimed showed him alongside Leap Somnang guards at two scamming compounds.

The rights group quoted a letter from Ban Sophat denying holding any ownership, director or management role in Leap Somnang, stating that he had “served as an adviser to the company owner”.

“The fact that I may appear in a photograph taken at a particular location does not mean that I have knowledge of, or involvement in, the activities or operations conducted there,” it cited him as saying.

Scam site survivors have described guards administering electric shocks and beatings, detaining people in “dark rooms” and standing guard while compound managers raped women.

Amnesty said it had identified more than 20 members of the military and police who were seen to have an active presence at the compounds, including working openly as guards.

With annual losses estimated at about $100bn – a sum that outstrips the GDP of several countries in the region – international pressure has grown on countries such as Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar to crack down. There are signs that some parts of the industry are moving to South Asia.

In July 2025, Cambodia launched its largest-ever crackdown on scam operations, promising to wipe out the criminal networks. Authorities claim to have shut down hundreds of scam centres, and Amnesty said the industry there was now “dormant”.

“Even if scamming compounds are dormant, our findings clearly show that the infrastructure of impunity has not been dismantled,” Callamard said. “Cambodia will not have ended this abusive industry until it has held to account those who staffed, managed, financed and protected this abusive system.”

Amnesty said it presented its findings to Cambodian authorities, and cited a response from the ministry of interior stating that it had, as part of its ongoing crackdowns, already disciplined 77 police officers, prosecuted six private security guards for using stun batons illegally and detained 17 military, police, and civil officials for colluding with criminals.

Authorities had sent 3,477 suspects to court, the letter says, citing a policy of “no tolerance, no exemption, and no retreat” to ensure Cambodia did not become a “haven or operating base for transnational criminal networks”.

Amnesty said it did not receive a response from Leap Somnang.

The Guardian has contacted Cambodia’s interior ministry, Ban Sophat and Leap Somnang for comment.

title: Angry Labour MPs urge leadership not to overrule energy secretary on Rosebank
excerpt:
Exclusive: Backbenchers voice alarm over ‘intolerable position’ faced by Miatta Fahnbulleh over oilfield decision

Furious Labour MPs have been lobbying the prime minister and chancellor not to overru...
body_text:
Exclusive: Backbenchers voice alarm over ‘intolerable position’ faced by Miatta Fahnbulleh over oilfield decision

Furious Labour MPs have been lobbying the prime minister and chancellor not to overrule the energy secretary should she decide to block the Rosebank oilfield.

MPs say they are alarmed at the cabinet splits that have emerged over the issue after sources told the Guardian that Miatta Fahnbulleh was minded to refuse environmental permission for the field.

Sources close to the chancellor, John Healey, have since made it clear he is in favour of the scheme, while some in government believe the prime minister, Andy Burnham, also wants it to go ahead.

Backbenchers worried about the environmental impact of the project are now urging their whips and Downing Street not to allow other ministers to intervene in Fahnbulleh’s decision.

Catherine Fookes, a Labour member of the energy select committee, said: “Approving Rosebank will blow a hole in our green credentials. A group of us is making it clear to leadership that this should be Miatta’s decision and I hope they listen.

“Labour MPs are really, really concerned about it – it would go against the thrust of our manifesto.”

Another MP said: “If Healey pushes through Rosebank, there will be blood. It’s economically shortsighted as well as politically explosive – they aren’t listening at all to the discomfort on the backbenches.”

Another commented: “Lots of us have raised this. I think the position Miatta has been put in by these briefings is intolerable.” Concerns are understood to also have been raised with Healey directly in budget meetings with MPs.

Fahnbulleh’s parliamentary aides have circulated a memo to MPs insisting she would have the final say on the proposals, after a number of MPs contacted them to raise concerns that she would be overruled.

“No decision has been made on Rosebank,” the memo said. “The energy secretary will consider all relevant factors in a case before reaching a decision.

“The energy secretary is the only decision maker and will consider all relevant factors as part of the quasi-judicial process. No other cabinet member or minister has any role in this decision and does not see the advice on it,” it added.

Burnham has promised to take a “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil drilling, calling the Jackdaw gasfield, which the government approved last week, “a bridge to the future”.

The prime minister insists the decision over Rosebank will be for Fahnbulleh alone to make.

But he prompted speculation about his support for the project on Wednesday, when he told the Commons: “Use of our reserves can support and accelerate a clean energy future, and that was very much the logic behind the decision that the government announced on Jackdaw last week.”

Many in government believe Fahnbulleh can approve the bigger Rosebank scheme without breaching the UK’s carbon commitments, in part because most of its oil would be exported.

The Guardian also revealed on Tuesday that the Treasury had already factored in tax revenues from the scheme, which are expected to hit about £500m by the end of this parliament.

Treasury officials said on Wednesday the money had been included in forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) since 2019, and that doing so would not prevent the energy secretary from blocking it.

The OBR said in its budget forecast on Wednesday: “The projection includes production from currently producing fields (including Jackdaw), and the North Sea Transition Authority’s estimate of production from development of new fields, which includes Rosebank, and from future discoveries.

“The forecast annual pace of decline [in oil and gas production] would be around 14% a year if there were no production from any new fields.”

The memo from Fahnbulleh’s aides added that decisions to score Rosebank as part of the forecast would be a decision for the OBR.

However, some Labour MPs believe the Treasury has been using aggressive tactics to strong-arm the energy department, with one describing the approach of No 11 as “macho bullshit”.

Clive Lewis, another Labour MP, said: “You cannot claim global climate leadership while approving new oilfields simply because you’ve already pencilled in the tax receipts. Tax ‘receipts’, as I understand it, that will be the operator’s estimate and not actual Treasury revenue.”

Analysis by Uplift, a campaign group, found that on the government’s and industry’s estimates, the tax take from Rosebank would probably be limited and could be outweighed by the tax breaks and incentives likely to be offered for the development and decommissioning of the fields.

Areeba Hamid, a co-executive director of Greenpeace UK, said: “Any tax revenues from this far-off field in a rapidly declining basin don’t just leave our public services at the hostage of future oil prices, they also leave taxpayers on the hook for the costs of decommissioning for decades to come. The truth is that approving new oil drilling in the North Sea will only add to the costs of climate impacts, costs not fully factored into forecasts such as those from the OBR. Any economist should be able to see that.”

MPs said there would be a significant parliamentary rebellion on Rosebank, unlike Jackdaw, where they were prepared to accept the argument to allow gas to be extracted for domestic consumption.

Fookes said: “The case was made for Jackdaw to some degree and we remained quite quiet over that. Rosebank, however, is a different issue.”

title: Neighbour of new Montenegro embassy in London sues council over impact on mental health
excerpt:
Case in Pimlico is latest instance of tensions between small countries seeking a space in capital and residents

It is not a classic neighbour-from-hell dispute, what with the protagonist inviting eve...
body_text:
Case in Pimlico is latest instance of tensions between small countries seeking a space in capital and residents

It is not a classic neighbour-from-hell dispute, what with the protagonist inviting everyone over for evening drinks and canapés. But the sudden conversion of a five-bedroom family home in Pimlico, central London, into the embassy of Montenegro has triggered a neighbourhood row that has gone all the way to the desk of a high court judge.

The first stirrings of trouble came when one resident argued in a submission to the council this spring that the new embassy’s “flagpole and rather tacky-looking flag stick out like a sore thumb” among Cambridge Street’s Grade II-listed homes.

A second person, who described Montenegro’s red flag with gold border as “gaudy”, suggested the embassy was “out of keeping with the quietly dignified” whitewash late-Regency frontages designed by Thomas Cubitt.

Some of those critics, frustrated by the lack of planning application before the installation of the embassy flagpole and plaque, were somewhat placated when drinks were put on by the chargé d’affairs of the west Balkans state. “Perhaps it would have been diplomatic to have done that at the start,” one resident commented drily.

But the party did not convince everyone, and an involuntary nextdoor neighbour to the embassy has now taken matters to the courts.

Diana Simpson, 35, a Stanford graduate who lives with her parents on Cambridge Street, is suing Westminster city council. She is applying for judicial review and potential damages on the grounds that when the embassy did belatedly seek planning permission for its change of use and flagpole, the local authority failed to take into account the impact on her mental health of the arrival next door of Montenegro, a country that has been involved in recent scrapes with Russia.

Simpson, the daughter of a former US diplomat who has lived on the street for more than three decades, is in receipt of disability benefits after being diagnosed with clinical anxiety, long Covid and a functional neurological disorder. So unsettling has the arrival of the embassy been to Simpson that her nights are regularly affected, she claims in her statement of grounds.

She alleges: “I frequently feel the need to sleep in an alternative to my lifelong bedroom, to gain some marginal relief; sometimes pre-emptively, sometimes in the middle of the night when I cannot reason with my activated primal ‘fear’ brain response (for example, upon hearing a creak, and immediately fearing an intruder accessing my room from the embassy, despite knowing the possibility is very slim and that this response is mostly irrational).”

Citing breaches of the human rights and equality acts, Simpson has said she had considered whether it “remains tenable for me to continue to live in this house, which I had anticipated having the option of living in for the rest of my life”, adding that leaving would wrench her from a “local tight-knit community”.

Simpson told the Guardian she was confident in her case, which alleges the council failed to take into account her conditions, acted irrationally and delivered a flawed public consultation by having a closed mind to objections after the Foreign Office gave its permission.

In its defence statement, Westminster city council denies the allegations and writes: “There is no plausible interference with the claimant’s home or her private and family life.” The council is seeking a summary judgment without a hearing.

A spokesperson for Westminster City Council said: “Councils are legally required to take decisions in line with existing planning policy. It would not be appropriate to comment further at this stage.”

The case in front of Justice Mould for consideration is perhaps unusual but it has highlighted a more common clash between smaller countries – as they move their embassies due to rent hikes or landlords selling up – and the residents of some of London’s more affluent streets.

The US has its London home in an intimidating purpose-built 12-storey cube structure south of the Thames. But for most of the major nations the natural home is Belgravia or perhaps South Kensington, Knightsbridge and Mayfair. There is a tendency for the lower-tier states to want to be close to these luminaries but spend not quite the same sums on rent.

It is for that reason that Montenegro has alighted in Pimlico, near Victoria coach station, and the Turkmenistan embassy has recently opened in another adapted family home on Victoria Road, in Kensington but a telling 1.4 miles from the splendours of France’s home opposite the Natural History Museum.

The move by Turkmenistan has led to some rancour, too. “I cannot understand the lack of courtesy afforded to immediate neighbours,” submitted one local to a Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea consultation. “I will find out if anything untoward has taken place and, if so, further newspaper action might be necessary.”

The correspondent added of the house in which the embassy is now located, which is owned by Tengku Fahad, 32, the Eton-educated son of the late king of Malaysia, that another location should be found for Turkmenistan, a former Soviet republic in central Asia.

“I was quite happy with the late king of Malaysia [who] lived there and I believe the property is still owned by his son,” she wrote. “We had a family living there for four years who left a while ago for tax reasons but the house has not long been vacant … I have no doubt that they are very pleasant people but, however you bill it, I for one don’t feel totally safe and the idea that there be signage and a flag up leaves me speechless.”

When approached at her home, the complainant, who asked not to be named, said the Turkmens had turned out to be “actually quite quiet” and there had been no problems “so far”.

Risks of such local hostility and scrutiny appear to have led some nations to go another way. North Korea has for two decades had an embassy in something of a place of exile in a seven-bedroom 1920s home off the A406 in Ealing, west London.

Colin Flood, a retired solicitor who lives two doors down, said they never heard a peep from them. A workman renovating the house next to the North Korean delegation added: “They are lovely people – we tidied up their greenery at the front and hope to get more work. Lovely people.”

title: Why a Democratic win in US midterms could adversely affect Europe
excerpt: The United States midterm elections appear stacked against the ruling Republicans, with polls suggesting the Democrats average an eight-point lead in the House of Representatives and the Senate. But i...
body_text:
The United States midterm elections appear stacked against the ruling Republicans, with polls suggesting the Democrats average an eight-point lead in the House of Representatives and the Senate. But if Democrats take one or both houses, could they affect upcoming elections in Europe?

Not fundamentally, analysts and observers have told Al Jazeera, but besides a welcome improvement in transatlantic relations, they point to two potentially adverse effects.

First, a Democratic Congress might produce complacency among Europeans regarding their own far-right movements.

Second, it might spur US President Donald Trump to raise pressure on Ukraine to make a deal it doesn’t want to make with Russia.

“If the Democrats win the House, let alone both houses, it will be read as, ‘you see democracies bounce back,’” said Catherine Fieschi, a nonresident scholar at Carnegie Europe, specialising in European far-right politics. It would introduce “the idea that these things don’t mean the advent of a fascist regime”, she said.

From her vantage point in Paris, Fieschi said she imagines a Democratic win leading to “a whole discussion about whether we should fear a Marine Le Pen election as much as some people say we should, or whether, in fact, it’s swings and roundabouts and, at some point, if people are really bad and really incompetent, then elections right the way,” she said.

French right-wing politician Marine Le Pen is currently leading the field in polling for presidential elections scheduled for April 18, with surveys indicating she has about 34 percent of the popular vote.

There is a precedent for the complacency Fieschi alludes to. In June 2025, the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), a think tank, polled Europeans following Trump’s first six months in office. Clear majorities in Western Europe said the US political system was broken. In Eastern Europe, majorities said it was working well – though they were weighted towards right-wing voters.

Greek Migration Minister Thanos Plevris warned against giving too much credit to the US for what Europeans think and do, however.

He said he believes European public opinion hardened against asylum and economic migration independently, but the US marked the shift by expressing it more violently, with military deportation flights and armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents sweeping American cities.

“I think there was a European about-turn on migration. We saw this in Germany, which had a welcoming attitude [to refugees] for many years, and they went to a more controlled policy. All northern European governments saw societies change,” he told Al Jazeera.

“But the US provided a change in tone, from induction and integration and benefaction to deterrence, border protection, increased returns and consequences if asylum is denied. I do think that pivot played a role in Europe,” Plevris added.

Should French voters decide that the only way out is through electing Le Pen – “like some kind of strong medicine that would wake us up to what we might lose”, as Fieschi put it – they would have to contend with three controversial propositions – cutting French financial contributions to the European Union’s federal budget to pay for earlier retirement, cutting military aid to Ukraine and possibly leaving the single currency, the euro, in favour of a devalued franc.

Any one of those policy moves would be a major setback for the European project, which has coalesced around trade, money and now security. A cut in assistance to Ukraine would remove 3.5 percent of its foreign military aid, according to the Kiel Institute’s Ukraine Support Tracker, which other allies would have to make up.

At the same time, “we could end up in a situation where Trump is basically clinching deals with Putin as fast as he can,” said Fieschi, referring to the US-Russian strategy to coerce Ukraine into a peace agreement that involves sacrificing its eastern Donbas region – something Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said would be a strategic error leading to renewed war, and which a majority of Ukrainians are against.

Trump has already leveraged US early warning on incoming ballistics and Starlink satellite navigation against Ukraine. He has twice echoed Russian calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced.

Compounding this renewed pressure from a beleaguered White House, Russia could intensify its “all-domain war”, which many European governments believe it is already waging against them, said Victoria Vdovychenko, a Ukraine expert at Cambridge University’s Centre for Geopolitics.

“Cognitive warfare never stopped on the European continent, and Russians are already using existing vulnerabilities to the utmost,” she told Al Jazeera. “I hope that the European partners will be staying very strong.”

Trump’s abandonment of the world order the US and Europe established after World War II, his disregard for democracy and human rights, and his betrayal of Ukraine have already transformed European public opinion, observers say.

Only 31 percent of Europeans see the US as Europe’s “most trustworthy ally”, down from 51 percent in 2024, when Trump’s predecessor, Joe Biden, was in office, according to a poll for the German think tank Bertelsmann Stiftung.

Seventy-three percent of Europeans across all age groups say Europe should “go its own way” rather than continue a close cooperation with the US, up from 63 percent in 2024, and that figure includes a clear majority among those on the centre-right and right.

In this year’s Spring Eurobarometer, a regular pulse-taking conducted by the European Commission, 68 percent of respondents wanted the EU’s role in protecting Europeans from global crises and security risks to increase, while 39 percent wanted it to be a top priority.

In a June poll for the European Council on Foreign Relations, the description of the US as an “ally” fell from 22 percent in November 2024 to 11 percent across all territories polled in Eastern and Western Europe.

In a June poll for the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based think tank, 76 percent of people polled in 36 countries, of which nine were EU members, expressed no confidence in Trump, and 57 percent expressed unfavourable views of the US.

It would appear that such shifts against the US and especially Republicans, formed over two Trump terms, would be difficult to reverse in a single congressional election, especially with a Russian war ongoing in Europe.

title: Defence backed claim that social media footage of public servants could invite bullying
excerpt:
Official’s controversial September request for Senate hearing footage to not be shared on social media has been heavily criticised

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The s...
body_text:
Official’s controversial September request for Senate hearing footage to not be shared on social media has been heavily criticised

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The secretary of the defence department approved a senior official’s controversial idea to tell a Senate hearing that footage of public servants giving evidence should not be shared on social media because it could invite online bullying and raise national security concerns.

Emails obtained by Guardian Australia under freedom of information reveal deputy secretary Celia Perkins’ planned request to the parliamentary inquiry was flagged with the offices of deputy prime minister Richard Marles and assistant defence minister Peter Khalil, and received the backing of department secretary Meghan Quinn.

Perkins – defence’s deputy secretary of security and estate – drew criticism across the political divide with her 4 September statement to a committee hearing, where she said defence witnesses “do not consent to the reposting of our evidence to social media sites”.

She pointed to a submission from the secretaries board of the Australian Public Service, which had raised similar concerns about evidence being taken out of context, and alleged “edited and embellished” videos from previous hearings had “generated significant highly inappropriate and highly personal commentary that was distressing for staff and invited ridicule, hostility and abuse”.

The Greens senator David Shoebridge instantly objected, saying: “This is evidence given in an open public hearing … These witnesses do not get to censor what the Australian public sees.”

The committee rejected Perkins’ request on the advice of the Senate clerk.

Newly revealed correspondence shows that concerns about online bullying, as well as national security fears, were used as a “defensible” reason to not share clips from hearings online – and that the plan was backed by the defence department.

“Meghan is fully supportive, as is [Khalil]. I discussed today in a meeting with [Khalil] and staff from [Marles] and his office,” Perkins told two fellow deputy secretaries two days before the hearing.

Guardian Australia requested documents under FOI from the defence department relating to the preparation of Perkins’ statement. Emails between senior department officials showed Perkins’ proposal to make such a statement had been strongly endorsed by her colleagues and superiors, and that she had told Quinn on 25 August that officials could be put in danger if their evidence before public committees was published online.

“As senior leaders in Defence – we actively discourage security clearance holders from a social media presence that identifies us and our roles,” Perkins wrote to Quinn, outlining “core arguments” to support her statement.

“And these post[s], designed to invite outraged responses – increase the personal risk from malign online actors, including cyber and foreign intelligence threats.”

The offices of Marles and Khalil were contacted for comment. Neither provided an on-record response, but Guardian Australia understands neither office directed Perkins on the content of her statement.

Defence did not supply a response to Guardian Australia, but a spokesperson pointed to Quinn’s opening statement to a Senate estimates committee on Thursday, in which she said she supported the submission from the secretaries board and claimed that the treatment of staff after committee hearings could sometimes conflict with an employer’s duty to ensure the health and safety of employees.

In the 25 August email, which discussed the upcoming hearing, Perkins told Quinn she wanted “to add an explicit statement that the Defence witnesses appearing do not consent to our evidence being reproduced in edited format on social media platforms”.

“We’d need to settle a form of words that is defensible,” Perkins wrote, outlining concerns about maintaining a safe workplace for staff and that previous hearings led to “significant vile, personal commentary that was distressing for staff and invited online bullying.” Perkins also raised the concern about cyber and foreign intelligence threats.

In response, Quinn wrote: “Very happy to support you using such words.”

On 2 September, Perkins emailed two other deputy secretaries in the department, John Reid and Cath Patterson, flagging her intention to make the statement and “to specifically call out the social media posting matter”, and seeking their feedback on wording.

Patterson responded to Perkins’ email: “Those words look fine – polite and clear and safe given in the Sec Board submission”.

Reid concurred: “I agree with Cath; this is a good statement and makes the point clearly and respectfully.” Reid suggested minor changes to Perkins’ original suggested wording, with that version read at the committee.

title: Spain begins mourning period after deadly train crash
excerpt:
Emergency services combed through the wreckage overnight as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims

Spain has begun three days of mourning after a h...
body_text:
Emergency services combed through the wreckage overnight as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims

Spain has begun three days of mourning after a high-speed rail collision – its second this year – killed 68 people and injured scores, with relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.

The trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling on Wednesday morning in the same direction on the line that stretches from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to the southern region of Andalusia. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near the town of Urda.

Officials said on Wednesday another 107 people had needed medical treatment in hospital, including 15 who were in a serious condition.

The disaster has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain’s rail network after the transport minister reported an “error” and “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash.

Emergency services combed through the wreckage overnight to find further victims, hoisting pieces of mangled metal with cranes, according to Agence France-Presse.

Emiliano García-Page, the leader of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, told reporters on Wednesday that more victims were likely as “it has not yet been possible to reach the bottom of the carriages”.

The Civil Guard has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Córdoba and Seville to enable relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims. Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid.

A school in the nearby village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid, is being used to allow relatives to enquire about their loved ones. Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who arrived, some of them in tears.

Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia said “long and hard hours” were in store because “every person will manage it in their own way”. “We have people who are in shock, who haven’t taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated,” Garcia said.

In January, 46 people were killed and dozens more injured after two trains – again, one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.

The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said it was “unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in the same year, as we have”.

The causes of the accident were under investigation, he added. If it emerged that it was due to failures in the security system or negligence, these shortcomings would be addressed with the “utmost severity”, he said.

The first victims to be named included a 31-year-old Guardia civil agent, José Manuel Chacón.

The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues. Spanish media said the missing included a former minister for the People’s party and several foreigners who were likely on holiday in the country.

The opposition People’s party leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.

title: Can Turkiye’s Libya breakthrough reshape Eastern Mediterranean diplomacy?
excerpt: Istanbul, Turkiye – Once adversaries, Turkiye and the leadership of eastern Libya are now building closer political and military ties. Ankara has also repaired relations with Egypt in the past few yea...
body_text:
Istanbul, Turkiye – Once adversaries, Turkiye and the leadership of eastern Libya are now building closer political and military ties. Ankara has also repaired relations with Egypt in the past few years after previous hostility, but a maritime dispute is testing how far those reconciliations can go.

On Wednesday, Turkiye’s Ministry of National Defence renewed its offer to sign a maritime boundary agreement with Cairo, arguing that Egypt could gain more than 15,000sq km (5,790sq miles) of maritime jurisdiction – a figure that is Ankara’s estimate – compared with a potential further agreement with Greece, with which Cairo signed a partial maritime deal in 2020.

The offer came eight days after Libya’s eastern-based parliament in Tobruk reversed years of opposition and approved a maritime agreement signed between its rival, the internationally recognised government based in the Libyan capital, Tripoli, and Turkiye in 2019.

The agreement delineates maritime jurisdiction areas claimed by Turkiye and Libya in the Mediterranean, but Greece, Cyprus and Egypt argued that it infringes on their sovereign rights while Turkiye maintains that it complies with international law.

A senior Turkish official told Al Jazeera that eastern Libya’s leaders had come to recognise Ankara’s intentions.

“Turkiye is not there to use Libya for its own purposes,” the official said.

“From the very beginning, we have supported a policy of one Libya,” the official added, stressing that the country’s stability and resources should benefit all Libyans.

Turkiye helped repel a 2019-2020 offensive on Tripoli by forces loyal to renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, leader of the military forces of the eastern government. Ankara has since expanded its relations with the eastern camp while maintaining ties with Tripoli.

The senior official said Turkish security personnel based in Tripoli had remained in contact with eastern Libyan forces even during the confrontation.

“There has actually been no change in our policy. Only the results it has produced have changed,” the official said.

The diplomatic outreach has been accompanied by military and intelligence contacts.

In May, Defence Minister Yasar Guler met Saddam Haftar, Khalifa Haftar’s son, and Abdulsalam al-Zoubi, a senior defence official in the Tripoli-based government.

Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin also met Saddam Haftar in Benghazi on June 23. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan followed in August, meeting both Khalifa and Saddam Haftar.

A change in Libya’s eastern parliamentary leadership also preceded the maritime vote. On October 6, lawmakers replaced Aguila Saleh as parliament speaker with Al-Salhin Abdelnabi al-Obeidi, who previously chaired the Libyan-Turkish parliamentary friendship committee.

Galip Dalay, a senior research fellow at Chatham House, sees Ankara’s engagement with its former adversaries as a strategic gain.

“This is not merely a pragmatic or tactical gain. It is a strategic gain for Turkiye,” he told Al Jazeera.

Dalay argued that closer relations with both Libyan camps make it harder to establish Eastern Mediterranean energy and security arrangements that exclude Turkiye.

The rapprochement also reflects political calculations within the Haftar camp.

Tarek Megerisi, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Saddam Haftar hopes Ankara’s influence could strengthen his own political prospects with many believing that he eventually wants to lead Libya.

The senior Turkish official said Ankara had made no specific political commitments to eastern Libyan officials beyond general principles and cooperation that would also benefit Libya.

Representatives of both Libyan camps held talks in Ankara on Friday about unifying their military structures, according to Libyan media reports. Differences over political oversight remain unresolved, and no final agreement has been announced.

But Anas El Gomati, director of the Sadeq Institute, cautioned that an understanding between Libya’s rival leaders would not necessarily produce an inclusive political settlement.

“An elite bargain between two camps can leave out everyone beyond them,” he said.

The Libyan eastern parliament’s reversal has also complicated Egypt’s position. Cairo has traditionally supported the eastern leadership but opposes the maritime agreement it has now endorsed.

On October 22, Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis announced discussions with Egypt on extending their partial 2020 maritime delimitation agreement eastwards towards Cyprus.

Four days later, Egypt joined Greece, Cyprus, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and the European Union in a statement at the United Nations rejecting the Turkiye-Libya accord.

Yet Cairo and Ankara have continued rebuilding their relationship.

Turkiye’s land forces commander, General Metin Tokel, arrived in Egypt on Monday for an official visit. The Turkish Defence Ministry has also announced a joint naval exercise in Alexandria from November 4 to 9.

The senior Turkish official told Al Jazeera that Ankara remained open to cooperation on maritime boundaries and energy but would defend what it considers its rights.

“Just as other countries say they will not give up the rights they recognise as their own, the same applies to Turkiye,” the official said.

Fidan has acknowledged Egypt’s concerns and discussed the possibility of cooperation with Italy. The official clarified, however, that no formal four-country negotiating mechanism between Turkiye, Libya, Italy and Egypt has been established.

El Gomati believes Cairo’s ability to influence decisions in eastern Libya has diminished.

“Egypt still has influence, but it no longer has a veto,” he said.

Megerisi, meanwhile, argued that Turkiye’s relationship with Egypt has become too important to sacrifice over the maritime dispute. He sees room for accommodation, potentially involving Italy’s energy company Eni, which has interests in Egypt and Libya.

Greece maintains that the maritime agreement disregards the rights of its islands, including Crete. Turkiye rejects those claims, arguing that islands should not automatically receive the same weight as mainland coastlines when mapping out maritime boundaries and exclusive economic zones.

Megerisi said the eastern Libyan parliament’s approval strengthens the agreement’s domestic legal footing but does little to resolve the wider dispute between the countries of the Eastern Mediterranean.

“I think both sides are maximalist,” he said.

The parliamentary vote gives Ankara greater political leverage, but it does not settle competing maritime claims or clear the way for offshore energy exploration.

Ankara now wants to build on its gains in Libya and improving ties with Egypt to strengthen its position in the Eastern Mediterranean. Its aim is to develop new partnerships and regional cooperation rather than remain outside arrangements shaped largely by Greece, Cyprus and Israel.

But that will require finding common ground with countries that continue to challenge Turkiye’s maritime claims.

The senior Turkish official said Ankara’s improved relationship with Cairo had opened the door to discussing those differences directly.

“We can now discuss every issue with Egypt, and we will discuss this one too,” the official said. “We do not have to seek the approval or consent of unrelated third countries.”

title: Russia says more than 600 drones launched towards Moscow overnight
excerpt:
Russia has downed most of the 613 drones launched towards Moscow overnight, in a major attack on the Russian capital, Russian state news agency TASS has reported.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on...
body_text:
Russia has downed most of the 613 drones launched towards Moscow overnight, in a major attack on the Russian capital, Russian state news agency TASS has reported.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram that air defence forces destroyed 231 of the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) on approach to the city, with the remainder neutralised on distant approaches between Wednesday evening and Thursday morning.

The attack marks the latest in a series of major drone assaults targeting the Moscow region, following a record attack in September during which air defence forces reported shooting down more than 1,600 drones.

Meanwhile, Russia attacked Ukraine’s Kharkiv, the country’s second-biggest city, damaging an educational institution, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said on Telegram.

title: Judge rejects Trump effort to block California ‘noncitizen’ ballots
excerpt: A United States judge has rejected a Department of Justice request to temporarily halt California from counting mail ballots from a list of 20,000 alleged noncitizens just six days before the country’...
body_text:
A United States judge has rejected a Department of Justice request to temporarily halt California from counting mail ballots from a list of 20,000 alleged noncitizens just six days before the country’s midterm elections.

US District Judge David Carter’s ruling on Wednesday came as US President Donald Trump expands efforts to search for alleged noncitizen voters, with subpoenas issued in at least 13 states.

“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter wrote on Wednesday.

The judge, a 1998 appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, said the Justice Department’s last-minute request to exclude more than 20,000 ballots ran afoul of “longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections”.

The Justice Department swiftly appealed the decision to the Ninth US Circuit Court of Appeals and did not immediately respond to requests for comment by the Reuters news agency.

The Justice Department filed the lawsuit on October 15, a rare intervention in the voting process weeks before Tuesday’s election, when voters will choose which party controls Congress as well as their state and local representatives.

The decision marks the latest setback in Trump’s effort to expand the federal government’s role in elections ahead of the legislative midterms, as his Republican Party fights to retain control of both houses of Congress.

The Trump administration issued more than 100 subpoenas demanding records on tens of thousands of voters in at least 13 states, both Republican- and Democratic-leaning.

Most of the subpoenas Reuters documented were issued to state and local election officials in the past three months, though some date to the start of the year. Many were previously unreported, revealing a federal effort to identify potential noncitizen voters that is broader than publicly known.

It is illegal for noncitizens to vote in US federal elections. Legal experts say the records could be used to contest close midterm results, despite scant evidence that noncitizen voting is widespread.

Also on Wednesday, Democracy Docket, a US media platform that tracks election litigation, reported that the Department of Justice list of alleged noncitizen voters “appears to have been created using a deeply flawed process” that could disenfranchise US citizen voters beyond California.

In a court filing, a government whistleblower revealed that voters were being scrutinised nationwide, not just in California, as part of the federal government’s “Unlawful Voter Initiative” investigation, the group reported. The whistleblower warned that “the current process is knowingly sweeping known US citizens in as potentially ‘unlawful voters'”.

California has said the state’s safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust. It said the Justice Department’s assertions relied on “suspect data” and that complying with its demands would risk disenfranchising eligible voters. Democracy Docket reported that in Los Angeles County, one in four voters on the “noncitizen” list were born in the US.

title: ‘The more you earn, the less you keep’: readers react to the budget
excerpt:
From a young chef and a single father to business owners and a pensioner, Guardian readers reveal how John Healey’s measures will affect them

Louie, 24, a chef living in London, says a lot of people ...
body_text:
From a young chef and a single father to business owners and a pensioner, Guardian readers reveal how John Healey’s measures will affect them

Louie, 24, a chef living in London, says a lot of people have “written off the idea of even considering getting a property” in their 20s.

He is optimistic about the government’s new Your First Home scheme, which will enable people to buy a new-build property with a deposit of just 2.5%, supported by an interest-free equity loan.

But he says a smaller deposit alone will not be enough for him. “I’ve found hospitality wages to be far too volatile to even consider saving for a property,” he says.

As a result, he is studying an access course with plans to start a physiotherapy degree next year. He hopes that by the time he graduates and gains some experience, he will have a stable enough income and sufficient savings to put down a deposit.

He says the new scheme “should encourage a lot of young people to buy earlier” and adds: “We are moving in a good direction, but I’ll still save and wait until around late 20s to early 30s to start [thinking about buying], just due to how much it may cost me.”

Louie earns between £37,000 and £40,000 a year and shares a three-bedroom rented property with two friends. But rent and bills take up an increasingly large proportion of his income, leaving little room to save towards buying a home.

“I was always told that a third of your salary should go towards rent and bills, but it’s coming up to about half now, which is a little bit mental,” he says.

His landlord recently informed the household that their rent would increase by £200 a month in November.

He has managed to build up some savings. Since he was 18, he has put between 5% and 10% of his earnings into a stocks and shares investment account, and over the past year has also started making regular contributions to an Isa specifically for a house deposit.

“Nobody really wants to be spending all their money on rent,” he says. “But with the amount of money we make, you kind of have to. ”

Graham Robinson is a business owner from Timperley, Greater Manchester, who runs the company KeySim. He earned £126,000 last year, but says that despite his six-figure income, he has virtually nothing left in his bank account at the end of each month.

Graham says he was “hoping for real help with the cost of employing people” from the budget. “Instead, the employment allowance stays at £10,500, while employers pick up the rising wage bill.”

He adds: “The minimum wage increase is welcome for workers, but the government gets the headline, businesses get the bill and the Treasury recoups some through tax and national insurance.”

The 45-year-old lives alone and shares care of his 10-year-old autistic son with his ex, covering all childcare costs himself.

“I know £126,000 sounds like an enormous amount of money, but after tax it works out at broadly £6,500 a month, and that really doesn’t go as far as people might think,” he says. “I don’t have expensive cars, I don’t go on extravagant holidays. I don’t really do anything particularly lavish, but at the end of the month it’s all gone.”

His mortgage payments have risen from about £900 a month to £1,300, while council tax, food, energy and other everyday expenses have also increased.

Normally earning approximately £100,000 a year, he has increasingly relied on additional dividends from his business to cover rising costs.

He is frustrated by the effective 60% income tax rate on earnings caused by the gradual withdrawal of the personal allowance on income over £100,000, which reaches zero when earnings reach £125,140.

“To put an extra £1,000 a month in my take-home pay, my salary would need to rise from £100,000 to £129,757 a year,” he says.

Helen, 40, lives in south-west London with her husband and two children, aged eight and five. She is the main breadwinner, working in communications, while her husband runs his own architectural practice.

Her house is in council tax band D, which means she will get a £100 energy payment this winter. She welcomed the extra money, but found the way it was being distributed strange, based on bands rather than financial need.

She says the change offering self-employed people paternity pay was “great”, though now her children are older it would not benefit her family. She adds: “It was lovely to hear Dolly Parton’s book scheme mentioned, as encouraging education for all is key.”

Her family’s biggest monthly expense is their mortgage, which increased by more than £600 a month when interest rates rose. They have now fixed it until 2028.

Helen says frozen income tax thresholds are one of her biggest concerns, alongside getting the economy growing and the pressures facing small businesses. Her husband’s architectural practice is less than four years old and has struggled with the rising costs of building and a wider slowdown in construction.

“The challenge comes down to the price of energy; for example, the cost of steel, transporting materials and building homes,” she says. “It impacts everything we make, build and buy.”

Peter Pillinger, 72, is a widower from South Ribble in Lancashire whose state pension makes up about half his income. He also receives a pension from his career as a Methodist minister, a small amount from his late wife’s pension and an allowance for his work as a local councillor.

He is pleased with one of the key announcements: the scrapping of standing charges on gas bills. These are fixed daily fees that households pay regardless of how much gas they use.

“My gas bill in the summer is almost entirely standing charge,” he says. “They are regressive. Putting all the costs in the unit charge will encourage people to reduce usage and to insulate their homes.”

But he wonders why it will take until at least next spring for the change to come in. He also wants to know what the government will do “for those who need higher usage for medical reasons”.

He supports the changes to the state pension triple lock and believes pensioners who can afford to pay tax should do so. “If my income is £25,000 or approaching £30,000, why should it not be taxed? If everyone else is paying tax at that level, why should I not?”

Conversely, he is concerned about those surviving on much less. “I don’t know how people live on just the state pension,” he says.

Danielle Walker, 37, is a self-employed florist based in Wakefield, West Yorkshire. She says rising fuel prices are squeezing her business from both sides, increasing the cost of making deliveries while also pushing up the price of the flowers she buys.

She welcomes the chancellor cancelling the planned fuel duty rise, but adds “it doesn’t undo the increases we’ve already faced or take away the pressure we’re under”.

Increasing the higher mileage rate from 25p to 35p a mile will not benefit her, she says, nor will the business rate threshold going up from £12,000 to £18,000, as she works from a studio.

Danielle has spent considerable time calculating delivery charges for different postcodes to ensure they cover her fuel costs and the time spent travelling. But she says she is increasingly having to absorb some of these costs herself.

“If I’ve quoted flowers for a wedding based on diesel being £1.40 a litre and it’s £2 by the time the wedding comes around, I’ve still got to get there. There’s only so much you can absorb for so long,” she says.

With customers already struggling financially, she feels unable to keep passing on rising costs without risking a loss of business.

“Flowers are a luxury item, and when people are feeling the pinch, they’re one of the first things people think to cut back on,” she says.

Danielle believes the government should look at the impact of fuel duty and VAT on small businesses that depend on driving, arguing that independent traders are particularly exposed to rising prices.

“Someone has to take it on the chin somewhere. I feel it’s unfair that small businesses are continually having to absorb these costs or lose customers by being honest about what delivery should cost.”

Jonny Roberts, 39, is a single dad from Newbury, Berkshire, with children aged 11 and eight. He works part-time at McDonald’s and as a tutor, while also studying for an online master’s degree. Between his two jobs, he works the equivalent of full-time hours. But even with support from universal credit, his income only just covers essentials.

“We had heard in the run-up [to the budget] there would be something on energy bills, and I’m sure millions of households are grateful for the extra £100 help towards that announced today,” he says. “But it was disappointing to see no announcement on whether local housing allowance [LHA] will be uprated.”

For Jonny, one of the biggest problems is the gap between the housing support available through universal credit and the reality of renting. He is entitled to the three-bedroom LHA rate, which gives him £1,200 a month towards his rent, but he pays £1,300 a month for a two-bedroom flat.

“The rent we’re paying isn’t particularly high for the area. It’s pretty much in line with the norm,” he says.

“Last year’s freeze and the cuts of prior government mean the housing element of universal credit seems to live in an alternate reality to the actual rents charged in the south of England.”

Jonny is also frustrated by the way universal credit reduces the financial rewards of taking on additional work.

For every extra pound he earns above his work allowance, his universal credit is reduced by 55p. Once income tax, national insurance and student loan repayments are taken into account, he says the amount he keeps from an additional shift can be surprisingly small.

With rent taking up the largest share of his budget, Jonny has little flexibility when other household costs rise. “I’m happy to go with less for myself to make sure I can feed all three of us,” he says.

Jonny was happy to see a “speeding up of the rollout of free breakfast clubs to an extra 2,000 schools” but adds: “It still seems a glacial pace when there are 17,000 primaries in the country.”

Jonny takes part in Changing Realities, a collaboration involving more than 200 parents and carers living on low incomes, researchers at the University of Glasgow and Child Poverty Action Group. The project documents families’ experiences of living on a low income and brings their voices into discussions about poverty and social security policy.

title: How will John Healey’s energy support package affect you?
excerpt:
Chancellor’s ‘new course’ includes a £100 one-off payment, low-carbon upgrade loans and an end to standing charges

John Healey has unveiled a package of support for households being buffeted by “glob...
body_text:
Chancellor’s ‘new course’ includes a £100 one-off payment, low-carbon upgrade loans and an end to standing charges

John Healey has unveiled a package of support for households being buffeted by “global economic storms”.

“I’m setting a new course to get energy costs down in line with Europe,” the chancellor said in his maiden budget. In the long term, he hopes that changes in how Britain covers the cost of renewables and grid upgrades will “drive down all aspects of energy bills”.

British households face some of the highest energy charges for three years, with the war in the Middle East driving up oil and gas prices.

Under the government’s price cap, average dual-fuel bills are £1,700 a year and could rise to more than £2,100 a year from January, according to industry forecasts.

So what has the chancellor offered hard-pressed households to help them through the coldest months of the year? And will it be enough to lower gas and electricity bills?

The government’s biggest bet on offering “breathing space” to struggling households this winter is a one-off payment of £100 in January for 20m households in council tax bands A to D. It is also the measure most likely to deliver real benefit for those in need.

The £2.6bn “household energy payment” will go directly into bank accounts to “take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people through to the spring”, according to Healey.

Martin Lewis, the founder of MoneySavingExpert.com, said households could face a 25% cost increase from January and shouldn’t expect to feel better off than they do today.

Officials are anxious to avoid handing public money to those who can get by without it but they lack household income data to target proposed support. Using council tax bands is “the least worst proxy”, Lewis said.

The payment will be in addition to the Warm Home Discount, which offers about 6m means-tested households in England, Wales and Scotland £150 off winter fuel bills.

This measure will offer a modest saving for most British households – but not all, and perhaps not until next winter.

Healey promised to end “unfair and outdated” standing charges on gas bills for 23m homes “in 2027 or as soon as possible after”. This could help almost two-thirds of households to save an average of £45 a year.

A standing charge is a fixed daily fee paid through all household gas bills, regardless of how much is used. It means homes that severely ration their gas use – or use none at all – still shoulder the same cost as a high-income household.

The charge typically adds about £100 a year to bills and the change means these costs will soon be recovered through a higher unit price for gas. For those with below-average gas use, bills should fall. But there won’t be savings for everyone.

Jonny Marshall, an economist at the Resolution Foundation, said households with high gas use might have higher bills when the unit rate increases. These could include low-income households who have bigger families or poorly insulated homes.

A home using 7,000 kilowatt hours of gas a year would save about £40 under the change, but a household using 14,000 kWh of gas a year could be £25 worse off, according to Richard Neudegg, a director at Uswitch.com. A household using the typical 11,500 kWh shouldn’t see any change, he added.

The government has already begun taking aim at taxes and policy costs loaded on to electricity bills that could over time mean removing hundreds of pounds from bills.

This month, it removed the 5% VAT levy on electricity bills for 29m households, effectively saving them about £45 a year.

This was supposed to help households through the coldest months of the year, until March. But Healey has promised to keep VAT off bills until July, extending the annual savings to £50 a year, according to the Treasury.

The move follows a string of cuts to electricity levies over the past year which have shaved about £150 a year off costs.

“For many years, under Conservative governments, policy costs were simply loaded on to household bills through levies,” Healey said. “Today, I am putting an end to that. We’ll introduce a new cost control framework to drive down all aspects of energy bills.”

Healey confirmed he would consider steps to remove standing charges on electricity too, which ​add about £200 a year to the average ​bill. The savings from this measure remain unclear, depending on which costs would move into general taxation and which would be covered through the unit price for electricity.

Healey will continue to alter a subsidy scheme for the UK’s oldest renewable energy projects, around three-quarters of which has been removed from bills and covered by general taxation. The research charity Nesta said this would lower electricity costs by £42 a year.

Healey has scrapped plans for a levy to support hydrogen projects that would otherwise have added £2.60 to £4.50 a year to the average dual-fuel bill.

The government believes that households could save up to £550 a year on energy bills if they invest in solar panels, home batteries and a heat pump. These savings could rise by a further £300 a year with a time-of-use tariff, according to the government.

To help households access these savings, a Warm Home Loans scheme, which launched on Tuesday, will offer government-backed loans of up to £35,000 for low-carbon energy alternatives.

The government said it was committed to rolling out heat pumps through its boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants of up to £7,500 to help meet the £13,600 cost of installing one.

Grants of up to £9,000 a year are available to households that are not connected to the gas grid and rely on high-cost heating oil.

For many, the government’s new measures will come too late to help this winter. But there could be support in the spring from a debt relief scheme.

The government said the delayed scheme will “provide targeted support to customers in genuine financial need”. Total household energy debt has tripled from 2021 to a record £5bn and could reach £7bn by the end of the year.

The one-off, targeted intervention has been designed to help those with debts from the 2022-24 energy crisis and little prospect of repaying them.

Nesta has suggested debt relief could be given to about 2m households for a one-off cost of £2.7bn. This would also cut the £29 a year paid by all households to cover the cost of unpaid bills.

More details on the scheme will follow in early 2027, the government said.

Barbara Barrie played Hal Linden's wife on "Barney Miller." (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

Barbara Barrie has died at age 95 after a terminal cancer diagnosis, according to a report.

The "Barney Miller" actress’s death at her home in New York City was medically assisted, her daughter told The New York Times.

The Oscar-nominated actress’s TV and film career spanned multiple decades from the 1950s until last year.

EVA MARIE SAINT, OSCAR-WINNING ‘ON THE WATERFRONT’ AND ‘NORTH BY NORTHWEST’ STAR, DEAD AT 102

Barbara Barrie, 95, died with medical assistance this week after a terminal cancer diagnosis. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

Barrie was known for her small screen roles as Barney Miller’s wife on "Barney Miller," a police series that ran from 1975 to 1982, and as Brooke Shields’ grandmother on "Suddenly Susan."

She was nominated for an Academy Award for 1979’s "Breaking Away," and she won best actress at the Cannes Film Festival for 1964’s "One Potato, Two Potato."

She lost to Meryl Streep for "Kramer vs. Kramer" at the Oscars.

She also played Goldie Hawn’s mother in 1980’s "Private Benjamin."

Barrie was also a prolific Broadway actress who was nominated for a Tony for her performance in the original 1970 cast of Stephen Sondheim’s "Company."

The 95-year-old made her Broadway debut in "The Wooden Dish" in 1955 after she moved to New York when she graduated from college in Texas, telling the Akron Beacon Journal in 1963 that she only went there because of a man.
