title: Yankees president Randy Levine says he is 'confident' MLB will avoid a lockout despite cap fight
excerpt:
Tampa Bay Rays' Kevin Cash spoke with Kevin Burkhadt, David Ortiz, Derek Jeter and Alex Rodriguez following 4-3 win over Milwaukee Brewers in Game 4 of World Series.

Game 5 of the World Series could ...
body_text:
Tampa Bay Rays' Kevin Cash spoke with Kevin Burkhadt, David Ortiz, Derek Jeter and Alex Rodriguez following 4-3 win over Milwaukee Brewers in Game 4 of World Series.

Game 5 of the World Series could very well be the last baseball game for the foreseeable future.

The league's current collective bargaining agreement with the players expires on Dec. 1, and the players and owners appear as far apart as they ever have been.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Assuming there is no deal, the owners are expected to lock out the players, as was the case five years ago which led to the season being delayed by one week.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The New York Yankees warm up during a workout ahead of the American League Wild Card Series against the Boston Red Sox on Sept. 28, 2026, at Yankee Stadium in New York, N.Y. (Getty Images)

Despite the apparently harsh circumstances at the moment, New York Yankees president Randy Levine is actually "confident" things will all work out.

"It's very, very early... They want to reach an agreement. It's always this way in every labor negotiation I've done. It's always posturing at this point in time, getting your position out," Levine said on "The Craig Carton Show."

"We have until December. I think they're really going to work hard, and I'm very hopeful they'll reach an agreement. I've seen circumstances where it looked harder than even this, and this one looks hard, but at the end of the day, I'm confident everyone wants to get a deal."

"The whole playoffs have been great, the whole season has been great. Baseball is regaining popularity, it's the national pastime, so we gotta work hard to just preserve it," Levine added.

Levine's boss, Hal Steinbrenner, said last week he "support[s]" the owners' proposals — all of which include a cap.

"I've said before — let me put it this way, as a member of the labor policy committee — I helped craft, one of many, the proposals that we have given at the bargaining table. And I support those proposals in their entirety. That's absolutely the case, so that should answer your question," Steinbrenner told reporters.

The Yankees' $336 million payroll was the third-largest in baseball during the 2026 season, behind the Los Angeles Dodgers ($422 million) and New York Mets ($338 million).

Randy Levine, president of the New York Yankees, attends the Bloomberg Power Players New York event in New York on Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

FANS DEBATE BREWERS DECISION TO KEEP JACOB MISIOROWSKI IN DUGOUT WITH CHANCE TO WIN FIRST EVER WORLD SERIES

Arguments skew both ways, but a constant has remained in that the highest payrolls continue to go up, while the lowest payrolls remain at a stall. The Marlins' payroll is actually roughly half of what it used to be in 2017, despite a sale of the team and everyone in the league making more money than ever. Meanwhile, the Dodgers have already committed more money in 2030 than 12 teams have this season.

MLB commissioner Rob Manfred has said that owners are simply "listening to our fans" regarding a salary cap and said it "defies human experience... to think that the bottom end of that [payroll] gap has the same opportunity to win the top end." It should be noted, though, that the National League-winning Milwaukee Brewers swept the Dodgers with the 11th-smallest payroll, and they are facing the Tampa Bay Rays, who have the league's third-smallest payroll. They defeated the Cleveland Guardians, who rank 29th in payroll, in the American League Division Series.

Major League Baseball has never had a salary cap.

"Salary cap is the ultimate excuse not to compete. It's the ultimate excuse for an owner to say, 'Gee, I would like to make the team better, but you know I can’t,'" interim MLBPA executive director Bruce Meyer said during the All-Star break. "Salary caps are bad for fans. Salary caps prevent teams from doing the things that they believe are in their interest to make the team better."

Major League Baseball Commissioner Robert D. Manfred speaks during the 2026 All-Star Legacy renovation event at the Veterans Multi-Service Center in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on July 13, 2026. (Daniel Shirey/MLB Photos via Getty Images)

"Every team in baseball can afford to compete, many are choosing not to," Meyer added. "To me, that's the biggest problem right now."

title: What’s next for Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro after election defeat?
excerpt: Sao Paulo, Brazil – Far-right Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, along with his wife and two daughters, landed in Miami, Florida, in the United States on Wednesday, days after he was defeated in Brazil’s presi...
body_text:
Sao Paulo, Brazil – Far-right Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, along with his wife and two daughters, landed in Miami, Florida, in the United States on Wednesday, days after he was defeated in Brazil’s presidential run-off election.

Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes issued an order late on Sunday night for Bolsonaro to turn in his regular and diplomatic passports, believing him to be a flight risk in connection with a money laundering and currency evasion investigation involving the senator and his friend Willer Tomaz — who the local press says already left Brazil for Miami two weeks ago.

Argentine immigration authorities said on Wednesday that Flavio and his family used a land crossing to enter Argentina late Tuesday night, and less than an hour later boarded a private plane operated by Baires Fly destined for Guayaquil, Ecuador. That plane arrived in Ecuador, and later took off for Miami, Florida, with Flavio and his family on board. The Bolsonaro family landed at Opa-Locka Executive Airport near Miami on Wednesday morning.

The US State Department confirmed on Tuesday that it will issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them to enter the country.

US President Donald Trump and Argentina’s President Javier Milei are the only two prominent world leaders who have not yet acknowledged Brazil’s Sunday election result, in which centre-left incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pulled off a jaw-dropping comeback to win re-election, scoring 51.8 percent of votes over Bolsonaro’s 48.2 percent. It was a difference of millions. Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump said Brazil’s election appeared to have been “rigged”, though he also expressed his admiration for President Lula.

News of Flavio’s abrupt departure drew swift indignation from some voters on the ground.

“He’s acting like a coward who’s unwilling to face the consequences of his actions,” said Cristiana Cunha, 36, speaking to Al Jazeera in Sao Paulo. She said she was unsurprised by news of his leaving the country.

Priscila Cardoso, a 45-year-old psychoanalyst also living in Sao Paulo, was even more scathing: “It’s a joke, it’s like a parasite fleeing through the sewer,” she said.

Political analyst Paulo Roberto de Souza of the Democracy in Check Institute told Al Jazeera that Flavio’s flight may kick off a new dispute for power among Brazil’s conservatives, in which the Bolsonaro family may be pushed to one side.

“By leaving the country, he’s made it easier for the right wing to start a fight over the Bolsonaro’s spoils,” he said, noting that, despite the relatively fine margins, Flavio’s defeat on Sunday was “humiliating” for the family.

“In 2022, [Flavio’s father] Jair Bolsonaro became the first incumbent Brazilian president to lose a re-election battle. And now, in 2026, Flavio became the first presidential candidate to lead after the first round and lose a run-off. It imposes a ceiling on the Bolsonaros’ power,” de Souza said.

In the aftermath of Sunday’s result, Flavio called a press conference in which he said it would be “impossible” for him to acknowledge the outcome of the vote, announcing he would pursue a petition to have the election annulled.

His claims were based on a last-minute Brazilian Supreme Court decision on Sunday that delayed the closing of polls by two hours, after both candidates had requested extensions due to insufficient availability of public transportation and adverse weather conditions. But official records show that fewer than 35,000 votes were recorded during the two-hour polling extension, and Lula’s winning margin was more than 4.4 million votes.

For some voters, Flavio’s call for an annulment came across as bad sportsmanship. Cardoso, who is a single parent, likened his behaviour to that of a “spoiled child who loses a game and takes the ball home with them”.

While Flavio has yet to concede defeat, his Liberal Party has recognised Sunday’s result, and prominent allies have sought to put the election behind them.

Sao Paulo Governor Tarcisio de Freitas, who campaigned alongside Bolsonaro and won re-election in a first-round landslide, published a two-minute video on social media on Tuesday outlining his own project for the country and mentioning Flavio only once.

“Without a doubt, Tarcisio is the main figure in this reorganisation process on the Brazilian right,” said de Souza. “For this election, he was the name floated and insisted upon by some key figures in Bolsonarism, as well as neo-Pentecostal leaders.”

His main obstacle, however, will be walking the tightrope between political pragmatism and continuing to convince hardline Bolsonaristas that he is a “loyal ally”.

It is unlikely, in de Souza’s view, that there will be a member of the Bolsonaro family on the presidential ticket come the next election in 2030. “They are much more likely to be figures that provide endorsement, rather than actual players themselves,” he said.

Among voters, however, Bolsonarism stepping into the background appears like a distant thought. “The Bolsonaro family is always trying to perpetuate its power in Brazil,” noted voter Cunha, pointing to the election of Flavio’s brother Carlos and mother-in-law Michelle to Senate seats.

“I definitely think there could be a Bolsonaro on the ballot in 2030; I just don’t know which one.”

title: Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show
excerpt:
Israel's election result is messy - here's why

Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot,...
body_text:
Israel's election result is messy - here's why

Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, but is still short of a majority in parliament.

With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48.

Both leaders have said they will try to form a governing coalition.

Arab-led parties, who are on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.

With between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots from groups including soldiers, diplomats and hospital patients yet to be counted, it could still take a day or two for the final election results to emerge.

Once they are confirmed, President Isaac Herzog will hold consultations with all the political factions and invite the leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a government - a process that could take weeks.

If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.

How could Israel break election deadlock? Here are four scenarios

Netanyahu and Eisenkot face difficult paths to power as neither set to win majority

During a meeting at his residence in Jerusalem, Herzog praised the 77.7% turnout in Tuesday's election, which was the country's highest in more than two decades.

"It is a badge of honour for Israeli society, and it was remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he said.

He added that he expected to receive the official results next week, after which he would begin discussions with every faction.

"We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So, I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."

Both the prime minister and his main rival have insisted that they should be tasked with forming a governing coalition.

Benjamin Netanyahu called for "a strong right-wing national government"

Eisenkot declared that the public had "spoken in favour of change", after initial exit polls published by three Israeli broadcasters projected that his "Change Bloc" would emerge with between 52 and 53 seats in the Knesset, compared to 50 seats for Netanyahu's bloc.

"The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust," he told supporters at Yashar's election headquarters in Tel Aviv. "I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government."

Later, the broadcasters updated their exit polls, with two projecting that the rival blocs would be tied on 51 seats and one giving Netanyahu's bloc a narrow three-seat lead.

Netanyahu then appeared at Likud's headquarters in Jerusalem and declared that his right-wing bloc had won a "great majority".

"We must put in place a strong right-wing national government," he said. "It is forbidden, simply forbidden, to endanger Israel by forming a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties."

As the votes were counted on Wednesday, it emerged that his bloc had done better than the exit polls predicted and was on course to win 53 seats. However, that figure is 15 seats fewer than it had once controlled in the last Knesset.

Tuesday's election was the first since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

It was also seen by Israelis as one of the most consequential in the country's history, because it could decide not just their leadership but whether the country continues on its current hard-line, religious-nationalist trajectory.

Key campaign issues included accountability for the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, the conduct of regional wars, conscripting ultra-Orthodox Jewish men into the military, judicial reforms and Israel's international standing.

Avigail Levine from Kfar Saba, who voted for former prime minister Naftali Bennett's opposition Beyachad party, told the BBC that she was disappointed with the election results.

"I was hoping for new leadership. I feel we need it as a nation," she said. "The people in power on 7 October should not be in power now."

She said people were frustrated that Netanyahu had not shouldered responsibility for what happened three years ago, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage. Her husband's grandmother was among those who died in Kibbutz Be'eri.

Gal from Ramat Gan said he voted for Netanyahu because Israelis "cannot relax and live in peace with neighbours when all they want is to erase us from the map".

He also said he was "afraid of the strengthening of the Arab political parties".

Likud complained on Wednesday that they had "stolen" the election. It alleged that they had resorted to "bribery, threats, violence, fraud and the use of prohibited software to encourage voters", without providing any evidence. The Central Elections Committee said it would examine the claims as part of a post-election review.

Gadi Eisenkot said the Israeli public had "spoken in favour of change"

The two Arab parties - the United Arab List and the Joint List - are set to almost double their representation because of a surge in turnout among Arab Israelis, who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Mahdi Kabaha from the Arab-majority city of Umm al-Fahm, who campaigned to get out the Arab vote, described the result as "historic".

"Arab citizens came out and said clearly: we want a real say in this country," he said.

The head of the Joint List, Yousef Jabareen, told the BBC that Arab voters had been motivated in part by the opportunity to remove far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir from office, whom he accused of racism and "provocation against our community".

Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party, has called for the annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians. Several Western countries have imposed sanctions on him for incitement against Palestinians.

United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas, who served in a short-lived governing coalition formed after the 2021 elections, said on Tuesday night that he hoped "the numbers will work out and we, the Change Bloc and the UAL, can ensure that there are 61 Knesset seats".

The leader of the left-wing Democrats party, Yair Golan, told his partners in Eisenkot's bloc that there was an "opportunity to form a change government in partnership" with the Arab parties and replace Netanyahu's coalition.

"We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't put an end to racism," he wrote on X.

Eisenkot has previously raised objections or attached conditions to that kind of alliance, including recognising Israel as Jewish and democratic, and Hamas as a terrorist organisation that must be destroyed. The right-wing parties in his bloc, meanwhile, have flatly rejected it.

"The opposition parties cannot dictate any conditions," Jabareen said. "If the opposition in Israel are willing to afford real and substantive change, and an alternative for the dangerous, extreme-right-wing government... they will have to negotiate with us."

The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future

How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election

Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters

title: Flávio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after defeat in Brazil's presidential election
excerpt:
Watch: Bolsonaro shielded from media by umbrellas at Florida airport

Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro has flown to Miami after losing the country's presidential election on Sunday.

His arrival in ...
body_text:
Watch: Bolsonaro shielded from media by umbrellas at Florida airport

Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro has flown to Miami after losing the country's presidential election on Sunday.

His arrival in Florida ends days of confusion over his whereabouts, after he was reported to have travelled to Argentina, and then prematurely reported to have already entered the US on Tuesday.

The US has said it would grant visas to Bolsonaro and his family, who travelled with him. Brazil cancelled his passport, after he failed to surrender it to authorities, due to an ongoing criminal investigation. He has denied any wrongdoing.

In a statement, Bolsonaro cast himself "as the true elected president of Brazil", and thanked the American government for granting entry to his family.

Newly reelected President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has criticised the departure, saying "those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear".

In a statement, distributed by the right-wing Brazilian influencer Paulo Figueiredo,  Bolsonaro thanked both the presidents of Argentina and the US, and the American public "who share the same values ​​as the good people of my own country".

"It was never my intention to leave my homeland, but I know exactly where this is heading," he said.

He repeated unfounded allegations of "electoral fraud" which he said allowed a "mathematical impossibility" to occur in the election.

He called himself a victim of a coup d'état and political persecution, and said his travel to the US was to protect his family.

"I want to tell not only my 60 million voters, but the entire Brazilian people, that I am the elected president," he alleged.

"The criminals who stole Brazil's election are part of a criminal organization that has established a tyranny."

After Bolsonaro won the first round of Brazil's election, Lula won the second round by more than four million votes, which was attributed to significantly higher turnout, and swaying more undecided voters.

The result was confirmed by the president of Brazil's top electoral court, himself appointed by Jair Bolsonaro. He said that an extension to voting hours did not impact the count or result.

Speculation about Bolsonaro's whereabouts was first triggered by a report on an Argentine news site, which claimed that he had crossed the land border between Brazil and Argentina and then boarded a private plane en route to the US.

Brazilian police took the rumours seriously. Early on Tuesday, they checked border crossings but found no evidence that Bolsonaro had left the country, and Argentine officials said they had no reports of him crossing.

For a little while, it seemed like Bolsonaro may just be keeping an uncharacteristically low profile after being unexpectedly beaten by his left-wing rival in the presidential run-off vote on Sunday.

When he failed to surrender his passports in time to meet a 24-hour deadline, Brazilian authorities cancelled the documents and ordered police to make checks at border posts.

With Bolsonaro's lawyers saying they did not know where he was, speculation quickly grew again that he might have left the country.

How did Flávio Bolsonaro end up in Miami?

Confusion about Bolsonaro's whereabouts as Argentina says he flew to Ecuador

Then, several sources told the BBC and other broadcasters he was on his way to the US.

The US State Department confirmed that it would issue Bolsonaro and his family visas to enter the country.

There were even reports that he had already landed. BBC Brasil and BBC Mundo were informed by three people close to the Bolsonaros that the senator had arrived in the US.

A cousin, who is close to Flávio Bolsonaro and his younger brother Eduardo, told BBC Brasil that the defeated right-wing candidate had arrived in Miami.

Another close aide to Eduardo Bolsonaro told BBC Mundo that Flávio was with his younger brother in Miami.

Neither Flávio nor Eduardo Bolsonaro could be reached directly for comment at the time.

Flávio Bolsonaro was seen getting off a plane in Miami on Wednesday morning

Hours later, however, Argentine migration authorities posted a tweet saying that Flávio Bolsonaro, his wife, and two daughters had only just crossed into Argentina over land on Tuesday night local time.

At around the same time, US President Donald Trump told reporters who quizzed him over the matter: "I heard he was in Argentina."

Flight tracking data verified by the BBC suggested the Bolsonaros departed from Puerto Iguazú in Argentina at 12:18 local time (03:18 GMT) on Wednesday to head to Guayaquil in Ecuador.

After a brief stop, the same private jet took them to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport, where they were pictured disembarking just before 09:30 local time (13:30 GMT).

Photographers, who had been waiting for his arrival to finally put an end to all the speculation, swarmed around Bolsonaro as he left the airport in Miami, while his team tried to cover him with umbrellas.

Flávio Bolsonaro is not the first member of his family to travel to the United States.

His father, Jair Bolsonaro, also left Brazil for Florida in December 2022 before his successor, Lula, was inaugurated.

Jair was still in the US when his supporters stormed Brazil's government buildings and Supreme Court on 8 January. He later used his absence as part of his defence in his coup trial, which led to a conviction and 27-year sentence.

Eduardo Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has been living in Texas after taking leave from Brazil's Congress. While in the US, he lobbied officials there in an attempt to influence the coup trial of his father, which led to the US imposing punitive tariffs on Brazil and sanctions on key officials.

Eduardo was convicted in absentia over this by Brazil's highest court earlier this year.

It is not yet clear what Flávio Bolsonaro's ultimate destination will be, nor how long he plans to stay in the US.

He is the subject of two investigations currently pending before Brazil's Supreme Federal Court.

One is regarding possible irregularities in the transfer of nearly $70m (£53m) from private bank Banco Master to the film Dark Horse – a biopic about his father.

The second investigation relates to alleged money laundering, both of which Bolsonaro denies.

He is set to lose his parliamentary immunity on 31 January, when his eight-year Senate term ends.

Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback

Lula's comeback in Brazil dents Trump's ambitions for Latin America

title: UN votes to condemn embargo of Cuba despite US lobbying push
excerpt:
The United Nations General Assembly has again voted in favour of a resolution condemning the United States’s economic embargo of Cuba despite a push by US officials to peel off support.

The resolutio...
body_text:
The United Nations General Assembly has again voted in favour of a resolution condemning the United States’s economic embargo of Cuba despite a push by US officials to peel off support.

The resolution passed on Wednesday with 130 countries in favour and 17 opposed, including the US and Israel. Another 25 countries abstained, including countries such as Germany and Italy, that had previously voted in favour. The General Assembly has voted to condemn the embargo annually for more than three decades.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said in a social media post after the vote that the US was “once again isolated in its attempt to continue strangling the Cuban people”.

“Neither its most insane pretexts nor its pressures nor media circus will prevail over the force of facts and truth,” he added.

The US embargo on Cuba, part of an effort to isolate the country and squeeze its economy that has lasted more than six decades, has been widely condemned on the world stage and linked to worsening hardship on the island.

US President Donald Trump’s administration has implemented a series of additional economic restrictions, including an energy blockade, to further tighten the screws.

That economic campaign has also been accompanied by a US diplomatic push to further isolate Havana, an effort that US officials said is apparent in the uptick in countries that abstained during Wednesday’s vote. Cuban officials accused the US of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions and other penalties if they voted to condemn the embargo.

“I’m satisfied that so many countries now, including major economies like Korea, like Germany and others have shifted their position,” US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told reporters after the vote.

“Diplomacy takes time, but now that we’ve had a tripling of countries that have shifted, we expect that to only continue to grow,” he added.

Tensions between US and Cuban officials exploded on Tuesday during a General Assembly debate with both yelling at the other and engaging in an apparent shoving match.

Waltz said on Wednesday that Richard Tur de la Concepcion, a first secretary at Cuba’s UN mission, would be expelled from the country for “assaulting an American diplomat”.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the US and Cuban missions for comment but has not received a response.

title: Dem AG’s ‘too many golf courses’ remark goes viral as critics tee off
excerpt: Former Louisiana Rep. Garret Graves joins 'Fox News Live' to analyze how artificial intelligence expansion is impacting local communities. As tech giants build data centers nationwide, voters voice co...
body_text:
Former Louisiana Rep. Garret Graves joins 'Fox News Live' to analyze how artificial intelligence expansion is impacting local communities. As tech giants build data centers nationwide, voters voice concerns over power grids and water usage.

Arizona’s Senate president took aim at viral comments about the future of golf from the state’s Democratic attorney general as their battle to be the state’s top law enforcement officer entered its final stretch before next week’s midterm elections.

A remark about potentially restricting golf courses and the Grand Canyon State having "too much grass" turned a debate over water conservation into a campaign flashpoint, with Sen. Warren Petersen accusing Attorney General Kris Mayes of targeting a multibillion-dollar industry in the desert state while Mayes later insisted her remarks were taken out of context.

"Kris Mayes thinks Arizona has too many golf courses. I think Arizona has too many radical politicians who believe government should dictate which industries get to thrive," Petersen, R-Maricopa, told Fox News Digital Tuesday.

100 DAYS UNTIL MIDTERMS AND DEMOCRATS ARE WINNING BECAUSE THEY ACTUALLY HAVE A MESSAGE

"Our golf courses support jobs, tourism, small businesses and communities across this state. Instead of attacking an industry that contributes to our economy, the attorney general should be focused on enforcing the law, protecting consumers and defending Arizona families."

In an interview with Politico delving into the data center debate and whether the proliferation of water-intensive buildings is wise, particularly in an arid state, Mayes cited neighboring states allegedly "backed by" the Trump administration as hindrances to Arizona’s local supply.

Mayes' golf course remarks came shortly after she warned that Arizona was headed toward a potential Supreme Court showdown over Colorado River water supplies.

"We could do a hell of a lot more when it comes to conservation," she said, citing tax incentives for catchment and removal of lawns.

GRAND CANYON WATER PIPELINE DAMAGED AGAIN AS FLOODING COMPLICATES REPAIRS

Arizona Senate President Warren Petersen speaks during a rally for vice presidential nominee JD Vance at Arizona Christian University July 31, 2024. (Imagn)

"We have way, way too much grass in Arizona. We probably, frankly — and I'm sure the golf industry is not going to like this when I say this — we probably have too many golf courses in Arizona right now."

That remark sparked blowback from Petersen and many others.

"We don’t have a golf course problem in Arizona. We have a dumocrat (sic) problem in Arizona," quipped Rep. Eli Crane, R-Ariz.

"Kris Mayes is promising to get rid of golf courses. I promise to get rid of Kris Mayes," Petersen added in his own tweet.

E-procurement software CEO Tom Spengler added that Arizona "honestly need[s] more golf courses."

"Tee times are very hard to get and rates have doubled or tripled since COVID," he said.

"We have too much grass — said no one ever, other than Kris Mayes," added Turning Point USA executive Justin Streiff.

Arizona’s business community also took notice, and Arizona Chamber of Commerce Vice President Courtney Coolidge responded to Mayes with several statistics about golf’s impact on the state.

Coolidge reported a $6 billion economic impact, 66,000 jobs, $2.3 billion in wages and $520 million in tax revenue. Most relevant to the water debate, she said golf courses collectively use 2% or less of the state’s water resources.

Those stats also lined up closely with separate figures in a 2023 study by the Arizona Alliance for Golf.

Popular golf satire site PGA Tuor shared a clip of Mayes’ comments, writing, "How to not get re-elected 101."

Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes speaks at an Arizona AFL-CIO Get Out the Vote canvass launch with union members and supporters Nov. 2, 2024, in Phoenix, Ariz. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

Another putting enthusiast said Mayes’ comments cost her his vote, saying, "[She] has no idea what the economic impact golf has on our entire state."

Fox News Digital reached out to Mayes for comment on the viral nature and content of her remarks.

The Democrat separately tweeted that she was intending to make a larger point about water usage.

"Relax, nobody's closing golf courses," Mayes said.

"My point is we need incentives to help all Arizonans and major industries swap thirsty grass and catch rainwater, especially if our water situation gets worse — while I take on the foreign mega-farms and data centers draining our water."

She then accused Petersen of spreading "false claims."

A golfer tees off during a tour in Flagstaff, Ariz. (Chris Coduto/Getty Images)

But Mayes’ response was also met with ridicule. X critics called it "condescending" while one also quipped, "you relax – we all heard you." Others characterized her stated approach toward the golf industry as "communist."

With Election Day just days away, Petersen is betting the controversy will resonate beyond the fairways, casting Mayes' remarks as part of a larger dispute over government intervention in Arizona's economy as Republicans seek to regain control of a state government they once reliably held.

Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: US ambassador suggests Trump could blame Canada if midterms don’t go his way
excerpt:
Pete Hoekstra, controversial US ambassador to Canada, has also accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections

The US ambassador has suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans perform ...
body_text:
Pete Hoekstra, controversial US ambassador to Canada, has also accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections

The US ambassador has suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans perform poorly in next week’s midterm elections, the latest intervention from a controversial figure who has been accused of inflaming a bitter dispute that has angered and baffled residents of both countries.

On Wednesday, CTV news reported that Pete Hoekstra told business leaders at a closed door meeting that if a number of swing races – including Maine and Michigan – go to the Democrats, it could make things harder for Canada because Donald Trump might try to blame the loss on it.

“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” the prime minister, Mark Carney, told reporters when asked about the allegations.

For months, Canada and the US have been locked in a bitter tariff war, with Ottawa retaliating against illegal US tariffs and targeting goods in states that rely heavily on trade with Canada.

Carney said that Canada “will pursue” such a deal if it presents itself, but that Ottawa’s trade negotiators are “not in that position right now”.

Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particular for his response to Trump’s rhetoric about making Canada the 51st US state. Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the threats as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”. He had previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election as “anti-American”.

This year a House of Commons petition signed by more than 225,000 Canadians called for his expulsion, suggesting his statements violated diplomatic protocols, including the prohibition on diplomats interfering in the internal affairs of a host country.

More recently, Hoekstra has accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections, pointing to Canadian politicians who have criticized the tariffs in US media, and the province of Ontario’s anti-tariff advertisement that ran on US television.

“We see all of that. We are monitoring it. We are evaluating it. And if some of it becomes election interference, America will respond to it,” Hoekstra, who comes from Michigan, recently told a Canadian podcast, adding that Canadians should “keep your nose out of American politics”.

Canada’s industry minister, Mélanie Joly, who was a target of Hoekstra’s comments, told reporters in Ottawa that her country “would never do that” and said Canada would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada”.

Carney, while in Turkey, told reporters there was “no merit” to the claims of interference and that he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.

Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, said the remarks were an “extraordinary thing” for a US ambassador to say about his host country and looked like an effort to “manufacture a pretext for the Trump administration’s own political difficulties”.

“The job of an ambassador is to represent the interests of his country, but it’s also to maintain channels of communication and build relationships and manage disagreements,” he said.

“His comments have repeatedly aggravated tensions instead of helping to manage them. I don’t think that he’s serving American interests very well. I’m not even sure that he’s serving the interests of his president.”

Paris points to polling in the US that shows voters have increasingly linked tariffs, the war and cost of living. There is also widespread confusion over why the White House has chosen to treat Canada as a trade adversary.

“It’s certainly not working in Canada. It’s on the contrary. It seems that every time Mr Hoekstra opens his mouth, the Canadians are more determined than before to stand up to the bullying of the Trump administration,” he said. “That’s not serving American interests.”

The US embassy denied Hoekstra said Canada would face blame for a poor Republican showing, suggesting the remarks were “grossly taken out of context” from a broader discussion.

“The ambassador has consistently said that the Canadian media is attempting to overstate the relevance of Canadian issues in American elections. As we have previously stated, Americans will decide American elections based on issues that are important to them,” the embassy said in a statement.

At a Canadian American Business event last year, Hoekstra delivered what witnesses say was an expletive-laden tirade at Ontario’s trade representative after the province ran a series of anti-tariff ads in the US that featured Ronald Reagan. Ontario’s premier called the outburst “absolutely unacceptable” and “unbecoming of an ambassador”.

Last week, Barack Obama noted the unusual choice to attack a longtime ally while speaking at a Democratic campaign rally in Detroit, mocking Trump’s fixation on Canada and jokingly referring to his northern neighbor as a “well-known evil empire”.

“That historical adversary of ours: Canada,” the former US president said. “It’s your neighbor! It’s a few minutes drive over the bridge. These are the people who gave us Martin Short … and maple syrup. They are the nicest people. And somehow we’ve gotten them so mad.”

title: Education secretary Linda McMahon plans to spend nearly $43,000 on office furniture
excerpt:
Trump ally, who is seeking to shutter the department, had said office relocation would save taxpayers $4.8m annually

The Trump administration has insisted its controversial education cuts are saving ...
body_text:
Trump ally, who is seeking to shutter the department, had said office relocation would save taxpayers $4.8m annually

The Trump administration has insisted its controversial education cuts are saving “millions of dollars” after it was reported that Linda McMahon, secretary of education, is planning to spend roughly $43,000 on new furniture for her office.

McMahon’s office told Congress that the secretary’s current furniture was worn out and “cannot be configurationally or aesthetically integrated into the agency’s new office space”, according to non-public records seen by the New York Times.

In March, McMahon – who is seeking to permanently shutter the Department of Education – announced the department would relocate from its headquarters in the Lyndon B Johnson building to a smaller building in downtown Washington DC, which housed the US Agency for International Development (USAID) before the Trump administration closed it down.

McMahon claimed the relocation would save taxpayers $4.8m annually. Now, the education secretary’s office needs new furniture for the office, including a new desk, conference table, chairs and other items, an unnamed senior official told the New York Times.

The new furnishings are expected to cost $43,278.64.

Savannah Newhouse, the education department’s press secretary, claimed in a statement the administration was “saving taxpayers millions of dollars” through its education cuts, adding: “Believe it or not, just like in the private sector, new federal offices need places to sit, write, and meet.”

Though McMahon is reportedly planning to furnish her new office at the department, her overall goal is to diminish staffing and remove responsibilities that her department oversees, in effect shutting it down.

Shortly after returning to office in 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order directing McMahon, a former executive at World Wrestling Entertainment turned cabinet member, to close the Department of Education.

The Department of Education was established by Congress and can only be dissolved at the direction of Congress, but the Republican-controlled chambers have not moved to do so. But the administration has taken steps to reduce the department’s power. So far, the administration has nearly halved the department’s staffing through workforce reductions and moved department-specific responsibilities to other agencies through “interagency agreements”.

Among those, special education services have been moved to the Department of Health and Human Services and civil rights enforcement efforts have been moved to the justice department.

Trump and McMahon have insisted that effectively shuttering the Department of Education will give states more authority over education, despite states already controlling most of their education policies, and eliminate unnecessary bureaucratic processes.

title: 'Never-ending' cruise grinds to devastating end, stranding over 200 passengers abroad
excerpt:
A residential cruise ship that offered retirees the chance to travel the world indefinitely suspended its voyage after mounting fuel expenses left its operator facing major losses.

A dream cruise aro...
body_text:
A residential cruise ship that offered retirees the chance to travel the world indefinitely suspended its voyage after mounting fuel expenses left its operator facing major losses.

A dream cruise around the world has come to an abrupt halt after two years at sea, reportedly leaving passengers scrambling to find somewhere to stay in Cambodia.

The Villa Vie Odyssey, a residential cruise ship that promised passengers the chance to make the ocean their permanent home, suspended its voyage Tuesday after its operator said soaring fuel costs had made it too expensive to continue.

CRUISE VACATION COMES TO CRASHING HALT AS SHIP SLAMS INTO 2 CARGO VESSELS

The ship was carrying 203 passengers, most of them Americans, and 156 crew members when it arrived in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, according to The Associated Press.

Passengers said they were given just seven hours' notice to leave the vessel Tuesday and had to make their own arrangements, despite the company's claims that it was helping residents find temporary accommodations.

In a statement, Villa Vie Residences, which is headquartered in Florida, announced that it had been "unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses."

The residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey arrived in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, carrying 203 passengers and 156 crew members.  (AFP via Getty Images)

The company said monthly fuel expenses per cabin had climbed from roughly $1,800 to as much as $8,000 in parts of Asia.

ANGRY CRUISE PASSENGERS SAY FRUSTRATING ISSUE SHOULD HAVE BEEN DISCLOSED BEFORE BOOKING

"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," the company said, according to the AP. "Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees."

The company added, "The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements."

The Villa Vie Odyssey, seen above, suspended its around-the-world voyage after its operator said soaring fuel costs had made continued operations financially unsustainable. (AFP via Getty Images)

The ship first set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024, on what was supposed to be a 3 1/2-year journey around the world.

For some passengers, the ship was supposed to be their permanent home long after the initial voyage ended.

MAJOR CRUISE LINE HIKES ITS POPULAR PACKAGE PRICES IN MOVE THAT COULD HIT VACATION BUDGETS

Fox Business reported in May 2024 that Villa Vie Residences was offering lifetime access to its Odyssey cruise ship through its "Endless Horizons" program for a one-time payment of $299,999 for a single-occupancy cabin or $499,999 for double occupancy.

At the time, the experience was billed as a budget-conscious alternative to traditional retirement.

"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk."

The company marketed the program to retirees concerned about inflation, rising living expenses and the possibility of outliving their savings.

CEO Mikael Petterson similarly promoted the experience as a way for retirees to live on a fixed budget without worrying about ongoing expenses.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"For less than the price of an average home, you can secure a lifetime of experiences," Petterson said at the time.

Speaking to AP, passengers expressed disappointment over the abrupt end to their voyage.

Passengers who had planned to spend years living aboard the Villa Vie Odyssey faced uncertainty after the company announced it could no longer continue the voyage. (AFP via Getty Images)

Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming who boarded the ship 17 months ago, said they purchased a cabin with plans to spend years traveling the world — but were repeatedly asked to contribute more money for fuel.

"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," Lynn Montoya said.

"We had hopes, but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole," the AP reported.

California sisters Carol Larson, 69, and Crystal Lavering, 72, also said they were heartbroken after spending 18 months aboard the ship.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Larson, who paid $120,000 for her cabin, said she hoped residents could buy the ship and keep the cruise going.

Despite the setback, she told the AP she had no regrets about her investment.

The Villa Vie Odyssey's operator said monthly fuel expenses per cabin had climbed from roughly $1,800 to as much as $8,000 in parts of Asia. (AP Photo/Heng Sinith)

"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk," said Larson.

"From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth. … I still feel that way."

Fox News Digital reached out to Villa Vie Residences for comment.

The Associated Press contributed reporting.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

The most difficult part of the suspension for Sweat may not have been missing two games, but facing Bears coach Ben Johnson.

title: Budget 2026: Healey hikes taxes on banks and landlords to fund £100 handouts to 20m households
excerpt:
Few surprises as chancellor uses low-key speech blaming ‘global economic storms’ for stoking energy prices and cost of living crisis

Briefing: key questions answered by Heather Stewart and Pippa Crer...
body_text:
Few surprises as chancellor uses low-key speech blaming ‘global economic storms’ for stoking energy prices and cost of living crisis

Briefing: key questions answered by Heather Stewart and Pippa Crerar

Editorial: Budget’s bold ambitions and welcome first steps

John Healey raised taxes on banks and landlords to fund a £100 winter handout for 20 million families as official forecasts made clear there is no end in sight for the cost of living crisis.

In his first budget, the chancellor blamed “global economic storms” for the grim outlook, as the war in Iran drives up oil and gas prices.

But he also faced criticism for failing to squeeze more money from profitable banks, punishing savers and not giving enough help to the poorest.

In a low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, Healey was at pains to stress he was sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules, and there were few surprises in his hour-long address to MPs.

But with households facing soaring energy prices, and mortgage bills rising amid higher interest rates, Healey offered a £100 cost-of-living payout, which will be sent to all English households in council tax bands A-D.

It formed the centrepiece of a cost of living package, which he said would “take the pressure off in the coldest months, and see people through to the spring”.

The £2.6bn cost of the £100 giveaway includes funding for the Scottish and Welsh governments, which Healey said he hoped they would use to implement a similar scheme.

“I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. I know that people look to government at times like this, not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space,” he said.

But the government’s independent forecaster warned households face a “grim picture” on living standards, as it slashed the outlook for the economy in 2027 and said there was “virtually no growth” in disposable income for households.

Healey also came under fire for an unexpected 2p increase in tax rates for income earned on property or savings. As well as hitting savers and landlords, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said it risks “leading to a steady rise in rents”, by deterring landlords from the market and cutting supply, as well as passing on costs to tenants.

Ruth Curtice, the chief executive of the Resolution Foundation thinktank, criticised the £100 handout, arguing it would have been better to give more generous support to the poorest consumers.

“The chancellor has missed the mark with badly targeted support that has left families facing a tough winter as energy bills rise,” she said.

As expected, the chancellor also cancelled fuel tax rises planned by Rachel Reeves, and extended the VAT cut on electricity prices previously announced to next summer.

Healey announced several measures intended to cut businesses’ costs – including raising the rates relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 for companies in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors. The change would be funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops, he said.

The cost of the household support measures will be met by a doubling of the additional levy banks pay on their profits, to 6%; as well as the higher taxes on income from property and savings.

The additional bank tax will only last for 15 months and marked a less significant rise than some in the industry had feared. Banks’ share prices were among the highest risers in the blue chip FTSE 100 index on Wednesday.

Laura Suter, director of personal finance at AJ Bell, said: “Savers will be hit with another hefty tax rise on their savings interest, adding to the squeeze on their savings over the past few years.”

She added that the higher tax on rental income “could be passed on to tenants, with rent hikes a potential lever for landlords to mitigate any increase in tax”.

“Equally, we could see yet more landlords selling up, in favour of investing their money in other assets that have lower taxes and less government tinkering,” she said.

The New Economics Foundation thinktank accused Healey of failing to be bold enough. Hannah Peaker, its deputy chief executive, said: “As households prepare to be hit by a wave of price rises this winter, the chancellor has shown the right instincts but not yet the right scale.

“The £100 support with energy bills will provide some welcome relief, but the chancellor could have been braver in the face of what we are up against.”

Energy provider EDF predicts that the Ofgem price cap – which determines consumer bills – is set to go up by £466 in January. And despite Healey’s promise of a “breathing space,” in the teeth of the crisis, official forecasts published by the OBR alongside the budget pointed to a challenging winter.

Presenting the forecasts, the OBR’s David Miles highlighted a “pretty grim picture” for household finances, as inflation rises to almost 4%.

Even by 2030-31, it only expects real disposable household incomes – its favoured measure of living standards – to be 2% higher than before the Covid pandemic. It now expects anaemic economic growth of 1% next year, about half a percentage point lower than expected in March.

Healey said higher inflation and interest rates had hit the government’s finances too, ratcheting up the government’s interest bill by £14bn this year alone, but promised to stick to Labour’s fiscal rules.

The OBR said Healey would meet the most important rule – to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues – with a diminished headroom of £15bn by the target date of 2029-30, against the £24bn Rachel Reeves had built up in the spring.

Borrowing is scheduled to be higher than expected in the short term, but the chancellor promised to rebuild the buffer against the rules to £22bn by the end of the five-year forecast period.

“That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can,” he said. Bond markets appeared unruffled by the higher-than-expected borrowing.

The deferral of some important decisions to next year’s spending review prompted the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, to argue Burnham was keeping his options open on an early general election.

Burnham doubled down on his promise not to call one, however, telling reporters on Wednesday that he could rule one out for at least 12 months. “I’m not thinking about my own party and its prospects. I am thinking about people, and I’m thinking about what I can do to help them.”

Badenoch said Britain had “overspent, overborrowed and overtaxed”, and criticised Healey for delayed decisions on defence spending and welfare cuts. Healey has said he will tackle welfare after reports from Alan Milburn on youth unemployment and Sir Stephen Timms on disability benefits, expected next month.

Helen Miller, the director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that by sticking to the tight spending plans bequeathed by Reeves, Healey could be storing up trouble for the spending review due next year.

“History warns us to be sceptical of tight spending plans in later years of the forecast. Next year’s spending review will be a crunch point, and looks very tough for many departments, whose budgets will be squeezed by higher inflation forecasts,” she said.

“The plans for overall spending set out in the budget mean that spending choices at next year’s spending review will be much harder than those made so far this parliament.”

Buried in the budget was a hint at an easing of some migration restrictions, including some industries that will be allowed to lower the salary thresholds for visas to allow companies across the country to hire international talent.

Among the winners was London mayor Lord Sadiq Khan, who received new powers to extend the Bakerloo line in London and a pledge that cross-Channel trains will now also stop at Stratford International in east London. There was also cash to explore hosting the Olympics in “a northern city” – and former Greater Manchester mayor Burnham may have a candidate city in mind.

title: Russell Brand tells court he ‘misused’ fame for ‘reckless philandering’ – latest updates
excerpt:
Brand, 51, who has been charged with three counts of rape says he acted ‘consensually’

Content warning: this article contains references to allegations of sexual abuse which some readers might find d...
body_text:
Brand, 51, who has been charged with three counts of rape says he acted ‘consensually’

Content warning: this article contains references to allegations of sexual abuse which some readers might find distressing

Russell Brand has denied all the allegations made against him as he took to the witness box to give evidence in his trial at Southwark crown court.

The comedian, 51, told the court that his “entire life has been consumed by these allegations”.

Brand said he struggled to find anyone to give evidence on his behalf, saying the consequences of the September 2023 investigation by the Sunday Times, Times, and Channel 4 Dispatches were “devastating”.

He told jurors that he believed consent was “fundamental, essential, necessary and, indeed, in many ways more important than sex itself”.

During cross-examination, Brand admitted he was “obsessed” with sex in his younger years but denied being unable to function without it.

He denied the accusation that he would pretend to be gay to make women trust him.

Russell Brand has finished giving evidence in court.

The judge has sent jurors home for the day, with the trial to resume tomorrow with the defence’s case.

Brand told the court that he was “in a position of fame, a successful person” and that he “misused that commodity foolishly” and “consensually”.

He added that he “was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access” and that he acknowledged it was “wrong”.

He told jurors he “dedicated” a lot of his life to “reckless philandering”.

Brand said it has been “deeply traumatic” since allegations have been made against him, adding that he has focused on recalling events “at the expense of my marriage, my children and my health”.

In response to questions from the prosecutor in relation to alleged inconsistencies in his prepared statement to police and what he has told the jury with regard to one of the complainants, Brand said: “Since these events occurred there’s been escalating recollection.

“Its been a deeply traumatic episode of my life.

“I’ve focused on it at the expense of my marriage, my children and health. I ask your forgiveness, well not your forgiveness, I recognise that this recollection includes small details that are inconsistent and I acknowledge that.”

Brand is being questioned by the prosecution on his statements about the allegations.

He denied constructing his account of events around what the complainants had alleged.

Karmy-Jones asked him about a statement he made in March this year, saying he had received accounts of the allegations from two of the complainants at that point.

She said: “So you knew what they said, and as I’ve already put to you, you constructed your account around some of what they said.”

Brand replied: “I disagree but I agree that you said it.”

During cross-examination, Russell Brand told the court he believes alcohol “makes people less effective as human beings”.

A woman who alleged he raped her in a Soho bar toilet in 2004 told the court in her evidence she had drunk six or seven vodkas before encountering Brand.

When prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told Brand it was “obvious she had been drinking”, Brand said: “Yeah, I suppose so.”

Karmy-Jones put to him that the woman was “more vulnerable”, Brand said: “I agree alcohol makes people less effective.”

When the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, interjected to ask him to clarify, Brand said: “Effective human beings. It’s a deleterious substance.”

Brand said it was a “marvellous night” when he had a threesome with two women backstage at Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.

One of the women accused Brand of anally raping her during a second meeting at his flat a few days later.

Karmy-Jones put to him that it was an example of Brand “never leaving without a conquest” because the woman had refused to have full sex with him backstage.

Brand replied: “That actually went down as quite a marvellous night by the criteria of the time.”

Brand said that “going in and out of bathrooms didn’t attract a great deal of attention” during the time of the alleged offences.

When asked by Karmy-Jones if his behaviour was “normalised” by his peers, Brand said: “In the media in the early 2000s, people going in and out of bathrooms didn’t attract a great deal of attention.”

He added: “Maybe an eyeroll, eyebrow raise.”

Karmy-Jones asked Brand about the woman who alleged he grabbed her breasts before pulling her into a toilet and orally raped her at a bar in Soho in 2004.

When Karmy-Jones put it to him that he groped the woman and dragged her into the toilet, he denied it.

“What were you inviting her into the toilet for?” Karmy-Jones asked.

Karmy-Jones asked him if he recalled telling the woman “don’t be a spoilsport, come on” when she protested, Brand said “I don’t remember”.

The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones, asked Brand about the alleged attempted indecent assault against a woman who worked at MTV in 2001, who alleged the comedian grabbed her arm and tried to drag her into a toilet.

She said to Brand if he “quite enjoyed having sex in toilets” at the time, he replied “yes”.

Karmy-Jones asked: “Sex in toilets happened a lot didn’t it?”

Karmy-Jones asked if he remembered there being a struggle when he grabbed the woman’s arm, he said he did not recall.

Russell Brand’s cross-examination by the prosecution continues.
