title: Fans debate Brewers decision to keep Jacob Misiorowski in dugout with chance to win first ever World Series
excerpt:
Brewers manager Pat Murphy discusses Milwaukee's Dramatic extra-inning Game 4 loss against the Tampa Bay Rays and preparing for Game 5.

It is hardly a new phenomenon to see starting pitchers - elite ...
body_text:
Brewers manager Pat Murphy discusses Milwaukee's Dramatic extra-inning Game 4 loss against the Tampa Bay Rays and preparing for Game 5.

It is hardly a new phenomenon to see starting pitchers - elite ones at that - get the final outs of the World Series, but the Milwaukee Brewers passed on that opportunity.

Up 3-2 heading into the bottom of the 12th, the Brewers were three outs away from a sweep to win their first Fall Classic. Having used up plenty of relievers, manager Pat Murphy decided to keep impending Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski in the dugout and go with Shane Drohan.

But Drohan, who got bitten by his defense, did not record an out, and a Game 5 will be played Wednesday night.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Milwaukee Brewers pitcher Jacob Misiorowski throws during the first inning of a baseball game against the St. Louis Cardinals on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026, in Milwaukee. (AP Photo/Kayla Wolf)

After the game, Murphy said Misiorowski, who was always slated to, and will, start Game 5, was not an option.

"You can't blow that type of situation on a one-run lead on the road," Murphy said. "If we were in the 13th inning and had a three-run lead, that might be a little bit different, and I probably still wouldn't have."

The move was highly debated on social media in the early morning hours after the game.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"I'm not crazy for thinking that the Brewers should have put in Misiorowski to start the inning, right? You need 3 outs, go use your best arm to get them," one X user said.

"Not sure it gets as utter woke nonsense as saving the best pitcher in the world for a hypothetical game 5 where you’d still be up 3-1," said another.

"Wouldn’t have needed a game 5 , congrats on out thinking yourself," added one more.

Milwaukee Brewers hard-throwing righty and presumptive NL Cy Young winner Jacob Misiorowski got his first postseason start in Game 1 of the NLDS against the San Diego Padres. (Photo by Rob Tringali/MLB Photos via Getty Images)

YANKEES LEGEND SAYS HE DOES NOT 'FEEL WELCOME' BY TEAM DESPITE LEGENDARY CAREER

"They had 3-0 game lead. No reason to throw Misiorowski in this game," one opposer said.

"What if he had and Tampa still won. He would have lost him for at least game 5," a Rays fan wrote.

Misiorowski pitched to an MLB-leading 1.80 ERA this season, and his 252 strikeouts and 13.0 K/9 were also league bests . He has not found similar success in October, but he's still fared quite nicely (2.70 ERA, 14 strikeouts in 13.1 innings spanning three starts).

Had Misiorowski blown the save (an unlikely scenario), who knows who would pitch Game 5, but it's hard to imagine that he would not be available in a necessary Game 6 at home.

Murphy went with seven relievers after starter Dustin May tossed just three innings. Trevor Megill was used for one batter in the eighth inning, and Aaron Ashby, who has now allowed a run in 18.0 innings, started the ninth and was taken out after recording one out in the 11th.

Milwaukee Brewers pitcher Jacob Misiorowski throws during the sixth inning against the St. Louis Cardinals in Milwaukee on May 25, 2026. (Kayla Wolf/AP)

After an error to start the inning, the Tampa Bay Rays rattled off four straight hits to force Game 5 at Tropicana Field. First pitch is shortly after 8 p.m. ET.

title: Woman woke up to see stranger invited into bedroom by husband, court hears
excerpt:
Jury at Winchester crown court sees video evidence by Joanne Young, 49, in trial of four men accused of sexual assault

A woman who was allegedly sexually assaulted by men invited into their family ho...
body_text:
Jury at Winchester crown court sees video evidence by Joanne Young, 49, in trial of four men accused of sexual assault

A woman who was allegedly sexually assaulted by men invited into their family home by her ex-husband described how she would wake in the middle of the night restrained and blindfolded and feeling “hazy”.

Joanne Young said that on one occasion she managed to remove her blindfold and was shocked to glimpse a stranger in her bedroom who her husband, Philip Young, had allegedly arranged to have sex with her.

On another occasion she came around feeling “terrified”, with her husband asking her: “Wouldn’t you like it if somebody else was here?”

Philip Young, 50, “advertised” Joanne Young on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court has heard.

He has pleaded guilty to multiple charges of abuse, but four men who allegedly sexually assaulted Joanne Young, having been invited into the couple’s home by Philip Young, are on trial.

Recorded video interviews of Joanne Young, 49, telling her story to the police were watched by the jury on Wednesday.

Joanne Young said she and “Phil” had been married for 20 years and had three children. She said they were a straight, monogamous couple. “It was always just the two of us,” she said.

On one occasion early on in their marriage, he “joked” about watching her when she was having sex with someone else but she “laughed it off”. She said: “That was never part of our relationship and was never going to be.”

He liked to restrain and blindfold her during sex. “I didn’t object, it was fine,” she said.

But she said she would wake up not knowing how she had come to be restrained. “I’d wake up and there would be a blindfold on and restraints and I wouldn’t always remember them going on. It was a bit like, when did that happen?” She described feeling “hazy” when she woke.

On a night in February 2023, Joanne Young woke up and removed the blindfold and restraints. “I wasn’t comfortable,” she said. “I don’t know what was bothering me.”

When she got the blindfold off, she realised there was a stranger in her room. Philip Young told the second person to “get down” and he ducked out of sight.

“I was in shock,” said Joanne Young. “There was this man in my house and I was naked.” She hid in a bathroom and the next day asked her husband: “What was that?”

He told her he had invited someone to watch them have sex. “I was shocked someone had been there, it was so intrusive.” He claimed it had not happened before. “I thought it was a one-off,” Joanne Young said.

She said she decided to “stick my head in the sand” and carry on. “You can’t forgive. You have to hope it won’t happen again.”

Joanne Young said that on the day of his arrest, her husband admitted to her that he had shared explicit images of her. “That was totally out of the blue. It was a kick in the stomach. How could he do that to me? That is so intimate, it’s not allowed.”

She asked him if the incident in February was the only time such a thing had happened. Joanne Young said: “He stood there and looked at me and said: ‘No’”.

After the arrest, Joanne Young recalled a “vague” incident some years before when she had woken up feeling “terrified” and saying: “No, no.”

She said: “I remember him [Philip] saying: ‘Wouldn’t you like it if somebody else was here?’ I was scared.” The next day she put it down to a nightmare.

Four men are charged with sexually assaulting Joanne Young jointly with Philip Young.

Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, of Swindon, Wiltshire, denies sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching in June 2016. Richard Wilkins, 62, of Toothill, Swindon, has pleaded not guilty to one count of rape and one of assault by penetration in July 2016.

Norman Macksoni, 48, of Sharnbrook, Bedfordshire, denies one count of rape in February 2017. Mohammed Hassan, 38, of Swindon, has pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual touching in February 2023.

title: US lawmakers demand action on overcharging at 7-Eleven, Dollar General and other chains
excerpt:
Democrats urge FTC to tackle ‘systemic failure’ of biggest convenience and dollar stores over pricing practices after Guardian investigations

Thirty-four members of Congress are calling on the Federa...
body_text:
Democrats urge FTC to tackle ‘systemic failure’ of biggest convenience and dollar stores over pricing practices after Guardian investigations

Thirty-four members of Congress are calling on the Federal Trade Commission to investigate reports of widespread overcharging by some of America’s most-recognized brand-name retailers.

The 28 October letter to the FTC comes in direct response to Guardian investigations of four of the nation’s largest dollar-store and convenience-store chains. Both investigations revealed pervasive mismatches between shelf labels and register prices.

The first, published in December, found that Dollar General had failed more than 4,300 government price-accuracy inspections in 23 states over a three-year period on items such as peanut butter, spaghetti sauce and Flintstone vitamins. Its smaller rival, Family Dollar, failed 2,100 price inspections in 20 states over the same period.

The second, published last month, found a similar pattern at convenience store chains 7-Eleven and Circle K. Consumer complaints, along with state and local inspections, revealed overcharges for snacks, beverages, toiletries, tobacco and medications. In addition, some stores charged more at the pump for gasoline than the prices displayed on their big road-facing signs.

“These reports show that these incidents are not isolated to a geographic area or to a handful of stores,” the Congress members’ letter said. “Instead, the scale of documented violations seems to be the result of systemic failure within corporate operations, leading to customers overpaying for their groceries, potentially without knowing.”

All four companies have told the Guardian in written statements that they try to keep register prices consistent with shelf prices.

The letter, written by US House Democrats from 17 states and the District of Columbia, was addressed to the FTC chair, Andrew N Ferguson, a Trump appointee.

It was sent two days after the FTC, along with 20 states, filed a federal lawsuit accusing Dollar General of a “pattern of inaccurate pricing” that “affects millions of purchases”. The lawsuit claims the company knew about the problem for years without correcting it.

Dollar General, in a statement, vowed to “defend this litigation vigorously”, saying it aims for 100% price accuracy and that it cooperated with the FTC’s investigation.

“While this step is positive,” the lawmakers wrote of the FTC’s lawsuit, “the widespread nature of the issue revealed by public reports and state inquiries warrants a full-scope probe.”

The congressional letter comes on the eve of a midterm election in which affordability has emerged as the major concern. In a recent Harris Poll conducted for the Guardian, voters listed gas prices, grocery prices and living expenses as their top three election issues.

In another poll, released by AP-Norc Center for Public Affairs Research, nearly 80% of voters disapproved of Donald Trump’s handling of the cost of living.

“Gas prices are at $4.50 a gallon in my district,” US representative Nikki Budzinski of Illinois, the letter’s lead author, told the Guardian. “Any uptick in a gas price, or any uptick in the price of a banana or the price of ground beef, means families, in reality, making very difficult decisions as to whether they’re even able to afford that item any more … They’re making decisions as to whether to fill their gas tank up completely or fill their grocery basket up.”

Back in December, Budzinski and 29 colleagues wrote to the CEOs of Dollar General and Family Dollar seeking internal documents about their pricing disparities. Neither company complied, she said, “so we’re taking the next step of going to the FTC and asking them to do enforcement”. The federal agency is charged with policing unfair, deceptive and anti-competitive business practices.

The Guardian has contacted the FTC and the four retail chains for comment.

Budzinski and her co-authors noted that many of their constituents live too far to walk or drive to independent grocery stores or chain supermarkets. A Dollar General or 7-Eleven might be the closest place for them to buy food.

“Because these stores are often the sole option for essentials in underserved neighborhoods and rural communities, these companies occupy a unique position of trust and responsibility,” the letter said. “It is deeply troubling to see that these limited options have been exploited to the detriment of working families.”

For one of the lawmakers who signed the letter, the issue is personal. US representative Shontel Brown lives near a Dollar General in Warrensville Heights, Ohio. She visited earlier this year to buy some soda pop. When she reached the register, she said, the total cost didn’t match the advertised price.

“I asked the cashier, ‘Wait a minute, how am I paying X amount when these items are on sale and I’ve applied these coupons?’” Brown recalled. “And she said, ‘Well, the system does that. It does it a lot with the pop.’”

The congresswoman left without making the purchase. “I have the luxury of not counting every single dollar in my budget,” she said. Many of her constituents don’t have that leeway. “I can’t imagine folks who are coming in there, who have to itemize every dollar, dealing with something like this. So when the letter was brought to my attention, I was a ‘hell yes’.”

title: Budget 2026 live: chancellor says scrapping of gas standing charges will save 60% of homes £45 a year
excerpt:
John Healey says UK faces ‘difficult moment’ as he prepares to deliver first budget of Andy Burnham’s government

You be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the books

Good ...
body_text:
John Healey says UK faces ‘difficult moment’ as he prepares to deliver first budget of Andy Burnham’s government

You be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the books

Good morning. When Andy Burnham became PM, he signalled that he wanted to end 40 years of neoliberalism. Judging by all the briefing about what will be in the budget today, neoliberalism is probably safe for another year or so because Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, have decided not to use this as a moment for big, transformative change, but to instead opt for a more low-risk, every-little-bit-helps fiscal statement. There are radical elements in the Burnham agenda, but mostly they will have to wait for another day. In a video setting the scene for the budget, Healey sums it up with the slogan: “Breathing space today, and fresh hope for the future.”

Here is Pippa Crerar and Heather Stewart’s overnight splash story previewing the budget.

And here is an analysis by Phillip Inman setting out the main items we are expecting.

Every chancellor, though, likes to have at least one big surprise for the speech. This is the headline they want for tomorrow’s papers. We don’t know yet what Healey has chosen, but there is a lot of speculation that it will involve energy bills.

We have already had an announcement from the Treasury at 7am this morning about standing charges being removed from gas bills. Julia Kollewe has the story here.

According to the Treasury, this could save around 60% of families around £45 a year. It says:

The chancellor will announce today an end to this unfair and outdated practice. He will ask Ofgem to deliver removal of these charges – which are £108 a year for the typical household on average – in 2027 or as soon as possible after.

Instead, these fixed costs will be paid on the unit rate, which could save 60% of account-holding households around an average of £45 off their annual bill.

While this might sound like a modest cost of living measure – almost an “everyday fix” – Burnham and Healey – perhaps sensitive to the charge that there is not much radicalism in the budget – are presenting this as the start of something more ambitious. In a statement this morning, Burnham said this shows he’s “determined to reform our broken energy market” and Healey says:

My budget will draw a line in the sand on an energy policy that has failed British billpayers for years, letting extra costs on bills pile high and leaving households even more exposed to global shocks.

Healey is speaking at 12.30pm. We have also got PMQs today, but I will mostly be focusing on the budget, with reaction and analysis, and Graeme Wearden, who writes the Guardian’s business live blog, will be joining too to provide added firepower.

And we will also have comments open below the line (BTL).

8.45am: Andy Burnham chairs cabinet, where John Healey, the chancellor, will brief ministers on what’s in the budget.

Noon: Burnham faces Kemi Badenoch at PMQs.

Around 1.30pm: After Healey finishes, Kemi Badenoch gives a speech responding to the budget. Other MPs respond as the budget debate continues through the afternoon.

2.30pm: Jonathan Haskel, chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, holds a press conference.

3.30pm: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, and Robert Jenrick, his Treasury spokesperson, hold a press conference to give their reaction to the budget.

If you want to get in touch, you can post a comment BTL and, if it’s addressed to Andrew, I may find it using a word search. But I am more likely to see it if you email politics.live@theguardian.com.

title: MEHEK COOKE: Trump’s record is the GOP’s best weapon in the midterms
excerpt:
A panel of independent voters Doug Boyer, Rick Gagliano and Eric Mitchell discuss their top priorities and the key issues impacting their midterm votes on 'Fox & Friends First.'

From campaign speeche...
body_text:
A panel of independent voters Doug Boyer, Rick Gagliano and Eric Mitchell discuss their top priorities and the key issues impacting their midterm votes on 'Fox & Friends First.'

From campaign speeches and television appearances to debates, Democrats have made their entire midterm strategy painfully clear: Repeat President Donald Trump’s name and blame him for everything. Since September 1, Democrats have spent more than $163 million on television advertisements mentioning Trump. They are betting that relentless attacks on President Trump will distract voters from their failure to offer solutions.

Republicans’ winning strategy is to go all in on President Trump’s record and his blueprint for public safety, border security, affordability and government accountability. A new Fox News Poll found that 72% of voters said one reason for their congressional vote would be to express either support or opposition to President Trump. Republican candidates should lean in because voters have already placed Trump at the center of the election.

Republicans have a clear roadmap to victory based on the numbers. Voters trust the GOP over Democrats by 10 points on crime, eight points on border security and three points on immigration. These issues powered President Trump’s 2024 victory and are now backed by measurable results: a secure border, stronger law enforcement, and safer communities. His broader record also includes an aggressive crackdown on government fraud.

‘PHANTOM’ OBAMACARE ACCOUNTS SPARK NEW CRACKDOWN AS OZ TARGETS BROKER FRAUD

Democrats may currently lead the generic ballot, but Republicans can close the gap by making the election about Trump’s winning record. That case begins at the border, where Trump has achieved one of the biggest policy victories in modern American history. New DHS data show that Border Patrol recorded fewer than 99,000 southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026, a 95% decline from the annual average of more than 1.8 million under former President Biden. It was also the first fiscal year in history with zero Border Patrol releases.

Democrats insisted that sweeping border legislation, more money and another Washington compromise were necessary to enforce the law, secure the border and protect American citizens. On day one, Trump used existing legal authority, restored consequences for those who entered the country illegally and proved that much of the crisis resulted from policy choices, not a lack of presidential authority. The loss of American lives, a deadly fentanyl crisis and federal failures that left vulnerable migrant children exposed to trafficking and exploitation were a direct result of political choices made by the Biden administration.

President Trump is securing America on two fronts: protecting families through immigration enforcement and protecting taxpayer dollars through his crackdown on fraud. The federal government loses an estimated $233 billion to $521 billion annually to fraud, and Trump is confronting that theft. His anti-fraud task force. The Trump administration also canceled approximately 315,000 confirmed unauthorized Obamacare enrollments covering more than 760,000 people, and those cancellations are expected to save approximately $2.2 billion in taxpayer-funded subsidies.

The difference between Republicans and Democrats is clear. President Trump believes government must protect law-abiding Americans, while Democrats repeatedly defend systems that protect criminals, fraudsters and illegal immigrants from consequences. Trump’s progress is undeniable, but voters still feel the cost of groceries, gas and health care. The same poll found that 60% consider the cost of living their top economic concern.

DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE

To address voters’ concerns, Republicans should explain that affordability involves more than what families pay at the grocery store or doctor’s office. It also includes the costs of failed border enforcement, what Washington takes from their paychecks and whether government protects that money.

The immigration surge that began under Biden in 2021 imposed costs on state and local governments, with the largest expenses falling on schools, shelters and border security, according to the Congressional Budget Office. The Federal Reserve has also acknowledged that immigration can increase rent growth in the short term when housing demand grows faster than supply. When Democrats failed to control illegal entry, local taxpayers and families searching for affordable housing faced the consequences.

TRUMP IS FIGHTING OBAMACARE FRAUD. DEMOCRATS ARE DEFENDING THE NUMBERS

Fraud follows the same pattern. When it goes unchecked, taxpayers finance improper payments while eligible Americans and legitimate programs compete for what remains. Every dollar Trump stops from reaching a fraudster is one taxpayers do not have to replace through higher taxes or additional borrowing. President Trump’s record makes the connection clear: Affordability begins with enforcing the law and protecting the money families already earned.

While Democrats burn time and resources making the midterms a referendum on President Trump, Republicans must double down on his accomplishments and show how America is safer and government is more accountable than it was two years ago. They must also remind voters what Democratic control could bring: impeachment hearings, targeted investigations and two more years of partisan warfare. Do Americans really want Congress focused on investigating the president instead of lowering costs?

Democrats made the midterms about stopping Trump. Republicans must make them about protecting what he delivered.

Mehek Cooke is an attorney, political strategist and former state and U.S. counterterrorism adviser.

title: Dem eyeing Sen comeback to fix ‘broken DC system’ raked in cash from establishment Queen: 'Jekyll and Hyde'
excerpt:
Mehek Cooke, a GOP strategist and attorney in Ohio, told Fox News Digital that former Ohio Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown has long been part of the "broken Washington system" he frequently condemns.

F...
body_text:
Mehek Cooke, a GOP strategist and attorney in Ohio, told Fox News Digital that former Ohio Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown has long been part of the "broken Washington system" he frequently condemns.

FIRST ON FOX: Former Ohio Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown has pitched himself as a Washington outsider fighting against a broken system, but records reviewed by Fox News Digital show his campaign pocketed tens of thousands of dollars from Nancy Pelosi, one of the most notable establishment figures in Washington, D.C., whose husband is a prolific stock trader.

A vocal critic of members of Congress "who are too busy lining their own pockets" and trading stocks, Brown's campaign has accepted a total of $33,000 from Pelosi-affiliated committees since 2006, including $28,000 since February 2024, according to Federal Election Commission records.

Brown has taken a firm stance against congressional stock trading, writing on his campaign website, "No one – NO ONE – who serves in Congress, or their spouse, should be able to trade stocks. They also shouldn’t be able to turn around when they leave office and become a lobbyist. If you can’t agree to that, you shouldn’t be in public office."

Just weeks after announcing his comeback bid last year, Brown received $7,000 from committees affiliated with Pelosi. PAC to the Future gave $5,000, while Nancy Pelosi for Congress gave $2,000.

WATCH: DEM CANDIDATE GRILLED ON STOCK TRADING AFTER BEING DUPED WITH SELFIE REQUEST

Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, addresses voters during a campaign event at the Athens Armory near Ohio University in Athens, Ohio, on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Mehek Cooke, a GOP strategist and attorney in Ohio, told Fox News Digital that Brown has always sided with the Democratic establishment and has "never worked for us."

"I hate when people present themselves as one thing and then turn their backs on you in Washington," Cooke said, calling it another example of Brown’s "Jekyll and Hyde" platform.

She pointed to Brown’s lengthy career in politics as proof that he has been part of a system for "50 plus years" that he frequently condemns.

The former House speaker and her husband, Paul Pelosi, have an estimated net worth of roughly $278 million, according to a 2026 Yahoo Finance report. A 2025 New York Post report also found the couple made more than $130 million in stock profits during her congressional career.

In statement to Fox News Digital, Nicholas Martin, a spokesperson for Pelosi, denied she had any involvement in stock trading.

"Speaker Pelosi does not own any stocks and has no knowledge or subsequent involvement in any transactions," Martin wrote.

Pelosi stood behind lawmakers trading individual stocks during a 2021 press briefing, saying, "We are a free-market economy. They should be able to participate in that," before changing course in early 2022. Last year, Pelosi supported a ban, saying, "We must have strong transparency, robust accountability and tough enforcement for financial conduct in office because the American people deserve confidence that their elected leaders are serving the public interest — not their personal portfolios."

FOX NEWS POLL: GENDER GAP AND POCKETBOOK PAIN SHAPE OHIO SENATE RACE

Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and her husband, Paul Pelosi, attend the dedication ceremony for the Barack Obama Presidential Center in Chicago on June 18. Paul Pelosi is facing a misdemeanor hit-and-run charge in connection with a Friday crash in Napa County, California, authorities said. (Jim Vondruska/Getty Images)

Brown’s position comes amid ongoing debate over congressional stock trading, with critics arguing the controversial practice gives lawmakers an unfair advantage. Last month, Senate Democrats blocked a Republican-backed bill, the Stop Insider Trading Act, that would ban lawmakers from trading stocks, arguing it wasn’t strong enough.

Brown, recruited to run by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, is looking to reclaim a seat in the U.S. Senate and will face Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio’s closely watched midterm race. Brown, a former chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, was first elected to the Senate in 2006 before losing his 2024 re-election bid to Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio.

EX-HOUSE DEM WHO RIPPED CONGRESSIONAL STOCK TRADING BAN AS 'BULLS---' CHANGES HER TUNE IN COMEBACK BID

Senator Jon Husted, a Republican from Ohio, during a Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee confirmation hearing in Washington, DC, on Thursday, Feb. 13, 2025. (Getty Images)

This is not the first time Brown has faced questions over his campaign donations. Fox News Digital reported in September that Brown targeted Husted over Ohio’s data centers in a campaign ad featuring a facility owned by Google, despite its PAC and lobbyists donating thousands of dollars to his campaigns.

Cooke said Brown will continue accepting money from prominent Democrats like Pelosi rather than fighting "for the working man."

"Sherrod Brown's always going to be part of the broken Washington system that President Trump just flipped upside down when he got into office," Cooke said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Brown's campaign for comment.

"Sherrod Brown spent 32 years in Washington literally building the system he now calls ‘rigged,’" Husted campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Brown is backed and funded by the same people he claims to oppose - this is just another stunning example of Sherrod Brown’s hypocrisy and the fact that he’s willing to lie to Ohio families."

Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: DSA-affiliated Senate nominee sparks bipartisan uproar with comments on communist dictatorship
excerpt:
Florida Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon responds when CBS News asks whether she considers Cuba a dictatorship.

Florida Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon is facing a wave of criticism over h...
body_text:
Florida Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon responds when CBS News asks whether she considers Cuba a dictatorship.

Florida Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon is facing a wave of criticism over her response to a seemingly straightforward question about whether Cuba is a dictatorship, months after joining the Democratic Socialists of America as she campaigns for statewide office in a state shaped by generations of Cuban exiles.

"You know, that is what people have told me. I have never been to Cuba, and so I will have to take their word for it," Nixon told CBS News when asked directly whether she considers Cuba a dictatorship.

Nixon later pushed back on critics who portrayed her answer as a refusal to acknowledge Cuba's government as a dictatorship, saying she was referring to Cubans she has spoken with who described the country that way and that she believes them.

WHO IS ANGIE NIXON? BULLHORN-WIELDING SOCIALIST UPSETS ESTABLISHMENT FAVORITE IN SUNSHINE STATE STUNNER

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon speaks during a visit to the Ball and Chain Cuban restaurant/nightclub as she campaigns in the Little Havana neighborhood on Aug. 29, 2026 in Miami, Fla. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

"It's disappointing to have to say this, but CBS News, this is a serious failure of editorial reporting," Nixon wrote on X in response to the network's initial post about the exchange. "I clearly state in this clip that while I have not personally been to Cuba, I have spoken with Cubans who have described it as a dictatorship, and I believe them," she continued. "To claim I declined to answer the question is categorically false. That is not journalism. It is misinformation."

CBS subsequently deleted its original post, which had characterized Nixon as declining to say whether Cuba is a dictatorship, and reposted the interview with an editor's note acknowledging that the earlier version "did not accurately portray Rep. Nixon's answer."

But Nixon's underlying response still drew criticism from Democrats and Republicans.

Among the Democrats criticizing Nixon was Phil Ehr, the party's nominee in Florida's 28th Congressional District, who tied his concerns directly to conversations he said he has had with Cuban-American voters while campaigning in South Florida.

VAN JONES WARNS FAR-LEFT SOCIALIST AGENDA IS 'REGRESSIVE' THREAT TO DEMOCRATIC PARTY

Fidel Castro observes the May Day parade at the Revolution Square in Havana, Cuba May 1, 1998. (Sven Creutzmann/Mambo Photography/Getty Images)

"I can't get past this after spending a week at early voting sites and seeing firsthand how frightened so many Cuban Americans are," Ehr wrote on X alongside a photo from an early-voting site. "People like this woman thanked us for standing up not only against DSA rhetoric, but for their dignity and humanity."

In a separate statement, Ehr called Cuba a "communist dictatorship" and said there was "nothing progressive about making excuses for communist dictatorships." He added that he would "not stand behind Angie Nixon or defend her remarks," declaring, "If the Democratic party is unwilling to condemn them, I will."

Ehr was not the only Florida Democrat to object. Elliott Rodriguez, the Democratic nominee in Florida's 27th Congressional District, said that while he and Nixon "agree on many issues," Cuba's status was not among them.

"Cuba being a dictatorship is not a matter of opinion. It is a fact," Rodriguez wrote, pointing to political prisoners, repression and Cubans who have died seeking freedom.

FLA DEM SEN-NOMINEE ANGIE NIXON BACKED ABOLISHING ELECTORAL COLLEGE, RANKED-CHOICE VOTING IN RESURFACED CLIPS

Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon campaigns during a tour of the Little Havana neighborhood on August 15, 2026 in Miami, Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Republicans criticized the exchange as well, including Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who argued Nixon's answer reflected a broader problem within the Democratic Party.

"Like many of her Democrat colleagues who can't seem to define what a woman is, we now have a candidate for the U.S. Senate who can't define a dictatorship," Scott wrote on X.

Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., was similarly blunt, calling Nixon's response "the craziest thing I've ever heard."

"Of COURSE the Castro regime is a dictatorship," Donalds wrote. "It's sad to see what has become of the Democrat Party. They are fully consumed by socialism."

Senator Rick Scott, a Republican from Florida, in the Senate Subway during a vote at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Friday, March 14, 2025. (Allison Robbert/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The controversy comes months after Nixon joined the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a membership that has previously drawn questions about where she stands on the organization's positions involving Cuba.

In an August interview with CBS Miami, Nixon was asked specifically about DSA's praise of Fidel Castro and distanced herself from the group's position.

"I don't believe he's someone that should be praised," Nixon said, while adding that she does not agree with every position taken by DSA.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: OLIVIA TRUSTY: FCC’s New Cyber Trust Mark aims to make all of our smart home safer homes
excerpt:
FBI Director Kash Patel discusses the bureau’s ‘Operation Blackout’ initiative aimed at cracking down on cybercrime on ‘Hannity.’

Before purchasing a new refrigerator, consumers can look for the Ener...
body_text:
FBI Director Kash Patel discusses the bureau’s ‘Operation Blackout’ initiative aimed at cracking down on cybercrime on ‘Hannity.’

Before purchasing a new refrigerator, consumers can look for the Energy Star label to understand how efficiently it uses energy. Before purchasing food at the grocery store, consumers can look for the USDA Organic label to understand how it was produced. But before purchasing an internet-connected camera, baby monitor or door lock that we put in some of our most private spaces, consumers have no comparably simple way to know whether that device was designed to keep hackers out.

The Federal Communications Commission is working to change that with the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark program.

This voluntary cybersecurity labeling program is intended to make security easier to understand by helping consumers quickly identify internet-connected products that meet established cybersecurity requirements. Some of these requirements include making sure the product protects consumer data, limits access to authorized users and securely updates software. Qualifying devices will also provide consumers with clear information about manufacturer support so that consumers do not need to become cybersecurity experts to protect themselves.

WHAT A SMART FIREWALL DOES AND WHY IT MATTERS ON HOME WI-FI

Products that meet the Cyber Trust Mark requirements will ultimately display a label with a distinctive shield that quickly lets Americans know the connected product they’re bringing into their homes meets certain baseline cybersecurity requirements. The shield will be accompanied by a QR code that consumers can scan to find accessible and up-to-date information about the product’s security. A buyer can learn, for example, how to change a factory-set password, where to find security updates and how long the manufacturer has committed to supporting the product.

Shopping for high-tech equipment could get a lot more efficient thanks to the FCC's Cyber Trust Mark program. (iStock)

The FCC is working to roll out the Cyber Trust Mark program to a retailer near you by next year.

FBI SAYS RUSSIAN HACKERS HIJACKED OLD WI-FI ROUTERS

The commission’s efforts have taken on new urgency as cyberattacks increase and American homes become more connected. On average, there are approximately 20 to 25 connected devices in a typical U.S. household, and close to 1 million Internet-of-Things-related cyberattacks per day.

To meet the commission’s 2027 implementation timeline, the ioXt Alliance, an organization with extensive security experience, was selected earlier this year as the lead administrator to manage the daily operations of the program. And in the coming months, the FCC will seek public comment on the design and use of the label, technical standards and testing procedures to determine product eligibility, and post-market surveillance rules to preserve the integrity of the Cyber Trust Mark label throughout the life of a qualifying product.

APPLE WANTS TO MOVE INTO YOUR HOME. SHOULD YOU LET IT?

As the FCC moves forward on each of these program elements, we welcome feedback from manufacturers, retailers, cybersecurity researchers, consumer advocates and other interested parties to make sure we get the details right. Because in addition to giving consumers more tools to protect themselves, our goal is to maximize participation in this program among product manufacturers.

Manufacturers that participate will have a visible way of demonstrating their commitment to security. They will also distinguish themselves from competitors that lack this certification and give retailers and online marketplaces the opportunity to highlight the trusted products they sell. And before long, this will create economic incentives for others to build security into their products at the design stage and not bolted on only after a vulnerability has been discovered.

CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN

These, among other benefits, can be expected from the Cyber Trust Mark program, but consumers should be aware that no label can promise that a product will never be hacked. This is why the Cyber Trust Mark program represents just one part of the FCC’s broader commitment to strengthening cybersecurity.

Other commission-led initiatives include removing untrustworthy equipment from U.S. communications networks, improving the integrity of our equipment authorization process and increasing transparency into the foreign ownership and control of entities operating critical communications systems across the country.

Products that meet the Cyber Trust Mark requirements will ultimately display a label with a distinctive shield that quickly lets Americans know the connected product they’re bringing into their homes meets certain baseline cybersecurity requirements.

Each line of effort addresses a different point of vulnerability. Secure networks require equipment from trusted sources. Resilient infrastructure requires responsible operators. And connected homes require products designed with cybersecurity in mind.

To be clear, the Cyber Trust Mark program is not intended to put the burden of cybersecurity squarely on consumers. It is a practical tool for consumers to protect themselves while continuing to implement strong passwords, multifactor authentication and security upgrades. And manufacturers are still expected to adopt reasonable cybersecurity practices whether or not they participate in the program. This is merely a way to keep consumers informed while rewarding companies that invest in security and raising expectations across the connected-device marketplace.

The bottom line is that the promise of the smart home should not come at the expense of the secure home. And by next year, the Cyber Trust Mark will help make security a standard feature of a connected home – not an afterthought.

title: Can a Democrat stop Iowa’s red drift? 5 moments from the governor’s debate
excerpt:
Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn discuss their positions on abortion during the Iowa gubernatorial debate on Oct. 27, 2026. (Source: KCRG-TV9)

Zach Lahn, a businessman, and Rob Sand, a form...
body_text:
Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn discuss their positions on abortion during the Iowa gubernatorial debate on Oct. 27, 2026. (Source: KCRG-TV9)

Zach Lahn, a businessman, and Rob Sand, a former Iowa assistant attorney general and two-term state auditor, are competing to succeed retiring Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds, who has served as governor for nearly a decade.

The opponents faced off Tuesday night for a 90-minute debate where they discussed fraud, culture wars and data centers, and even found agreement on some issues.

The race in Iowa is the state's first open gubernatorial showdown in 20 years, with Reynolds last year announcing she wouldn't seek re-election.

Sand, the only Democrat to currently hold statewide office in Iowa, quickly became his party's frontrunner and faced no opposition in this year's primary.

Lahn, a self-described entrepreneur and farmer, had to navigate a crowded and contentious primary battle. He won a five-candidate Republican nomination race that included Rep. Randy Feenstra, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump.

Sand is aiming to become the first Democrat in two decades elected governor in Iowa, a one-time swing state that's shifted to the right over the past decade. The final Fox News Power Rankings ahead of Election Day rated the race between Lahn and Sand as Lean Democrat.

DRAG QUEENS, TRANS PASTOR, ABORTION RALLIES: INSIDE DEM GOVERNOR HOPEFUL'S PROGRESSIVE CHURCH

A split-screen showing Iowa Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn speaking after being invited on stage during a rally with U.S. President Donald Trump at Sioux Gateway Airport in Sioux City, Iowa, on October 22, 2026 (left), and Democratic gubernatorial candidate, state auditor Rob Sand speaking during a campaign stop at the state Education Association in Des Moines, Iowa, on October 08, 2026 (right). Polls released show Sand leading the race to replace retiring Gov. Kim Reynolds against Lahn. (Anna Moneymaker / Scott Olson / Getty Images)

The candidates differed on several culture war issues, such as abortion, parental rights and childhood transgender concerns. Sand affirmed that he would refuse to sign any new bill that he deemed culturally "divisive."

"The divisive stuff that people don’t agree on, let’s end that," Sand said. "So vetoing culture war bills to me is just a different way to say I want us to put 100% of our legislating time into issues that impact 100% of Iowans."

Sand also said that there is pressure from Republicans and the right to implement greater restrictions on abortion, even though the state has already implemented a six-week ban.

"It’s incredibly restrictive," Sand said. "I do not think we have to go further but a lot of the folks in the legislature said when that ban became law that they want to go further. I would veto going further."

Meanwhile, Lahn said he is "100%" behind culture battles being fought by conservatives.

"There is an issue with these ideologies infiltrating into our culture and I think parents, especially when we talk about some of these issues coming up in schools, they’re just looking for something they should be able to count on. And I think it is absolutely important that we put every single protection in place to make that our daughters are protected, that girls are protected, that women’s sports are protected," Lahn said.

Lahn also said that he was motivated to run for office to protect the most vulnerable.

"That's the lives of the unborn. That’s our daughters. That’s the young kids in school," Lahn said.

MEDICAID PROVIDER ALLEGEDLY BILLED $165K FOR DEAD PATIENT'S RIDES AMONG FRAUD EXPOSED IN EXPLOSIVE REPORT

Iowa Republican nominee for Governor Zach Lahn speaks to fairgoers at the Iowa State Fair on Aug. 14, 2026 in Des Moines, Iowa. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

Fraud and improper spending of taxpayer dollars was top of mind for both Lahn and Sand, but the candidates differed in their approaches to tackling corruption.

Sand, who used to be the state's auditor, pushed for mandated audits on the state's Education Savings Account program, calling it "common-sense."

"They're not required to have audits, and they need to have rules for how that money gets spent," Sand said. "Same things that would get you in trouble as a public school should get you in trouble as a private school if you're taking public money. If you don't want to abide by those rules, then you can continue to not take public money."

Lahn said during his time as auditor he saw payments being made to dead people and accused Gov. Reynolds of signing a law known as Senate File 478, claiming it made it harder for auditors to do their job.

"They changed the law to make it harder for us to find misspent tax money," Sand said. "This is something that every single government watchdog in America that weighed in on said would be a terrible law that would lead to an increase in waste, fraud and abuse."

Meanwhile, Lahn maintained that schools should be audited by third parties instead of being under government oversight.

"I think third-party auditing is where it should go," Lahn said. "I think we could do something very similar, which allows these schools to still have their privacy, but make sure that the funds are being spent properly."

Lahn also raised concerns of improper Medicaid payments, pointing to the fraud allegations from Minnesota's state program.

He argued for implemented advanced technologies like blockchain to ensure that money is being properly spent.

"This would create thousands of citizen auditors trying to find every single dollar that the government is wasting. And we start at the state level. Then we go down to the county level as well, where we can have radical transparency in spending," Lahn said. "We all want to have more efficient government. One of the best ways to do it is through radical transparency."

DEMOCRATS AIM TO KILL SCHOOL CHOICE FROM WISCONSIN TO THE REST OF THE US

Gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand speaks to voters during a campaign visit to the Carroll County Conservation Classroom on Aug. 20, 2026 in Carroll, Iowa. (Leon Neal/Getty Images)

Iowa's Education Savings Account program, which provides taxpayer dollars to families to cover tuition for private schools, faced scrutiny by Sand, who called for income restrictions on the program, pointing to the state facing a $1.1 billion deficit.

"We are putting hundreds of millions of dollars every single year into the pockets of people who have plenty of money, good for them, and are already going to send their kids to private school, fine by me, but your tax dollars don’t need to go pay for that," Sand said.

Lahn argued that the program was a "foundational freedom" and that when a school program isn't meeting a child's needs, parents should be able to go elsewhere regardless of their income.

"I think that there's no such thing as government money," Lahn said. "There's the people's money, this is their money."

The candidates also disagreed over whether private schools that receive public funding should be allowed to turn away students — an issue the Supreme Court will consider this term in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a case from Colorado.

"Private schools that are taking public money should have to take which ever students say they want to attend there," Sand said. "The fact that they don’t have to right now exposes the gulf between the rhetoric around this program and what it actually does because right now private schools can pick and choose which students can come in the front door."

Lahn said the "best model" is for parents to have different options for what fits their child's needs best.

"If you put these restrictions on schools, many of them, especially the smallest ones, will be burdened to a great degree," Lahn said.

Sand and Lahn both agreed that data centers need to pay their "fair share" if they want to be building in Iowa.

The topic of data centers — which has become a flashpoint issue this election cycle — was first raised by Sand when discussing his plan for balancing the state's budget was to cease giving data companies tax breaks.

"Data centers should be paying all their taxes and then some," Sand said. "If they need to build the grid out to do what they need to do, they can pay for that."

"Financially speaking, they should be contributing to the state of Iowa, and if they don't want to contribute, they can build somewhere else," Sand continued.

Lahn said that he agreed with his opponent, noting it may be "the one thing" that they both agreed on.

"A hundred billion dollar multinational company does not need welfare from the people of Iowa," Lahn said.

He said that there was a data center receiving $529 million in property tax abatements and were only required to create 30 jobs to receive the tax break.

"Not only is this happening too quickly with data centers, but it's also happening in a way that we feel like we're being take advantage of," Lahn said.

"What they need to do is pay their fair share, and we need to actually create a new class of property tax, which would be above industrial, because these are employing far fewer people per square foot, and we need to have a higher rate of property, a property tax there," Lahn said.

To end the debate, the moderators asked Lahn and Sand, who both have pledged support to protecting Second Amendment rights, if there was any legislation that they would sign to restrict or regulate firearms.

Lahn shared that he's not in favor of signing any new restrictions, saying the state is in a "good place." Sand said that its important for law abiding citizens to be able to exercise their Second Amendment rights, but that he supported background checks.

The question comes weeks after three children were gunned down in an elementary school in Oregon. Lahn pointed out that the school shooter was killed by a parent, who had a concealed carry permit.

"I think that the last thing we want to do is restrict the ability for lawful, citizens that are carrying firearms to protect the people they love in their communities. That's something that we need to make sure we're protecting," Lahn said.

Sand shared a story about how he, while prosecuting a man who was out on bail, he learned the man had received a concealed carry permit.

"If I convicted him, and I knew that he could be following me to my hotel, or following me to dinner at night, or following me to court in the morning, this suit was one of the suits that I was carrying that weapon in," Sand said.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

Exclusive: Health secretary to extend role of watchdog, which backers say helps hold service in England to account

Yvette Cooper has abandoned plans to abolish the NHS’s independent patient champion after an outcry from MPs across the political spectrum.

The health secretary has decided to keep and extend the role of Healthwatch England, which was due to be axed as part of the government’s reorganisation of the health service in England.

The move is the latest in a series of U-turns by ministers on core elements of the health bill since Andy Burnham became prime minister in July.

The rethink means Healthwatch England and its 150 branches will continue to collect and analyse feedback from patients about their experiences of the NHS and where its services need to improve. Its many supporters in parliament say the statutory body helps to identify areas where NHS care is lagging behind patient needs and hold the service to account.

Cooper told the Guardian: “Patients need a voice in our NHS. I’ve always been clear on the importance of people and communities having a say in local services and that’s why I said I would review all reforms in this area.

“We will retain Healthwatch England and Local Healthwatch, while strengthening them to ensure patient voices are heard and can influence real change across health and care services.”

Gillian Merron, the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) minister in the Lords, will confirm the change of plan when peers debate the health bill on Wednesday. Labour, Conservative and Liberal Democrat parliamentarians had criticised the planned abolition.

Healthwatch has gained respect for publishing reports highlighting issues such as declining patient access to NHS-funded dental treatment and years-long waiting times for ADHD assessments. It has also exposed flaws in the way the service communicates with patients, for example telling some of them about appointments after the date has already passed.

Cooper reprieved Healthwatch after MPs and peers from all sides in parliament raised serious concern that scrapping it would mean the loss of important oversight of the NHS.

Thea Stein, the chief executive of the Nuffield Trust thinktank and a former head of an NHS trust in Leeds, said: “Abolishing Healthwatch would have thrown away the independence that gave it credibility, without doing anything to address the reasons the NHS often don’t listen.

“It was the wrong solution to a real problem. Healthwatch has played a valuable role in making it more difficult for the NHS to ignore patients’ often frustrating experience of using it.”

Until now, the government had planned to transfer Healthwatch’s functions into NHS regional integrated care boards (ICBs) and local councils. But Healthwatch will now play a greater role in identifying recurring concerns and highlighting where action is needed to improve quality, safety and patient experience.

The Local Government Association had warned that abolishing Healthwatch “risks [NHS] organisations being seen to mark their own homework” and could create “confusion” for patients.

Other recent government climbdowns on the health bill include ministers dropping plans to:

axe the Health Services Safety Investigations Body.

end councils’ automatic representation on the boards of ICBs.

remove the requirement for a nurse on every NHS foundation trust board.

The U-turns show Cooper is closely examining the legacy bequeathed to her by her predecessor, Wes Streeting, and tearing up elements of the bill she thinks are misguided.

DHSC sources said her decision to retain and strengthen Healthwatch and its network of branches illustrated her strong belief – which Burnham shares – in public and local accountability.

Stein said: “This retreat needs to be followed by a cultural shift away from a health service where patients’ voices are all too often at the bottom of a long and impossible list.”

Sitting on a couch, they were a perfect couple making light of serious allegations.

There was some unintelligible banter about "Botox faces" and "fascists." The usual drivel. It seemed scripted.

Once they took the stage together, at the "I'm the Host Now!" event, Piker kicked his defense of Omar into overdrive with a litany of wretched insults. "Republicans… are the most un-American force in this country. They are terrorists," he proclaimed.

This has become a standard refrain for Piker.

HASAN PIKER LASHES OUT AT REPUBLICANS, CALLS THEM 'TERRORISTS' IN EVENT WITH ILHAN OMAR

Then he zeroed in on the accusations that Omar may have lied about her birthdate and true identity to gain citizenship. With the conviction of a zealous preacher in his pulpit, Piker declared, "A paperwork violation does not require deportation."

This would appear to be the first time that anyone speaking on Omar’s behalf has conceded that something in her background or citizenship filings may be amiss. Piker did not explain what the "paperwork violation" was, as convenience would have it.

HOMAN SAYS ILHAN OMAR COULD BE STRIPPED OF NATURALIZATION, DEPORTED IF IMMIGRATION FRAUD IS PROVEN

But his assertion also had the inconvenience of being wrong. A violation or false statement on U.S. citizenship or naturalization paperwork can, indeed, carry grave consequences. A material omission or misrepresentation can lead to revocation of citizenship and removal.

Far-left streamer Hasan Piker deserves to be ostracized, not embraced.

It does not have to be a criminal act such as fraud to become actionable. Denaturalization can occur —and often does— through civil proceedings in federal court. The standard of proof is "clear and convincing evidence," which is far lower than in criminal prosecutions.

REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES

Even if Omar did not herself misrepresent anything in her paperwork, she could still see her citizenship status vanish.

If her father lied in his application, that could nullify his daughter’s citizenship since hers was derivative of his. If he never obtained legitimate citizenship at all, that would invalidate Omar’s citizenship.

FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE

An honest clerical error or misunderstanding of a question might be forgiven. But that is clearly not what federal authorities are investigating. A U.S. District Court judge in Washington —a Democrat— approved the search of Omar’s home based on compelling evidence of suspected criminality.

That kind of judicial order is not the result of an innocent "paperwork violation," as Piker unknowingly contends.

ILHAN OMAR IS NOT THE MINNESOTA CONGRESSWOMAN’S 'REAL NAME': SOURCES

In the past, he has happily exploited the Omar case to accuse the Trump administration of targeting her for "political intimidation." This ignores the fact that the original investigation of the congresswoman began under Joe Biden’s presidency.

Piker has also decried the long-running rumors that Omar married her brother to gain immigration benefits as a "heinous lie." How exactly does Piker know that? He wasn’t there when the nuptials took place. Has he ever met the alleged brother-husband, who is reported to be living in London? Doubtful.

OBAMA BACKS ILHAN OMAR AMID PROBE, ACCUSES TRUMP ADMIN OF 'APPALLING' TARGETING IN LENGTHY STATEMENT

The unvarnished truth is that Piker doesn’t know what he’s yapping about.

But DNA evidence would know. That is probably why the feds were so interested in obtaining it. Testing could answer a multitude of vexing questions.

Are Omar and her ex-husband genetically proven siblings? Is Omar the person she purports to be? She is identified as someone else with a different surname in recent court filings by the U.S. Attorney in Washington.

ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND INSISTS HE HAS ‘NO CONCERNS’ AMID FEDERAL IMMIGRATION INVESTIGATION

Platforming Hasan Piker at a campaign event tells you everything you need to know about extremist Democrats who have infected the party like a modern plague.

Sponsoring his appearance implicitly condones his loathsome opinions. Judging him by his ugly rhetoric, this is a guy who is virulently antisemitic and a purveyor of hate.

Yet, there was Ilhan Omar. She appeared all too happy to sit alongside him. Does she share the incendiary and bigoted views that Piker routinely spews? She did not disagree with him when he condemned Republicans as un-American "terrorists."

Nor has Omar ever denounced Piker’s other grotesque statements. He said that America deserved 9/11 but later apologized for the word "deserved" amid a severe backlash. But he has never retracted —and apparently does not regret— the dehumanizing insults that he has hurled at Jews and Israel. They are too disgusting to repeat here.

Other prominent Minnesota Democrats have castigated Piker. But not Omar. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who is running for governor, characterized his sickening statements as "reckless and unacceptable." Rep. Angie Craig called Piker’s demagoguery "polarizing and dangerous."

Piker deserves to be ostracized, not embraced.

Since Ilhan Omar has made little effort to distance herself from his beliefs, one can reasonably conclude that she countenances them. She reveals her true self, relishing his disdain for all things American.

Perhaps it is true that a person is known by the company they keep.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM GREGG JARRETT

Gregg Jarrett is a Fox News legal analyst and commentator, and formerly worked as a defense attorney and adjunct law professor. His recent book, "The Trial of the Century," about the famous "Scopes Monkey Trial" is available in bookstores nationwide or can be ordered online at the Simon & Schuster website.  Jarrett’s latest book, "The Constitution of the United States and Other Patriotic Documents," was published by Broadside Books, a division of HarperCollins on November 14, 2023.  Gregg is the author of the No. 1 New York Times best-selling book "The Russia Hoax: The Illicit Scheme to Clear Hillary Clinton and Frame Donald Trump." His follow-up book was also a New York Times bestseller, "Witch Hunt: The Story of the Greatest Mass Delusion in American Political History."

body_text:
Opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s coalition predicted to fall short of 61 seats needed to form a government, while Palestinian parties set for big gains

Full report: Coalition talks loom as Israel exit polls suggest Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs tied

Analysis: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape

It’s just after 9am in Tel Aviv where Israelis are grappling with the results of yesterday’s elections, with no clear victor and uncertainty guaranteed at this point.

With 50% of the vote counted, Israeli media report that Netanyahu’s bloc is ahead, with projections he could take 55 seats under the current vote share. The projections put Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc on 49 seats and the Palestinian parties on 16 seats. Sixty-one seats are needed to form a majority to govern in the Knesset, and the final seat projection will probably be updated as more votes are counted.

Exit polls published by Israel’s major TV networks show Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing bloc tied with the opposition grouping led by Gadi Eisenkot on 51 seats each. Earlier exit polls had Eisenkot winning most seats in the Knesset by a slight margin. Israeli exit polls are often revised after publication and are notoriously imprecise, with the final count often swinging by several seats.

Voter turnout surged to the highest level in more than two decades, underscoring the stakes of an election that has been labelled the most important in the country’s history. More than 77% of eligible voters cast a ballot, according to Israel’s central elections committee, about 7 percentage points higher than in 2022.

The Palestinian parties are projected to dramatically increase their representation in the Knesset, with exit polls showing they could win as many as 18 seats, up from 10. Experts have said that if Eisenkot falls short of a majority, as the exit polls suggest, he would be obliged to sit down to talk to the Palestinian groupings, the Joint List and Ra’am, to try to form a government – which could take weeks.

Netanyahu took the stage at a post-election rally in Jerusalem just after 3am, telling his supporters official results will show that “Likud is the largest party in Israel”. He told his supporters that the country must “establish a strong, right-wing national government” – adding that a government that relies on the support of Palestinian parties must not be formed.

Eisenkot told cheering supporters in Tel Aviv that the “Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu’s service as Israel’s prime minister … a worthy leader would have accepted the people’s non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics.” In his speech, he also warned Netanyahu not to “use Israel’s security” for political ends, playing on fears that the prime minister could use this period of uncertainty to launch a new attack on Iran.

The exit polls were released after a last-ditch effort by Netanyahu and several other parties to keep polling stations open beyond their 10pm deadline was rejected by the Central Elections Committee. The prime minister suggested publicly that efforts were being made by the “left and Arabs” to steal the election, a claim rejected by the committee, which said it had seen no evidence of systematic tampering.

As the vote count flows in, Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, issued a strong statement rejecting attempts to frame results as a tie, and warning against the racist exclusion of Palestinian representatives from a future government.

Golan leads the only centre-left party in the Jewish-Israeli opposition bloc. Many of the parties in that anti-Netanyahu ‘Change’ grouping have explicitly ruled out governing with Palestinian Israeli parties.

The unofficial leader of the bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, has laid out conditions for joining his coalition that effectively bar the Arab parties.

double quotation markThere is one resounding lesson from the reality we face: we have no future here unless we stop being afraid. And unless we put an end to racism. We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes.

The vote of an Israeli citizen casting a ballot in Tira is worth exactly the same as the vote of an Israeli citizen casting a ballot in Givat Shmuel. Not less. Not approximately the same. Exactly the same.

Anyone who tries to erase the votes of Arab citizens is surrendering to Netanyahu and giving up on Israel.

The largest Palestinian-Israeli alliance, the Joint List, is expected to get significantly more seats in the Knesset than the Democrats. With two thirds of votes counted, the Joint List is on track for 12 seats, and the Democrats for 8.

Golan said the clearest message from voters was that Netanyahu’s coalition has lost its majority, and its mandate to rule.

double quotation markI know how to count to 120 [the number of seats in parliament]. 65 is more than 55. That is how Israeli democracy works. Period.
  
  
  We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Arab citizens of Israel—a government that serves all Israeli citizens.

It’s worth noting the front page headlines in Israeli media today, printed before dawn so slightly out of date on some of the projections.
 
 
 But the top headlines for each masthead are notable – with most highlighting the rise in the Palestinian-Israeli parties. The fact that there is no clear government formation had been expected; as we’ve reported, no single political party has ever won an outright majority in Israel’s political history so governments have also been coalitions of multiple parties. The papers did indicate a slight lead among the opposition bloc.

Small Parties Fall Beneath the Electoral Threshold

Exit Polls on All Channels: Pro-Change Bloc: 52; Netanyahu Bloc: 50; Arab Parties: 18

Exit Polls: 70 Seats for Opposition, 18 of Them from Arab Parties

Voter Turnout was 77.7%, Highest Since 1999

We’re expecting a sharper picture of results just after 10am local time, where a majority of votes will be tallied and crucially, key counting from areas supporting Palestinian parties will have come in.
 
 
 As of 9.16am local time, 65% of the vote had been counted showing the Netanyahu bloc on 56 seats, the Eisenkot-anchored ‘Change’ bloc on 48, and Palestinian Israeli parties with 16.

Hours after Israel’s polling stations closed, and with more than half of votes counted, several things are clear.

Benjamin Netanyahu’s current coalition has lost its mandate, Palestinian citizens of Israel have secured a key bloc of seats on the back of historic turnout, and the main Jewish-Israeli opposition bloc has no clear path to power without their support.

By 8am Israeli time, partial results put the opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot on 49 seats, behind Netanyahu’s coalition at 55 seats. Palestinian-led parties are forecast to secure the remaining 16 seats, but several key towns were yet to report their counts.

A more complete picture is expected by late morning. Exit polls had put Eisenkot in a stronger position, and Israeli political analyst Nadav Eyal said around 6am local time that the pollsters were standing behind their samples.

double quotation markThey haven’t corrected further, and apparently validated their exit polls against the true results at the polling stations. In their view, these will be the final results.”

He noted that samples in Israel have historically been very accurate in forecasting the size of potential coalition blocs, but also that Likud’s strength is often underestimated.

Exit polls also do not capture absentee ballots, although these are fairly restricted under Israel’s voting system. Eligible groups include diplomats, serving soldiers and people medically unable to reach polling stations.
